items.body_text:
Es la película más vista de Netflix a nivel mundial: un thriller inspirado en hechos reales y con un ganador de Oscar
Lleva dos semanas en el top 1 global y de España y reúne a las estrellas protagonistas de 'Gladiator', 'Peaky blnders', 'Wonder' y 'Divergente'
Las visitas a Netflix se disparan durante el fin de semana. La gente espera hasta sus días de descanso para ver esa miniserie que tiene guardada desde el lunes o esa película que no siempre se puede ver entera de una sentada.
Si eres de los que entran sin un objetivo fijo, esperando a que la plataforma le recomiende esa historia que le deje huella, hoy te traemos una película basada en hechos reales que puede ser la elegida para estos días de pleno octubre.
Se estrenó hace dos semanas directamente en la plataforma de la 'N' roja, sin pasar por los cines, y ya ha conseguido la aprobación del público. Es la película de habla inglesa más vista de Netflix a nivel global y también la más vista en España.
Noticia relacionada
Hablamos de 'Unabomber', el largometraje que ha ocupado el top 1 estas dos semanas. Está dirigido por Janus Metz, conocido por 'Armadillo' y su experiencia con documentales y otras narrativas con el crimen como protagonista.
Trailer de 'Unabomber' en español
Un Premio Oscar y un niño prodigio en el reparto
Antes de revelar la trama de este thriller tan bien acogido por los usuarios de Netflix, queremos destacar al reparto. Los actores hacen de esta película una reunión de talento, premios y taquillazos; en la que el elenco es uno de los motivos que más ha llamado a la audiencia.
Está protagonizada por Russell Crowe ('Gladiator', 'Nuremberg'), ganados de un Premio Oscar por el drama romano del año 2000; Jacob Tremblay ('Wonder'), Annabelle Wallis ('Peaky Blinders', 'Annabelle') y Shailene Woodley ('Divergente', 'Bajo la misma estrella'). La lista de estrellas se completa con Alexander Ludwig, Steven Ogg y Marc Menchaca.
El caso real de 'Unabomber'
'Unabomber' cuenta la historia de Ted Kaczynski, un caso real de un asesino en serie que aterrorizó a Estados Unidos a finales del siglo pasado. El criminal fue un matemático y escritor que envío cartas bomba entre 1978 y 1995 y consiguió 3 víctimas mortales y una decena de heridos por la metralla y la explosión de los paquetes. Murió en 2023 mientras cumplía su pena en prisión.
El nombre hace referencia al mote que le adjudicó el FBI durante su investigación, cuando era un terrorista anónimo. Había atacado una universidad y un avión, y por ello se inventó el nombre 'Unabom', del inglés 'University and Airline Bomber'.
En la película, que dura 1 hora y 40 minutos, se recorre la vida de Unabomber desde sus años en la universidad hasta su detención, 20 años más tarde.
Russell Crowe interpreta a Henry Murray, el psicólogo fundador de la Clínica Psicoanalítica de Harvard que utilizó al futuro terrorista para sus investigaciones cuando era solo un estudiante de la prestigiosa facultad. Jacob Tremblay da vida a Unabomber en su juventud y esos primeros años de deformación moral.

items.title: The midterm elections: Seven battles that will define the post‑Trump future
items.summary: Under a month from Election Day, control of the Senate hinges on a handful of seats. In a deeply polarized country, everything will depend on which party can better mobilize its voter base
items.body_text:
The midterm elections: Seven battles that will define the post‑Trump future
Under a month from Election Day, control of the Senate hinges on a handful of seats. In a deeply polarized country, everything will depend on which party can better mobilize its voter base
There is less than a month left until the midterm elections on November 3. The outcome will determine which party controls both houses of Congress and begin shaping the post-Donald Trump era.
The cost of living, the course of the economy, prices — especially gasoline — and the war in Iran are some of the issues voters care about most, according to polls. That turns these elections into a referendum on the president, whose approval ratings are at the lowest levels of his term, around 37%. But in a deeply polarized country, everything will depend on which party can better mobilize its voter base — and on a handful of very close contests in a few states.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs. Democrats need to gain at least three net seats to take control of the body responsible for the national budget, something most experts — and the betting markets — think they are very likely to achieve. Polls currently give them an 8.5% lead over Republicans in voter intention.
One third of the 100 seats in the Senate are being contested. To win control, Democrats must gain four net seats, from the 47 seats they hold now to 51. These are the key battlegrounds for control of the Senate.
Texas: the seminarian and the sinner
Democrat James Talarico, a state legislator and seminarian, was virtually unknown until last February. He is now his party’s best hope to win a statewide contest in Texas for the first time since 1994, and he holds a slight lead in the polls against his rival, Republican Ken Paxton, the attorney general of the Lone Star State.
Under other circumstances, Talarico —who advocates a populist platform and has said provocative things such as that there are “six genders”— would likely have had no chance in deeply conservative Texas. But this time general voter discontent has been compounded by the Republicans’ choice of the controversial Paxton as their candidate.
Paxton narrowly won his party’s primary with the support of Trump and the party’s most conservative wing, but his political career has been marred by scandal. In 2015, he was accused of fraud, though he reached a deal with prosecutors to avoid trial without admitting guilt. The Republican-majority Texas House impeached him on corruption charges in 2023, although the state senate ultimately acquitted him.
The RealClearPolitics poll average gives Talarico a 2.4% lead over his rival.
Michigan: The progressive Muslim and the interventionist former FBI agent
If the progressive physician Abdul El-Sayed wins the Michigan seat he is contesting against Mike Rogers for the Democrats, he will become the first Muslim U.S. senator in American history. His victory would allow the party’s left wing to argue that its progressive positions can also win in swing states —a claim potential 2028 presidential contenders such as New Yorker Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will weigh carefully. Conversely, if El-Sayed fails in a year favorable to Democrats, the message will be one of caution.
Republicans see his candidacy as a major opportunity to seize this Senate seat in Michigan from the Democrats. His opponent, former congressman Mike Rogers, has rushed to label him a dangerous “extremist” with “dangerous rhetoric.” El‑Sayed, an advocate of universal health care, has moderated some of his positions.
Rogers presents a profile opposite to his rival’s. A former FBI agent, he is a conservative Republican, anti-abortion, pro-business, and has a history of supporting overseas military interventions. He ran two years ago for Michigan’s other Senate seat, losing narrowly to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by 0.3 percentage points.
Voter intention gives El‑Sayed a 3.5 percentage-point advantage.

items.title: From police officer to store employee: The life change of a ‘Dreamer’ who turned in his badge
items.summary: Édgar Vázquez Silva, a DACA beneficiary, stopped being a law enforcement officer because he was required to be a US citizen or legal resident
items.body_text:
From police officer to store employee: The life change of a ‘Dreamer’ who turned in his badge
Édgar Vázquez Silva, a DACA beneficiary, stopped being a law enforcement officer because he was required to be a US citizen or legal resident
Édgar Vázquez Silva’s worst fears came true. His boss at the Stone County sheriff’s office in Mississippi called him and asked him to turn in his badge and uniform. The order was clear: all department officers had to be U.S. citizens or, at minimum, permanent residents.
Born in Mexico and brought to the United States without papers by his mother as a child, Vázquez Silva held neither status. For several years he had relied solely on a work permit obtained under DACA, the immigration program enacted by then-president Barack Obama to shield from deportation those who arrived in the country as minors without authorization.
“I felt awful. I held back the tears, but I went into the department and handed everything over,” Vázquez Silva recalls about the moment he returned his badge and uniforms, which he kept in a purple plastic bag. It was a quick procedure, and he was accompanied by his young son. There were no farewells, hugs or words of encouragement: none of his colleagues were at the station. “You have a dream and they take it away from you,” he laments.
Vázquez Silva is not the only one in this situation. Several officers in California have had to surrender their badges and guns or been placed on unpaid administrative leave because they could not renew their DACA status in time. The process has become increasingly complex and slow; it must be completed every two years and affects about 500,000 beneficiaries.
Those affected worked in the police departments of Los Angeles and Santa Ana. Others, like Vázquez Silva, lost their jobs after supervisors imposed stricter requirements on immigration status.
Amid the campaign against the DACA program under the Trump administration, processing times have increased and, for some, submitting a renewal months in advance was not enough. Average wait times rose from 15 days in 2025 to 70 days this year, an increase of more than 360%, according to data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).
The end of a police career
Vázquez Silva had spent months lobbying for a green card that would allow him to keep his job at the Stone County sheriff’s office. He thought going public with his case might help. He gave interviews to several media outlets, met with the governor of Mississippi and with a congressman, and maintained an active presence on social media under the name “Deputy Dreamer.” Nothing worked.
The order to require immigration status for all law enforcement officers came directly from Amy Vanderford, head of the State Department of Public Safety. “The sheriff told me he was very sorry, but there wasn’t much he could do. He told me he needed me to hand over the badge,” he recalls.
That ended a five-year law enforcement career in Mississippi, which he had managed to extend despite losing authority and ending up in a part-time role where he couldn’t even carry a firearm. He now works as an assistant manager in a store. “They paid me well and I have benefits. But it’s very different compared with being a police officer,” he says.
Vázquez Silva was born 36 years ago in the border state of Tamaulipas. He has no memories of Mexico. He was only three when his mother crossed with him into Texas, without documents. His stepfather’s construction work moved the family from state to state until they finally settled in Mississippi. When he was 12, his mother told him something that would change how he saw himself. “Son, you don’t have papers,” she said. He understood the meaning of those words years later, in high school as he began to plan his life. “And now what am I going to do?” he recalls asking his mother.

items.title: Are men turning away from Trump?
items.summary: Polls point to a decline in support for the president, particularly among voters who no longer trust him to improve the economy
items.body_text:
Are men turning away from Trump?
Polls point to a decline in support for the president, particularly among voters who no longer trust him to improve the economy
In early 2025, Donald Trump became the first sitting president to attend the Super Bowl. He had just returned to the White House and his approval ratings were higher than ever. A few months earlier, he had won the election with a 12-point lead among male voters, which encouraged him to embark on something of a tour of some of the principal cathedrals of American men’s sport: on December 14, he attended the traditional Army-Navy college football game; on February 9, he was at the Super Bowl; on February 16, he attended the NASCAR Daytona 500; and on June 8, he was present at UFC 316, shortly after which he announced that he would stage a UFC fight at the White House to celebrate his 80th birthday.
Trump’s message was clear: American men once again had a president who represented them. For many, the idea was more than popular. It was seen as a lifeline after years of supposed “silent suffering.”
Male workers were hit hardest by the factory closures and decline in manufacturing jobs that accompanied the surge of Chinese imports into the United States at the start of the 21st century. And since the end of the last century, their dominant position in society has steadily eroded: the share of men in employment has fallen, while their earnings have stagnated or declined, particularly among those with lower levels of education. All of this occurred as gender-equality policies began to produce results, however incomplete, and women made advances on a scale never seen before.
Against this backdrop and after twice defeating what many saw as the threat of a female commander in chief, the immediate future seemed promising for these men. Trump returned to the White House promising to revive U.S. manufacturing and to avoid wasting time on military adventures abroad that drained the nation’s resources and diminished its standing. He also launched an offensive against equality and diversity initiatives. It was time, the message went, to do away with governments that favored minorities and once again place the emphasis on the long-neglected heterosexual white man
But the fantasy does not seem to have had a happy ending. The tariffs Trump said would revive domestic manufacturing have done little more than drive up the cost of imported goods, while the war in Iran, questioned even by MAGA influencers themselves, has consumed more than $40 billion, weakened America’s standing abroad and pushed the price of a gallon of gasoline back above $3.50 for the first time in four years. This was not what men were promised, and many have taken notice. According to YouGov’s tracking poll, since the start of the year more Americans have disapproved of Trump’s performance than approved of it.
On 10 August, 52.9% disapproved of Trump’s performance, compared with 45.2% who approved of it. That represents a decline of more than 10 percentage points from the beginning of his second term in January 2025, when Trump was in the middle of his sports tour. Among men under 30, a demographic that was key to his return to the White House, the picture is even worse. A recent survey by Harvard University found that, looking ahead to the next midterm elections, these voters favor Democratic Senate candidates by a margin of eight points.
Since 2016, Trump’s political career has rested on two pillars: the support of less-educated men and the belief that he is better equipped to manage the economy than his Democratic rivals. Both assumptions are beginning to crack. His decline among male voters is due largely to the fact that many no longer trust him to improve the country’s finances. According to NBC’s latest poll, for the first time since 2017, more Americans believe that Democrats are better at handling the economy.

items.summary: Problems related to the overloaded grid network in the Netherlands continue popping up, FD reports.
items.body_text:
Real estate agents now also report that grid congestion is delaying housing projects
Problems related to the overloaded grid network in the Netherlands continue popping up, FD reports. Now, real estate agents are reportedly noticing delays in a growing number of housing projects because of the grid congestion.
“Grid congestion was previously mentioned as a future scenario, but agents now see delays caused by grid congestion in about a quarter of projects,” said Lana Goutsmits-Gerssen, chair of the association’s housing section. She spoke Thursday during a presentation on third-quarter housing market developments.
The electricity grid is full in many parts of the country, forcing more companies and homes to wait for new connections. Grid operator Netbeheer Nederland said last month that there is no room for nearly half of the homes that have applied for electricity connections over the next three years.
Long permitting processes and capacity problems at municipalities had already strengthened construction times. These factors now cause delays in about half of projects, the association told FD. Grid congestion and weak sales add to those causes.
In the third quarter, association members sold fewer newly built homes than in the same quarter a year earlier. It was the fourth consecutive quarter of year-over-year declines. The association called the drop notable because supply has increased. Potential buyers are pulling back because of long construction times and uncertainty about the sale proceeds of their current homes, Goutsmits-Gerssen said.

items.title: Dutch turn in 7,650 kg of fireworks in first nationwide drop-off campaign
items.summary: People brought in about 7,650 kilograms of fireworks during the first nationwide campaign
items.body_text:
Dutch turn in 7,650 kg of fireworks in first nationwide drop-off campaign
People brought in about 7,650 kilograms of fireworks during the first nationwide campaign to turn them in. The Ministry of Justice and Security announced the figure after the 35th and final drop-off point closed Friday in Hoorn.
The campaign began more than a month ago. Enschede recorded the highest total, with 686.5 kilograms, followed by Leeuwarden, 609 kilograms, and Zwolle, 528 kilograms. Less than 11 kilograms came in in Ternezen. In Venlo, Emmen, Tilburg, Maastricht, Den Helder, Den Bosch, and Almere, the amount also stayed under 100 kilograms.
Most of the fireworks, more than 6,500 kilograms, consist of consumer fireworks. Those were still permitted to be set off at last New Year’s but are banned for the upcoming New Year’s Eve. People also turned in nearly 600 kilograms of fireworks containing flash powder, such as crackers. More than 500 kilograms of distress signals were also collected.
The amount of voluntarily surrendered fireworks pales in comparison to the quantities seized. Toward the end of the year, customs and police typically intercept more fireworks in a single week. How much remains undetected is unknown.
According to the ministry, the drop-off days were not intended “to collect a certain amount" but to “inform citizens about the fireworks ban” and to give people who still had fireworks “the opportunity to comply with the new rules in a safe and penalty-free manner.” Whether New Year’s Eve will be quieter than in previous years also depends, the ministry said, “on enforcement, the local approach of municipalities, and people’s own behavior.”
Reporting by ANP

items.body_text:
Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.
The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.
Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.
Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”
The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.
The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.
The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.
The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.
The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.
In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.
Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.
The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.
If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.
Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.
Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.
“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”
The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.
The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.
“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.

items.title: Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar
items.summary: The Bangladeshi and Indian men said they did not know the practice was prohibited in Poland.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.
They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków…
— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026
The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.
After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.
The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF
A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.
However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”
Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.
The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat.

Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons.
Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday.
The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly.

On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack.
That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations.
In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely.
One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil.
Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026
Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”.
Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group.
Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources.
At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained.
Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”.
In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack.
In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy

An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours.
The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved.
#PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6
— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026
The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package.
The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently.
Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales.
In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements.
The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400).
Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage.
The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks.
Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops.
The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026
In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP).
The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment.
Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it.
Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show.
The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005.
They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv

items.title: Week in Review: Realities Old and New
items.summary: A string of long-awaited elections, as well as changing international dynamics, are reshaping the region, as our selection of Balkan Insight Premium stories this week highlights.
items.body_text:
Week in Review: Realities Old and New
Winners and losers
A new election in Bosnia and Herzegovina came with new technologies intended to increase the integrity of the voting process, sparking speculation ahead of the vote about how this might affect the results. Ultimately, the new technologies proved to be about the only novel thing in the elections.
Contrary to the expectations of many, voters reaffirmed support for entrenched nationalist parties even more strongly than they did four years ago. Nominally civic, leftist or pro-Bosnian parties were big losers. Our two analyses take a look at who the winners and losers of the elections were, as well as the prospects for government formation at state and entity levels.
Read more: Bosnia’s 2026 Elections: Fewer Votes, Familiar Winners (October 8, 2026)
Read more: Nationalist Parties Celebrate Wins in Bosnia Election, But Many Voters Stay Home (October 6, 2026)
Calmer waters?
After a rollercoaster political week, is Kosovo sailing into calmer voters? A drama was triggered by the guilty verdict handed down to former Kosovo Liberation Army leader and former Kosovo president Hashim Thaci for war crimes by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in the Hague.
All this converged with an October 6 deadline set by the Constitutional Court for Kosovo’s parliament to elect a new President, or face dissolution and yet another election. At the 11th hour, political leaders struck a deal to elect Justina Shiroka Pula as President. Our analysis looks at who the new President is and what her election could mean for Kosovo.
Read more: Kosovo President’s Election Kindles Hope of Return to Stability (October 9, 2026)
Read more: Justina Shiroka Pula, Another Woman at Kosovo’s Helm (October 8, 2026)
Changing world
Kosovo may have snapped out of its cycle of institutional blockage with the election of a new President, but what does the future hold? Internationally, the country has never looked more isolated.
In an opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Fron Nahzi examines the US’s changing relationship with Kosovo. Gone are the days when Washington was interested in nurturing Kosovo’s statehood and political development. It remains to be seen how the political actors in Kosovo adjust to this reality.
Read more: For the Trump Administration, Kosovo is Now Just a Bargaining Chip (October 9, 2026)
Electoral test
Serbia’s two-year-long political crisis, triggered by the collapse of the railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people, is reaching its culmination. Parliamentary elections on October 25, followed by presidential elections at an unspecified later date, will test popular support for the ruling Progressive Party and its main challenger, the Student List.
The Student List began as a university-centred protest movement demanding justice and rejecting politics. Since then, it has transitioned, somewhat reluctantly, into a movement competing for power. Our analysis tracks this evolution and weighs the Student List’s prospects of success.
Read more: From Streets to Polling Stations: Serbia’s Student Movement Takes Electoral Test (October 6, 2026)
End of the road?
Albania’s Special Prosecution Office Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, has scored many a success in prosecuting high-profile political figures since its creation in 2016. So much so that many across the region are watching in amazement and wondering how such prosecutions are possible.
But could its days of fighting corruption and organised crime be numbered? An attempt to rewrite large chunks of the country’s criminal code, some of it merited, is raising concerns that the real agenda of the legal amendments is to defang the SPAK.
Read more: Albanian Criminal Procedure Bill Slammed as Bid to ‘Neuter’ Anti-Graft Body (October 8, 2026)

items.title: For the Trump Administration, Kosovo is Now Just a Bargaining Chip
items.summary: Washington no longer sees Kosovo as a strategic obligation but as an asset of diminishing value, to be leveraged in the service of US interests.
items.body_text:
Kosovo has finally broken its political deadlock, with parliament electing a new President after 20 months of wrangling that produced two early elections and brought the country to the brink of a third.
But the political turmoil is far from over. Demonstrations have erupted over the indictment of four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders and the country remains deeply divided over its political future.
For a young country still struggling to find its political footing, one thing has been conspicuously missing: the United States. Washington once played a parental role for Kosovo, stepping in to broker deals and settle disputes, as US Ambassador Christopher Dell famously did in 2011, when he helped propose a presidential candidate after Kosovo’s political leaders could not agree on one. Today, Washington appears reluctant to play that role.
Since the end of the Kosovo war, Washington has envisioned its role as having a defined endpoint: the US would win the war, and Europe would take responsibility for maintaining the peace. Kosovo, and more broadly the Balkans, would eventually become a European responsibility.

The Hungarian State Opera has selected some of Zoltán Kodály’s most iconic works for its “1956/70 – Kodály Gala Concert”. At a press conference on Wednesday, held to mark the centenary of the Opera House premiere of the composer’s Háry János singspiel and the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, Opera House Director General Szilveszter Ókovács said that Háry János, which has close ties to the institution, would feature prominently in the program. The work premiered at the Ybl Palace on October 16, 1926.
Kodály’s works will be performed at the Opera’s concert commemorating the events of 1956, coinciding with the centenary celebrations. He also recalled that in 1956, the Hungarian Revolutionary Council of Intellectuals elected Kodály as its president. Throughout his work, the composer strengthened Hungarian national identity, said the director general.
The program features works from Kodály’s middle and later periods: on the one hand, hymn-like compositions imbued with a sense of responsibility for the fate of the Hungarian nation; on the other, music of varied character associated with Háry János and the Opera House.
Saturday’s concert will feature Psalmus Hungaricus and the Háry János Suite, as well as the singspiel’s ballet music, also known as the Dragon Dance, and Song to Saint Stephen, King of Hungary. The program will also include soldiers’ songs from the composer’s Hungarian Folk Music series.
Several events had been organized to mark the centenary of the premiere of Háry János. The folk opera will be staged under the direction of Attila Béres, with seven performances scheduled between October 17 and 25 as part of the anniversary series. A large-scale production is being prepared, starring Csaba Sándor and Gabriella Balga and conducted by Péter Halász.
Péter Halász said: “Conducting Háry János is a great honor and a wonderful challenge.” He emphasized that
the work had never before been performed in this particular form.
In 1962, when Kodály was elderly, he submitted a score to Universal Publishing House, declaring it to be the definitive version. The work has existed in numerous versions, but this time the team intends to perform it as Kodály envisioned it in his later years. Halász stressed that they would remain faithful to the score and strive to interpret everything in the spirit of Kodály, preserving the folk-song character of the vocal parts and performing the folk melodies with their original purity and naturalness.
Ókovács said that, as part of the “Háry100” anniversary program, the Opera House would hold a morning concert of Kodály folk songs on the day after the anniversary performance. The children’s production Háry Jánoska (Johnny Háry), which premiered in September, will also be performed on weekends at the Eiffel Art Studios.
The director general also announced that,
as part of the 70th-anniversary commemorations of the 1956 Revolution, a double-bill program will pair the mockumentary Kádár’s Record with a documentary drama titled Last Speech of Kádár.
The production will premiere on October 22 and be performed five times at the Eiffel Art Studios through November 1.
Historian and documentary filmmaker Tamás Novák adapted his chamber drama The Last Speech of Kádár, originally created in 2016 for the 60th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution, for the stage based on Mihály Kornis’s book János Kádár’s Last Speech. Ókovács explained that the production would be presented in a new format alongside the mockumentary, moving from the auditorium beneath the Opera House to the stage of the Eiffel Art Studios.

items.body_text:
It is capable of transporting necessary equipment and paramedics to the scene even in difficult terrain.Continue reading
Hungary’s National Ambulance Service (OMSZ) has completed a comprehensive modernization program. With nearly 20 billion forints (55 million euros) in EU funding, the organization has upgraded its infrastructure and equipment, the ambulance service announced on social media.
The project focused primarily on modernizing medical equipment. A total of 256 new ambulances have been put into service. The upgrades also include 572 advanced defibrillators with integrated multiparameter ECG monitors and accessories, 234 Doppler devices, 166 standalone ECG machines, as well as other medical equipment and IT infrastructure.
The new equipment is expected to help make prehospital emergency care faster, safer, and higher in quality.
Alongside the completion of the investment program, the OMSZ is continuing its transparency initiative announced in late summer. Since September, the organization has been publishing detailed monthly figures on response times and call volumes on a dedicated online platform.
The data is based on a new calculation method that measures the time from receipt of a 911-equivalent emergency call (112) to the arrival of ambulance crews at the scene. Direct comparisons with older statistics are therefore not possible, as those figures often measured response times only from the moment the ambulance station was alerted.
The latest figures for September present a mixed picture:
- Total call volume (P1–P4): The service recorded 84,963 calls nationwide across priority levels P1 to P4, including 15,903 in Budapest. Compared with August, the number of calls fell 11% nationwide and 5.8% in Budapest, although it remained above the level recorded a year earlier.
- Most critical emergencies (P1): A total of 10,638 calls nationwide were classified as the highest priority. Ambulance crews arrived within 20.10 minutes in 75% of these cases.
In 90% of life-threatening emergencies, paramedics reached the scene within 25.75 minutes. Despite a slight improvement compared with August, the service has yet to meet its own target. In the longer term, it aims to ensure that ambulance crews reach 90% of P1 emergencies within 15 minutes of receiving the emergency call.
Regional figures for September varied. Western Transdanubia recorded the shortest response time nationwide, with crews arriving within 23.16 minutes in 90% of cases. Central Hungary had the longest response time, at 27.75 minutes. Budapest presented a mixed picture. The response time for 75% of calls improved slightly to 19.84 minutes, while the time for crews to reach 90% of incidents increased to 24.89 minutes.
The ambulance service stressed that
response time is an important logistical indicator, but on its own it does not provide a complete picture of the quality of treatment and care.
The organization said it would publish the data in full every month to track progress transparently and document areas where further improvements are needed.
Via MTI, Featured image: MTI/Bodnár Boglárka

With the highest rate in the region, Hungary maintains its leading position among the Visegrád countries. According to the international software company’s quarterly Global AI Diffusion report, Hungary (33.3%) ranks 20th globally, ahead […] The post Hungary Leads Visegrád 4 Countries in Generative AI Use appeared first o
items.body_text:
At the AI Summit 2026, Hungarian media professionals discussed how artificial intelligence is reshaping journalism. Continue reading
One-third of Hungary’s working-age population uses generative artificial intelligence, Microsoft’s latest report revealed. This puts the country ahead of its regional neighbors.
With the highest rate in the region, Hungary maintains its leading position among the Visegrád countries. According to the international software company’s quarterly Global AI Diffusion report, Hungary (33.3%) ranks 20th globally, ahead of Poland (32.3%), the Czech Republic (31.2%) and Slovakia (27.1%).
The share of technology users in Hungary increased by 1.1 percentage points in a single quarter, while Poland recorded an even faster increase of 1.3 percentage points, said Microsoft Hungary in a press release.
Worldwide, 18.8% of the working-age population used generative AI in June, up one percentage point from the first quarter.
The highest rates were recorded in the United Arab Emirates (73.3%) and Singapore (64.3%), with Ireland moving into third place at 49.9%.
Microsoft experts point out that the spread of AI does not in itself mean that the technology will automatically boost productivity or economic performance. To achieve this, companies also need to transform their workflows, train employees, and promote the conscious and responsible use of the technology.
In education, efforts should focus on ensuring that AI genuinely supports learning, the development of critical thinking, and teachers’ work, rather than serving merely as a tool for providing quick answers, the analysts warn.
Microsoft’s annual Work Trend Index, based on a survey of 20,000 AI-using employees across 10 countries, shows that two-thirds of workers fear they will fall behind if they do not adapt quickly with the help of AI. Nevertheless, 45% feel safer focusing on their current objectives rather than using the technology to redesign the way they work.
The statement quotes Barbora Paulovic Deckerova, president of Microsoft’s Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia region, as saying that
in Hungary, the next phase of AI adoption will be driven less by increasing the number of users and more by improving the quality of how the technology is used.
Microsoft’s Global AI Diffusion report covers 147 economies and estimates the share of generative AI users among the working-age population aged 15-64.
Via MTI, Featured image: Pexels

items.body_text:
Police Car Ends Up in Vltava River, Three People Treated for Hypothermia
Prague Morning
A police car plunged into the Vltava River in Prague on Saturday morning after crashing through the guardrails of Hlávkův Bridge.
The vehicle’s two occupants and a man who jumped into the water to help them were treated by emergency crews for hypothermia.
The accident was reported to police at around 8 a.m. on October 10. A man and a woman, both approximately 30 years old, were inside the car when it went into the river.
A witness jumped into the water after the vehicle fell from the bridge and helped the occupants. Emergency services subsequently treated all three people at the scene.
Prague Emergency Medical Service dispatched three ambulances, a medical inspector and a rapid response vehicle to the incident.
All three were suffering from hypothermia but were not in life-threatening condition, according to emergency responders.
“We are very grateful to the rescuer for their help,” Prague Emergency Medical Service said in a statement, confirming that all three people were in its care.
Police are investigating the circumstances of the crash, including what caused the vehicle to break through the bridge’s guardrails and fall into the Vltava.

items.body_text:
Prague Outperforms Vienna and Berlin in Visitor Ratings
Prague Morning
Prague has received higher visitor satisfaction ratings than Vienna and Berlin, according to the latest Global Tourist Perception Index by Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence.
The Czech capital scored 92.7 out of 100, compared with 85.6 for Vienna and 78.4 for Berlin, Prague City Tourism (PCT) announced on Thursday.
The results reflect six years of efforts to improve tourism services, visitor experiences and the city’s destination branding, the organization said during International Customer Service Week, held from October 5 to 9.
The Global Tourist Perception Index assesses several aspects of the visitor experience, including hotel satisfaction, safety and tourism products. Prague scored highest among the three capitals, according to PCT.
Visitor spending rises as tourism shifts upmarket
Data from Mastercard transactions indicate that spending by visitors from key foreign markets increased by 18% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while the number of visitors rose by approximately 1%.
Social media analysis also points to Prague’s growing association with culture. More than a third of social media posts shared by visitors about the city focused on art and culture, an increase of around five percentage points year-on-year. Nightlife accounted for just 4.5% of reported reasons for visiting, according to PCT.
The Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence Platform also gave Prague a score of 80 out of 100 for hotel service satisfaction, ahead of Vienna at 75.8 and Berlin at 71.8.
Figures from hotel data provider STR point to further growth in the market. Between January and August 2026, hotel occupancy in Prague increased by 4.9% year-on-year, while the average room rate rose by 5.1%.
Occupancy reached 84.7% in August. According to a recent overview of Prague’s tourism sector by the Czech Institute of Tourism, the average room rate was approximately €123, rising to €170 in the city center and €241 in the luxury segment.
Prague attracts hotel investors
The city is also gaining ground among hotel investors. According to the Cushman & Wakefield Hotel Investor Compass 2026, published in March, Prague ranks among the 15 most attractive European cities for hotel investment, ahead of Vienna, Zurich and Budapest.
Investor interest in Prague’s hotel market has increased for two consecutive years. In the previous edition of the study, the city recorded the largest year-on-year increase in investor interest among the markets surveyed, at 14%. The latest edition showed a further increase of 7%.

Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
Prague Morning
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.
The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.
On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.
Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.
The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.
There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.
Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.
The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.
The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

items.body_text:
Russia Suspends Sale, Import of Drinks From Several Georgian Producers, RBC Reports
Russia has suspended the import and sale of alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks — including Nabeghlavi and Coca-Cola — from several key Georgian producers, Russian media outlet RBC reported, citing a document from the Russian consumer rights and public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor, as well as sources from the “alcohol market” and retailers.
Among the producers subject to “temporary sanitary measures” are Nabeghlavi mineral water produced by Healthy Water, Coca-Cola produced in Georgia, beer produced by Georgian Beer Company, wines produced by Teliani Valley, Tbilvino, and Wineman, as well as wine and cognac produced by Askaneli Brothers. The report does not indicate the period of suspension.
The outlet says that according to the Rospotrebnadzor document, “a temporary sanitary measure was introduced to suspend the import and circulation within the country of products that do not comply with established requirements for organoleptic and physicochemical indicators, as well as safety indicators.”
RBC quoted representatives of the retail industry, including the Association of Companies of Omnichannel Retail Trade (ACORT) and Auchan, the Russian subsidiary of French retailer Auchan recently placed under temporary administration by Russian authorities, as confirming that the products were being removed from stores following instructions from Rospotrebnadzor.

items.body_text:
Botchorishvili Says ‘Number of’ EU Countries Support Georgia’s OSCE Bid Amid Reports of Objections
Georgian Dream Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili says Tbilisi is aware of “a number of” EU member states supporting Georgia’s bid to chair the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) in 2027, despite reports of objections within the EU.
She has also cited a lack of consensus over the candidacy of Cyprus as an argument for Georgia’s aspired chairmanship, while noting that the OSCE is “not only an EU region.”
“Slovakia has openly stated that it will support Georgia’s candidacy for the OSCE chairmanship in 2027,” Botchorishvili said in her October 7 remarks to the pro-government Imedi TV. “Behind closed doors, we are also aware of the positions of a number of EU member states that they will support Georgia’s candidacy,” she added, acknowledging, however, that a single country can block a decision.
The OSCE, which brings together 57 participating states from Europe, North America and Central Asia, makes major decisions by consensus, meaning a single state can block it.
According to Botchorishvili, Georgia made its first-ever bid for the OSCE chairmanship in January, expecting the decision by the OSCE Ministerial Council scheduled to take place on December 3-4 in Lugano, Switzerland. Botchorishvili has openly campaigned for Georgia’s chairmanship on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York in September.
Her remarks come after Brussels-based news outlet Rapporteur reported earlier in October that the EU was standing in the way of Georgia’s bid, with Cyprus enjoying support from EU countries and the bloc as a whole despite a deadlock caused by Turkish objections over its candidacy.
Citing diplomats, the outlet said that the Baltic states were particularly opposed to Georgia’s candidacy, “reflecting concerns over Tbilisi’s increasingly difficult relationship with the EU and its approach to Russia,” while Serbia was also considering a bid to chair the organization next year.
According to Botchorishvili, the EU member states “can agree to adopt a common position, but within the OSCE, it is the position of each individual participating state that is recorded.”
She said Tbilisi deliberately refrained from actively campaigning until September as it was ready to back Cyprus in case of a consensus. “Unfortunately, no decision could be reached because of Turkey’s position, which has not changed to this day,” she said, adding that the EU “can, of course, support Cyprus, but we all know very well that reaching consensus on Cyprus is impossible.”
“A fact is a fact. Today, Georgia is the only country on which we do not know whether there is a final decision. We do know that no consensus has been reached regarding Cyprus.”
OSCE ‘Not Only EU Region’
The GD Foreign Minister further cited Georgia’s geographical position as an argument to support its aspired chairmanship, noting that “no country from our region” has previously held the position, and even from Central Asia, it was only Kazakhstan, which chaired OSCE in 2010.
“The organization covers a vast region. It is not only an EU region,” she said. “Georgia is, in a sense, in the middle of the organization.”
Botchorishvili said Tbilisi plans to host OSCE Chairperson-in-Office Ignazio Cassis, the foreign minister of Switzerland, a country that holds the OSCE chairmanship in 2026.
Georgia’s bid comes amid strained relations with the EU over concerns about “democratic backsliding” and Georgian Dream’s anti-Western rhetoric.

TI Georgia Says ComCom ‘Banned’ Use of 93 Phrases for Government-Critical Broadcasters
Transparency International (TI) Georgia, a local civil society organization, says it identified 93 distinct words and phrases that the Communications Commission, Georgia’s media regulator, “prohibited” government-critical broadcasters from using following last year’s amendments to broadcasting laws, which gave the regulator greater control over TV and radio content.
The watchdog said it identified the phrases after reviewing seven decisions issued by ComCom, a public agency chaired by a former ruling party MP, concerning government-critical broadcasters TV Pirveli and Formula. Both of these channels have been fined several times after the regulator found them in violation of amended broadcasting laws.
“The review found that the Commission prohibits critical broadcasters from using a total of 101 words and/or phrases: 33 in the case of TV Pirveli and 68 in the case of Formula,” TI Georgia said in its October 9 report. In some cases, the words and phrases prohibited for the two critical broadcasters overlap. Overall, the Commission prohibits the use of 93 distinct words and phrases.”
The list includes terms such as “regime,” “prisoners of conscience,” “oligarch,” “false-witness police officers,” “political prisoners,” “political hostages,” “repressive policy,” “Ivanishvili’s prime minister,” “the so-called education reform,” “Georgian Dream police,” “unlawful imprisonment,” “the Scroll-Screenshot Department,” “Georgian Dream government,” “repressive laws,” “the regime’s court,” “Ivanishvili’s president,” “Georgian Dream’s State Security Service,” “judicial clan,” among others, according to TI-Georgia.
In addition to prohibiting specific words and phrases, the watchdog argued that the regulator “requires critical broadcasters to report the news in a dry manner, stripped entirely of commentary and analysis.” According to TI Georgia, the memoranda also identify statements by journalists and presenters that the Commission considers unacceptable, citing several examples.
The watchdog emphasized that it is “deeply concerning” that ComCom “has the power to regulate broadcasters’ content and, on this basis, impose financial sanctions and suspend their broadcasting licenses.” It also argued that, amid what it described as “firmly established and clearly evident state capture in Georgia,” the Commission has for years been composed of commissioners “loyal to and affiliated with Georgian Dream.”
TI Georgia noted that questions remain over the Commission’s decisions and concerns persist that “it has acted to advance the interests of the ruling party and in a biased manner,” warning that “the Communications Commission should not operate as a censor, nor should it be used as a mechanism for punishing critical broadcasters.”
Citing “international practice,” the organization said that “disputed issues should instead be addressed through self-regulatory mechanisms,” and that “promoting and supporting self-regulation should be one of the Commission’s primary objectives — rather than serving the interests of Georgian Dream and penalizing broadcasters for criticizing and exposing representatives of the ruling party.”
The watchdog also warned that the ComCom “continues to act as a censor,” citing its October 1 decision to fine Formula TV GEL 10,000 (USD 3,850) over what the regulator described as violations of impartiality requirements, arguing that the broadcaster’s coverage was based on “personal views.”

items.title: Abkhazian media claims no danger from Sochi oil tanker fire
items.summary: The BBC Russian Service reported earlier in the week that the oil spill was visible from Sukhumi (Sukhum).
items.body_text:
Abkhazian media claims no danger from Sochi oil tanker fire
The BBC Russian Service reported earlier in the week that the oil spill was visible from Sukhumi (Sukhum).
Abkhazian government-controlled media has interviewed a representative of a local ecology institute, who claimed there is no evidence that the Aframax Rio oil tanker fire off the coast of Sochi has polluted the coastline of Abkhazia.
The tanker which appeared to be carrying crude oil from Novorossiysk, Russia to India was attacked by drones, leading Sochi to close beaches to the public as a plume of black smoke set over the city on 6 October, with the BBC Russian Service suggesting earlier in the week that the oil spill was visible from Sukhumi (Sukhum). OC Media had not independently verified this claim. Greenpeace analysis found that as of 9 October, an oil slick covering about 25 square kilometers was visible on satellite images.
Beaches in Sochi were temporarily closed to the public but were quickly reopened with Russian authorities claiming no threat to humans. Sochi Mayor Andrei Proshunin claimed ‘no pollution’ from the spill had been detected in the sea.
In the Gagra district, local Telegram channels reported it was the end of the summer swimming season, vaguely citing the safety of residents and visitors. Early October is a normal time for the authorities to do this; last year, the swimming season closed on 15 October.
Roman Dbar, who directs the Academy of Sciences’ Ecology Institute and serves as the State University’s First Vice-Rector, claimed that due to the wind direction, any potential air pollution was ‘carried away in a direction opposite to our coastline and waters’.
He claimed that ‘Even if there was potential water and air pollution, it did not enter our airspace or our seaspace’.
Abkhazian government media published the interview denying harm after moderate concern was expressed on local social media, with one user worrying ‘which way will the oil products drift now, and where should we expect the next environmental disaster?’
Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine has been heavily harmful to marine life in the Black Sea, but it is difficult to assess how detrimental the situation is off Abkhazia due to the lack of public monitoring.
In December 2024, two aging oil tankers — part of Russia’s so-called shadow fleet used to circumvent sanctions imposed after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine – capsized in the Kerch Strait. The tankers carried approximately 9,200 tons of oil, and according to Russian authorities spilled around 2,400 tons of that into the Black Sea.
In 2025, the Russian-state run medi outlet Sputnik interviewed a local climate expert, who acknowledged that oil from the Kerch spill reached Abkhazia’s shores. Asida Akhsalba told the outlet that the pollution posed no threat to humans, but also acknowledged that Abkhazia lacked the equipment to fully assess the extent of the pollution.
For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

items.title: Georgia plans $200 million railway link to Anaklia port, Kobakhidze says
items.summary: The construction tender is expected by October’s end.
items.body_text:
Georgia plans to build an 18-kilometre long railway connecting Anaklia port, with the construction tender expected to be awarded by the end of October. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said on Friday that the World Bank would support the estimated $200 million project.
The Anaklia Deep Sea Port project has a long and politically complex history in Georgia, which dates back to its initial development idea in 2006, and continued until the end of Mikheil Saakashvili’s presidency and the subsequent rise of the Georgian Dream government.
Kobakhidze says the railway project is part of wider changes to Georgian Railway, which he claims have already generated ₾190 million ($73 million) in savings.
Work on the Anaklia railway connection project was ongoing, Kobakhidze said on Friday, adding the announcement about the total estimated cost of the planned 18-kilometre section and that the World Bank would be contributing funding.
The construction tender would be announced by the end of October, he said.
Kobakhidze also highlighted changes within Georgian Railway, saying he had presented an overview of reforms in the economic sector when Mariam Kvrivishvili was nominated as deputy prime minister. He said the presentation focused primarily on changes implemented over the previous year and a half, with Georgian Railway being a key part.
Georgia said that China had officially exited the Anaklia Deep Sea Port project in July; the move was expected by many experts and critics, as rumours of China’s exit had been circulating for months.
Following completion of the dredging works, the seabed in the Anaklia Port area will be deepened to approximately 17.5 metres, with the project plans including the construction of a 1,376-metre breakwater. The depth will enable the port to accommodate some of the largest and highest-capacity vessels operating in the Black Sea, while the breakwater will create a sheltered harbour basin and facilitate the development of deep-water container berths, as well as berths for dry and bulk cargo. The design targets annual operational availability of at least 95%.
The construction of the initial land-based section of the breakwater is underway, involving the placement of stone and aggregate. Once this phase is completed, construction will move into the sea.
The project is being developed under a landlord port model, under which the state develops and owns the core port infrastructure, while private partners are responsible for developing and operating terminals. The Economy Ministry says this model is intended to foster competition, attract international partners and cargo flows, and support the port’s efficient operation.
The state is also responsible for developing the transport infrastructure connecting Anaklia to the wider network, including a new road and railway.
During a recent inspection of the ongoing works, Anaklia Sea Port LLC director Zurab Sichinava, Maritime Transport Agency head Ivane Abashidze, and Jan De Nul’s Anaklia director Eric Bates reviewed progress at the site.
Bates described the Anaklia Deep Sea Port as an important project for Georgia’s economy, saying it would contribute to increased employment as well as growth in Georgia’s GDP and global GDP.
In 2016, the Georgian government selected the Anaklia Development Consortium LLC to build and operate the deep-sea port on the Black Sea coast. The $2.5 billion project was presented as a major strategic investment that could strengthen Georgia’s role as a regional trade and transportation hub by creating a direct link between China and Europe along the historic Silk Road.
However, the project soon became mired in political and financial difficulties. By 2020, the Georgian government argued that the consortium had failed to meet its contractual obligations and terminated the agreement, prompting the consortium to challenge the government’s decision. items.title: Azerbaijan students launch school strike over hijab restrictions
items.summary: As pupils protested, the Baku City Education Department announced that it would conduct monitoring visits to schools.
items.body_text:
Students at two schools in Azerbaijan have boycotted classes in protest of restrictions on hijab-wearing pupils, local media are reporting. Imprisoned journalist Polad Aslanov has also launched a hunger strike over the changes to school uniform regulations which were adopted by Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers on 21 September, alongside new requirements governing teachers’ clothing.
The Baku City Education Department has announced they will begin monitoring how the new requirements have been implemented in public schools.
The measures have prompted criticism from students and parents, who say they restrict the right to education of girls wearing the hijab. According to the Constitution of Azerbaijan, the state guarantees the right to free and compulsory general secondary education. There is no specific clause in the constitution that grants individuals the right to wear hijabs in schools.
Students at School No 69 in Baku and B Shiriyev Secondary School in the village of Mollaoba, Masally district, reportedly refused to attend classes and demanded that their hijab-wearing classmates be allowed to return to school, according to Meydan TV reports and footage circulating on social media.
Jailed journalist launches hunger strike
Polad Aslanov, the jailed head of the Xeberman news website, announced that he had begun a hunger strike on Thursday in protest against the restrictions.
His wife, Gulmira Aslanova, reported the decision in a Facebook post, saying that Aslanov was being held at Penitentiary Facility No 15.
Aslanov said the hunger strike was intended to draw attention to hijab-wearing students being barred from schools and restrictions on teachers’ clothing. He also said his own child’s right to education had been restricted.
‘I declare that I have begun a hunger strike to defend the rights of my own child and all hijab-wearing students whose right to education is restricted, as well as all hijab-wearing female teachers who are being forced to choose between education and wearing the hijab’, he said.
Aslanov added that he had appealed to Allahshukur Pashazadeh, the head of the Caucasus Muslims Board, several days earlier but had received no response.
He argued that the clothing restrictions violate article 48 of Azerbaijan’s Constitution, which guarantees freedom of conscience.
Aslanov was arrested in 2019 on treason charges and initially sentenced to 16 years in prison. His sentence was later reduced to 13 years. He denies the charges and says he is being punished for his journalistic work.
Separately, a hijab-wearing teacher at Richard Sorge Secondary School No 90 in Baku has been dismissed, according to Medyan TV, whose footage shows crying students hugging the teacher.

items.title: Court fines man for storing dead parents in freezers for 30 years
items.summary: The 81-year-old defendant was ordered to pay about 2,000 euros in income-linked fines.
items.body_text:
A court in Turku has fined an 81-year-old man about 2,000 euros after finding him guilty on three counts of violating the sanctity of a grave, as well as the unlawful concealing of an unburied body.
Police discovered last year that the man had stored the bodies of his parents in freezers for over 30 years.
The case first came to the police's attention when the defendant, a trained physician who is also listed as an executive at a firm described as offering funeral services, was found digging up a family grave last autumn.
His 70-year-old brother was also charged with and convicted of violating the sanctity of a grave in relation to that incident, and the court fined him a total of 640 euros.
Decades-long concealment
The court heard that the brothers' parents died of natural causes in 1994 and 1995 and their bodies were released to the family for burial.
However, the older of the two brothers took possession of their parents' remains in 1995 when he collected one body from a hospital and the other from the University of Turku's department of pathology.
Police found the bodies in an outdoor storage unit at a detached house in Turku in 2024.
The 81-year-old defendant told the court during the trial that he was "only acting in accordance" with his father's wishes.
When police found the bodies, the electricity had been cut off to one of the freezers.
"The photographs presented by the prosecutor show that the freezers were under various pieces of junk amid general disorder, and had lain undisturbed for a long period," the court's ruling noted.
The court further found that the parents' wish for their bodies to be frozen did not absolve the man of criminal liability, as he was found to have violated statutes intended to protect people's basic understanding of how the dead should be treated.
Finnish legislation concerning the violation of the sanctity of a grave changed in 1999. Before the change in the law, the offence was called unlawful concealment of an unburied body.
Because the timeline of the crimes preceded and followed the law reform, the man was found guilty of both offences.
The court's ruling is not yet final, meaning it can be appealed to a higher court.

items.title: Nordic public broadcasters deepen cooperation to prepare for crises
items.summary: The broadcasters commit to helping their Nordic neighbours in times of crisis.
items.body_text:
Nordic public service media companies have agreed to prepare for crises by increasing cooperation.
Among other things, the unified work will aim to prevent cyber threats and the dissemination of disinformation.
Yle published a statement about the agreement on Friday.
At the same time, the broadcasters made a commitment to help their Nordic neighbours if a crisis should strike. For example, if one country loses access to their own news and information sources, residents will be able to get the necessary updates via another Nordic public broadcaster.
Apart from Yle, the Finnish Broadcasting Company, the participating public broadcasters include:
- RÚV (short for Ríkisútvarpið), the public broadcaster of Iceland.
- DR, the Danish Broadcasting Corporation.
- NRK, Norway’s state-owned public service broadcaster.
- SVT, the Swedish national public TV broadcaster
- SR, Sweden's national publicly funded radio broadcaster.
- UR, the Swedish Educational Broadcasting Company.
The media companies emphasised that journalistic independence is a core principle of the agreement. Cooperation therefore doesn't mean one company could decide what another broadcasts.
