items.title: Inside Sweden: Remembering what I love about this country
items.summary: In a political climate that often feels hostile to immigrants, it can be easy for those of us stuck in Sweden's immigration system to sour on the country. This week, Mandy Pipher takes a step back to remember why she wanted to come here to begin with.
items.body_text:
In Sweden's public discourse it's usually referred to as a "paradigm shift" on immigration, but for those of us directly affected, it can feel more like racing frantically around trying to catch new things being randomly shot out at us from one of those t-shirt launchers – if the t-shirts weren't free and also contained the basic right to keep living the lives we've been building in this country.
In such a context, keeping track of rapidly changing and complex immigration law changes in Sweden is as anxiety-inducing as it is necessary. For me, whose job it is to report and explain those changes to other foreigners in Sweden, while still on temporary permits myself, the sense of being rather under siege can, at times, threaten to overwhelm.
On the bad days, this means that the regular immigration policy news coming out of Stockholm combined with the most recent deportation stories we've been covering at The Local can congeal into a heavy film over my eyes, one which affects how I move through my daily Swedish life. I've always found Umeå, where I live, to be a calm, peaceful, welcoming place (well...welcoming in a passive Swedish way!), but on those bad days, that heavy film gets between me and the real place where I live.
It's not like I start walking around suspecting every blonde blue-eyed person I pass of being a Sweden Democrat voter. It's more like the regular world seems overall darker, heavier, more hostile. It's like a dim spectre of racially-charged venom and xenophobia starts hovering in the very air.
But on lighter days, or when I have the wherewithal (and energy) to blow that spectre out of the air, I realize that the immediate community around me is as it always was.
The walk to my daughter's preschool features trees, cute colourful houses, and more bicycles than cars. At the preschool itself, I am greeted by the wonderful staff, who chat calmly and wisely with me about my child's day – or about the weather. They are patient with my Swedish and treat the diverse children in their care with warm attention and respect. My daughter is usually busy running away from me, into the rambling forest they have on the grounds, yelling over her shoulder that she doesn't want to go home yet.
Back at our apartment, I exchange a few words with my neighbours as they, too, are arriving back from collecting their kids. The reserved Swedish way of interacting can feel remote, but I find that once I get a bit past the taciturn exterior, there's often a gentle, respectful warmth – and a good-natured, matter-of-fact attitude to life that, along with a dark sense of humour seems to me like a pretty great way of dealing with the world.
I feel at home here – here, in my neighbourhood, and in my adopted city. And I'm determined that no amount of dog-whistle political posters featuring a cartoon bee and a certain party leader hanging out of a car is going to change that.
What have we been writing about this week?
Sweden's government-formation process is (sort of) dribbling slowly along, as the four centre-left parties met together in person for the first time since the September 13th election.
We did more digging into the previous government's family immigration bill that became law on October 1st, publishing a Q&A explainer on how it will affect researchers, and an interview with a lawyer about how the law may create a new type of teen deportation case.
Speaking of teen deportations, the centre-left parties this week put forward their first joint motion: to halt all 'teen deportation' cases until the issue can be comprehensively dealt with.
And an AI consultant named Anna Bärlund has successfully appealed her Swedish citizenship rejection.
We also wrote about our reader survey on what you miss from home – and Richard and I talked about our own 'misses' on this week's Sweden in Focus.
Want to relax with some games on the weekend? The Local's got you covered: find the Swedish word in WordroW and crack the daily sudoku with The Local Games.
T

items.title: AI consultant wins appeal under Sweden’s new citizenship rules
items.summary: The AI consultant Anna Bärlund has become one of the first to successfully appeal a citizenship rejection under Sweden’s new longer residency requirements. Her arguments won't work for everyone, but the ruling could have wider implications if upheld.
items.body_text:
When Sweden tightened its citizenship laws on June 6th, the roughly 100,000 applicants already in the queue were judged overnight against new and much harsher rules than before. Anna Bärlund, an AI consultant originally from Russia, was one of them. She had applied for citizenship back in 2023 – long before any bill to change the rules was put forward by the government.
She had also had a request to conclude her case granted by a court in the spring of 2025, which is meant to fast-track your application, but often doesn’t work as intended and has been criticised by the Migration Agency and authorities for clogging up the system.
“The only thing they did [in response] was that they took away my passport, and I had to live for more than a year without my passport, without being able to travel to see my relatives, to see my friends, or do any work abroad, which was very important for me as well,” she said.
READ ALSO: How to appeal if your application for Swedish citizenship is rejected
Married to a Swede, Bärlund and others like her are the ones hardest hit by the changes, with the residency requirement for partners more than doubling from three to seven years. And so, after having waited almost three years, just nine days after the new citizenship laws came into force, the Migration Agency finally finished processing her case. Rejected.
“I cried, if I’m honest, because it felt so deeply unfair,” she said.
But she appealed, and on October 7th, the Migration Court in Malmö ruled in her favour.
“The Migration Court overturns the appealed decision and remits the case back to the Migration Agency for further processing,” reads the court decision, read by The Local.
Due to her long wait, Bärlund was rejected right at the finishing line, when she was just three months away from meeting the new seven-year requirement. As a result, she ended up reaching those seven months while waiting for her appeal to be processed by the court.
“Upon review of the case documents, the Migration Court notes that Anna Bärlund's period of habitual residence in Sweden now exceeds seven years,” the decision continues.
READ ALSO: Migration court rules that new Swedish citizenship requirements apply to pending applications
Essentially, the ruling indicates that an applicant has to meet the new rules by the time a court makes a decision on their appeal, even if they did not meet them when the Migration Agency made their decision. This is an existing legal principle, but it was not yet clear whether or not it would apply in cases relating to the lack of transitional citizenship rules.
Youstbi Djuanvat, a lawyer for Edelweiss Legal KB, which represented Bärlund, welcomed the judgment, but warned that the Migration Agency could still appeal it, so the ruling is not set in stone.
“I spoke with my client today and we are ready to fight this in the court of appeal if the Migration Agency decides to challenge the court decision,” he told The Local.
But he said that the ruling does suggest that rejected citizenship applicants who are close to meeting the new requirements might benefit from appealing their rejection.
“Absolutely, and it can be applied in different circumstances. If you do not fulfil the language or civic knowledge requirement, then maybe you can appeal that and then you complete your SFI and by the time you finish, you just send it to the court and say ‘there you go, now I fulfil the requirement – I would like my citizenship’,” he said. “But again, this decision is not final, so we don’t yet know the final outcome.”
In any case, Bärlund will still have to show that she meets all the other requirements for citizenship. She just took a Swedish test to be able to demonstrate her knowledge of the language, but she doesn’t know when she might get a chance to sit the civics test.
“I have mixed feelings. I feel good in the sense that someone would feel if they won something, but I don’t feel relieved. I don’t feel overjoyed, simply because I know it’s (...) go

items.title: OPINION: Sweden's Migration Agency is not fit for purpose. It should be scrapped
items.summary: An interview by the The Local's Richard Orange with the Migration Agency's legal chief about Sweden’s large number of deportations of British people makes for depressing reading. It demonstrates why the agency is no longer capable of doing its job and now needs to be replaced, argues James Savage.
items.body_text:
Sweden has deported more British people than any other EU country.
These were people who had moved to Sweden under EU freedom of movement, who had made their lives here, who were often extremely well-integrated and had half-forgotten that they weren’t technically Swedish. People whom the EU and Britain had promised could stay, and who were nonetheless kicked out.
In her interview with Richard Orange, Migration Agency legal chief Susanne Fonsell comes across at times as evasive.
At one point she tries to deflect Richard’s questioning by claiming, hilariously, that she’s “not a specialist” on applying the Brexit migration rules. But if the head of legal at an EU country’s immigration authority is not a specialist on applying EU immigration law, who on earth is?
But the interview was also revealing of the agency’s culture: it sees its job is to be a control agency, not a service agency.
Brits who lived in Sweden prior to Brexit kept rights that were already theirs.
That contrasts with asylum and family reunification, the cases the Migration Agency is used to dealing with, which work the other way round. There, the state grants permission — and in the past decade the state has been turning the screws to make this harder.
It’s clear from her interview that this culture has pervaded all aspects of the agency’s work.
Fonsell also demonstrates a peculiar understanding of proportionality. Under EU rules, her agency was not permitted to deny Brits residency permits if to do so would have been disproportionate. But in response to our question about proportionality she protests that “the legal system must be based on rules and not emotion”.
And so, she seems to effectively dismiss the whole legal concept of proportionality as being a matter of emotions.
If the failures at the Migration Agency were limited to Brexit it would be a short-term problem: incredibly, cases are still emerging, but in a year or two they will stop as Britain’s exit from the EU recedes into the rear-view mirror.
But the incompetence over Brexit is only a symptom of a wider malaise.
For years, The Local has been highlighting the Migration Agency's failures: its staff regularly give incorrect advice to work permit and citizenship applicants, it issues deportation orders over minor admin errors, even when those concerned are willing to correct them.
It repeatedly denies people the right to stay, or even citizenship, for being in Sweden illegally — even when the only reason their permit has expired is that the agency has let their case sit in a pile for too long.
Most Swedish parties want Sweden to limit the numbers of refugees and discourage low-skilled migration. At the same time they actively want high-skilled immigrants. They also have a duty to apply EU law correctly and to give Swedes who fall in love abroad the chance to bring their partners home.
It is clear that the current system is not set up to do all of this at once. The Migration Agency gives shoddy advice, lets cases pile up and then issues rejections on technicalities, even when those rejections are clearly disproportionate. The Migration Courts act as industrial-scale rubber-stampers of agency decisions.
Here, Brexit is an excellent illustrative example: the courts haven’t referred a single Brexit case to the European Court of Justice, despite the fact that important points of EU law are at stake.
Absurdly, the Migration Court of Appeal will only take up cases if they set a precedent, a rule it interprets so narrowly that we are not aware of a single Brexit case that has been heard there.
The agency would presumably point to the fact that it is underfunded. It would also say that it is only applying the law. But how agencies apply the law, how they treat the people that interact with them, is also a matter of culture.
And the culture of the Migration Agency is one of control, when many of its tasks demand a culture of service. The current system is no longer fit for purpose.

items.title: Inside Germany: How joining sports clubs helped me find my place in Berlin
items.summary: Sports clubs have a knack for turning strangers into locals. In this week's Inside Germany, journalist Tom Pugh explains how playing football and tennis helped him find a home in Berlin.
items.body_text:
When I moved from London to Berlin in 2008, I had a single contact in the city, a friend of a friend who agreed to meet me for a drink.
On the evening we met he brought along another friend who mentioned that he played for a hobby football team that trained on Sunday afternoons close to Schönhauser Allee in Prenzlauer Berg. They were always on the lookout for players, he said.
Looking back, a surprising amount of my life today can be traced back to that conversation.
At the time I wasn't looking for a wife or children or a way to integrate into German society. I just wanted a kick-about.
One of the advantages of sport when you're new to a country is that it requires so much less language than many other activities. Had I been invited to join a book club or take part in amateur dramatics, I’m sure I’d have spent the evening staring blankly into space and never gone back.
Football was easier.
I began to feel at home in Berlin – and at home with the people in Germany – running up and down a football pitch, trying to develop that almost telepathic understanding with teammates that allows you to deliver a perfect pass or get on the end of a cross.
I also think it’s the only time I’ve ever improved my German without making a conscious effort to do so.
Geh Drauf! (Press!), Zum Ball! (Go to the ball), Hintermann! (Man on!) – my first German phrases all came with exclamation marks.
READ ALSO: 'Vereine' - How you can start your own club in Germany
The process was so automatic I didn’t register what was happening until a trip back to the UK when I went to watch England play Germany with a group of friends.
I didn't realise I was shouting at the television in German until people I’d known for years started shuffling away from me.
I should stress I was shouting for England. As much as I love Germany, football allegiances are for life. But my non-German-speaking friends had no way of knowing that.
I should also stress that while I don’t quite have two left feet, I’m no great catch when it comes to football. Fortunately, Germany's Vereinskultur, its long-standing culture of clubs or associations, seems just as willing to reward the simple act of showing up as any actual sporting ability.
Building a life
Apart from the odd, awkward moment, my very amateur football career in Germany was a joy. Beyond the pleasure of just playing, I also travelled to new parts of the city, went up against legendary clubs like SC Tasmania 1900 Berlin (still famous for having conceded more goals than any other team in a single Bundesliga season back in 1965/66) and nearly came to blows with a Green Party team over a dodgy penalty decision.
But undoubtedly the moment which had the greatest impact on my life came on the day a teammate introduced me to the woman who would become my wife.
For years, football remained a constant. Even after our first child arrived, I managed to keep playing semi-regularly.
But when the second came along and we moved to another part of Berlin, disappearing for hours at a time to play football became increasingly difficult.
READ ALSO: Jugger to Sporthocking - Six off-the-wall German sports everybody should try
Eventually, though, the children got older and more independent, and I suddenly felt that familiar yearning to chase a ball again.
I briefly considered returning to football, but bones don't get stronger with age and I’ll admit I’d lost my nerve a little.
My second sporting life
Most days, between work and the school run, I walked past the gate of a tennis club in Kreuzberg. I’d played the game as a child and managed to persuade them to take me on as a member. Within weeks, I was happily obsessed with my new hobby.
My German is obviously much better now, but I don’t think I talk with my tennis buddies much more than I did with my football teammates. We don’t need to know that much about each other. We don't work together. We're not related and we don't see each other at parents' evenings.

items.title: 'Prost!': A short history of the German Kneipe
items.summary: Somewhere between a pub, a dive bar and a community living room, the mighty Kneipe is a ubiquitous cultural cornerstone in Germany. Here's a pint-sized guide to its history.
items.body_text:
If you've spent any amount of time in Germany, from the biggest cities to the smallest villages, you will have encountered one – the lace-curtained windows, the faded gold lettering and the cast of characters murmuring Prost (cheers) around their Stammtisch (regulars' table) – the German Kneipe is an institution.
But as the skylines of our cities shift under the weight of glass-fronted developments and the younger generation swaps pilsner for matcha, Kneipenkultur could well be entering its most challenging phase yet.
A tight squeeze
Sitting somewhere between a traditional pub and a dive bar, the term Kneipe emerged in the 18th century as a shorthand for Kneipschenke.
The name is rooted in the verb kneipen; literally "to press together". These were premises so cramped that guests had no choice but to sit shoulder-to-shoulder.
At this time, beer was primarily the drink of the lower classes, consumed in modest local taverns. But the Kneipe was never just about alcohol alone. In the 19th century, these premises were vital refuges for the labour movement.
During the era of the Anti-Socialist Laws, they became central political spaces where the resistance could meet under the guise of a quiet pint.
READ ALSO: 'Beer is cheap and everywhere' - How Germany's drinking culture surprises foreigners
While you might hear more formal terms like Schankwirtschaft, Taverne or Spunten across Germany, Kneipe remains the definitive term.
But a word to the wise. While you may hear a Kneipe be referred to as a Lokal, the general term for a place to eat and drink, a Lokal is rarely a Kneipe. One serves simple drinks; the other serves three-course meals.
Germans, particularly those of a certain generation, take this distinction very seriously.
A shelter during tough times
In the early 20th century, Germany’s drinking culture formed the foundation for numerous livelihoods. Many people worked in the hospitality industry, and positions as innkeepers, waiters, beer drivers and brewers were common.
During the hyperinflation of the 1920s, Kneipen kept a roof over people’s heads in an even more immediate way.
"Bum pubs" or vagrant bars provided an alternative to police-monitored shelters. In unlit back rooms, the unemployed and "shady characters" would doze in armchairs, while early-morning trade in bread, potatoes and liquor took place before the city fully woke up.
Following the devastation of the Second World War, the Kneipe took on a new role as a symbol of Germany’s reconstruction. By the 1950s, you could find a pub on literally every corner on some city intersections.
They became vital community pillars in a country still lying in ruin and with a limited number of social spaces outside the home or workplace. Despite their increasing number and proximity to one another, patrons tended to stay loyal to their local pub.
READ ALSO: 10 fascinating facts you never knew about German beer
Gentrification and changing tastes
Today, statistics paint a sobering picture for the Kneipe. Between 2009 and 2015, the number of pubs and restaurants across Germany plummeted from nearly 36,700 to around 31,100.
Hamburg was at one time the leader in closures, losing 48.1 percent of its establishments in a decade, closely followed by Lower Saxony.
The reasons for the downturn are many and varied. People have been steadily drinking less beer since the 1970s, and younger generations are opting for different leisure activities over the smoke-filled corners of a traditional pub.
Rising rents, higher living costs and changing demographics are also dealing a heavy blow to the humble "corner pub" in favour of more profitable, high-end ventures.
READ ALSO: Everything you need know about Germany’s sacred 'Biergarten' culture
A space for community (and conflict)
Despite the decline, the Kneipe remains a central pillar of community identity for many. They are often the headquarters for local clubs, sports associations and neighbourhood groups, proudly displaying club flags and trophie

items.title: Indonesia proposes ASEAN journalistic copyright consultation forum
items.summary: Law Minister Supratman Andi Agtas proposed establishing an ASEAN Press Council consultation forum to align copyright ...
items.body_text:
Kabupaten Badung, Bali (ANTARA) - Law Minister Supratman Andi Agtas proposed establishing an ASEAN Press Council consultation forum to align copyright protection for journalistic works with digital regulatory developments.
"Through sustained dialogue, mutual trust, and concrete action, ASEAN can foster a digital environment that respects rights, supports responsible journalism, and serves the public interest," Agtas said in Badung District, Bali, on Saturday.
He made the remarks while attending the ASEAN Forum on the Protection of Journalistic Works in the Copyright Regime in the Digital Era.
Agtas stated that ASEAN nations must build a shared understanding that protected journalistic works require safeguarding while balancing public interest, freedom of expression, and information access.
This shared understanding does not require member states to adopt identical legal frameworks, according to the minister.
Instead, regional alignment requires agreement on core protection principles, respect for rights, and interest balancing among journalists, media organizations, digital users, and the public.
Agtas emphasized that cross-border cooperation is crucial to enhancing the interconnectivity of regional copyright systems.
Effective linkage requires aligned information on rights holders, licensing mechanisms, usage records, and remuneration arrangements across borders.
Through information exchange, the identification of best practices, and technical cooperation, ASEAN nations are expected to reduce barriers to rights identification and facilitate the cross-border use of journalistic works while respecting each country's national laws.
Agtas noted that the forum is expected to yield three concrete outcomes. First, a shared understanding at the ASEAN level regarding the importance of copyright protection for journalistic works.
Second, preliminary recommendations to strengthen cross-border cooperation and system interconnectivity, including through information exchange and the identification of best practices.
Third, a follow-up framework to encourage the transparent use of journalistic work and fair remuneration, thereby supporting the sustainability of the journalism profession and a healthy digital information ecosystem.
He hopes the forum's outcomes will serve as a foundation for ongoing dialogue and practical, measurable technical cooperation, while respecting the national laws of each ASEAN member state.
“Indonesia believes that ASEAN has ample scope to strengthen cooperation in this area. We do not need identical rules to achieve our shared goals,” Agtas said.

items.title: Jakarta government manages 367 disability-friendly health facilities
items.summary: Jakarta Governor Pramono Anung Wibowo said that the provincial health office oversees 31 public hospitals and 336 ...
items.body_text:
Jakarta (ANTARA) - Jakarta Governor Pramono Anung Wibowo said that the provincial health office oversees 31 public hospitals and 336 community health centers (puskesmas) that have been designated disability-friendly.
"Jakarta has 44 puskesmas, 31 hospitals, and 292 supporting puskesmas, all of which are friendly to people with disabilities," he said during the Special Kids Expo (SPEKIX) 2026 in Senayan, Central Jakarta, on Saturday.
He added that Jakarta is among the few regions in Indonesia where all government-run healthcare facilities are disability-friendly.
"Not many provinces provide comprehensive health services [to people with disabilities]," Pramono affirmed.
The governor also highlighted the White Troops program, describing it as an initiative designed to serve older adults and residents with disabilities, including children.
"There are a total of 584 White Troops personnel tasked with providing services from one village to another," he said, noting that the program is intended to improve access to ambulances and other public services.
Women's Empowerment and Child Protection Minister Arifatul Choiri Fauzi praised the Jakarta administration for setting an example through concrete efforts to create a more inclusive environment for children, including through pilot projects.
She expressed her ministry's commitment to continuing collaboration with the provincial government and SPEKIX organizers on strategic initiatives.
"Let us synergize and take further steps to create bridges and solutions for the needs of our children," Fauzi said.
The minister also voiced her appreciation for parents caring for children with disabilities.
"Being parents to children with disabilities is not easy. Nevertheless, we must be grateful. To fathers and mothers, keep in mind that you are not alone; let us do this together," she said, assuring them of the government's support.

items.title: Eight orangutans rescued from W Kalimantan fires released into wild
items.summary: Eight Bornean orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus) rescued from forest and land fires in Ketapang and North Kayong districts in ...
items.body_text:
Bengkayang, West Kalimantan (ANTARA) - Eight Bornean orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus) rescued from forest and land fires in Ketapang and North Kayong districts in West Kalimantan were released into the Batu Nyambu Protected Forest in Ketapang District.
"Amid forest and land fires that are still ongoing, we are faced with a difficult situation," Indonesian Nature Rehabilitation Initiative Foundation (YIARI) Operations Director Argitoe Ranting said in a statement on Saturday.
He noted that many orangutans have lost their habitat, while safe forest areas capable of accommodating them remain limited.
Batu Nyambu Protected Forest was selected as the release site due to its adequate ecological carrying capacity, covering approximately 23,000 hectares with primary and secondary canopy cover, abundant food and water sources, roaming space, and connectivity with adjacent forest corridors.
The eight orangutans comprise three mother-and-offspring pairs and two juvenile males, all rescued from fire-impacted locations across Ketapang and North Kayong between August and September 2026.
One pair, Mama Man and her offspring, Man, were evacuated from Tempurukan Village in Ketapang District. They had been monitored since mid-June 2026 in residents' plantations bordering the forest, and were evacuated on September 3 after the fire moved closer to their habitat.
The four other orangutans, Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, along with two juvenile males named Naufal and Nopan, were rescued from Pemangkat Village in North Kayong District on Sept. 4, 2026. They had survived in coconut and rubber plantations after the fire burned down the forest and cut off the corridors connecting areas.
Meanwhile, Mama Lifa and her offspring Lifa were rescued on Sept. 18, 2026, from Pelang Village in Matan Hilir Selatan Sub-district, Ketapang District, where they were found isolated among a plot of about 400 square meters acacia trees surrounded by oil palm plantations.
Prior to release, all eight orangutans underwent health checks, medical care as needed, and observation at YIARI's rehabilitation facility in Sungai Awan, Ketapang. All the animals were reported to be healthy and still showed natural behavior.
Moving them to the release site required about six hours by land, followed by one hour by boat and around two hours on foot.
"The release was carried out in turns at several points about 80 meters apart to minimize disturbance to the animals," Ranting said.

items.title: With power bills already high, Meralco wins approval to raise own fees after 15 years
items.summary: After its first rate review in 15 years, Meralco has won regulatory approval to raise its distribution charges even after already posting a record P51.13 billion in profits in 2025
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- Meralco customers will experience higher electricity bills due to a distribution rate increase approved by regulators, marking the first hike in 15 years.
- The new average distribution rate will rise from P1.35 to P1.48 per kilowatt-hour, impacting household budgets already strained by inflation and rising living costs.
- Despite the rate increase, Meralco reported record profits and continues to pursue modernization projects, while the government is under pressure to lower electricity costs.
MANILA, Philippines – Meralco customers will face higher electricity bills after regulators approved the utility’s first distribution rate increase in 15 years, pushing up already-high energy costs and further tightening household budgets strained by rising food, fuel, and other living expenses.
The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) approved a new average distribution rate of P1.48 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), up from the existing P1.35 per kWh, an increase of around 13 centavos. The actual increase will depend on the final residential rate, though Meralco has yet to clarify how exactly this will raise consumer bills.
The regulator and Meralco has also not mentioned when the new rate will reflect in consumer electricity bills.
Meralco’s overall residential electricity rate already stood at P14.7424 per kWh in September, meaning a household consuming 200 kWh already paid nearly P2,950 monthly. This is before the latest rate hike was factored in.
The distribution charge accounts for only one portion of the electricity bill, alongside generation, transmission, taxes, and other charges. However, it is the portion that actually goes to Meralco to cover its distribution operations and earn a profit.
Meralco’s distribution rates were last reviewed in 2011 and have effectively been frozen since 2015, as successive ERC administrations did not complete regular rate reviews. The prolonged delays kept the utility from raising its distribution charges.
Meralco originally asked for P532 billion in revenue requirement over four years, but the ERC cut this to P342 billion, 36% less than what the energy giant asked for. Even with this reduction, the approved distribution rate is still higher than what customers currently pay.
“We trimmed capital projects that were not yet justified, disallowed excessive operating costs and bad debt provisions, removed contingencies and duplicated assets from the asset base, and used a lower return on capital than what Meralco proposed,” ERC Chairperson Francis Juan said in a statement.
“The approved revenue gives Meralco a clear path to operate more efficiently and to roll out the capital projects needed for a more reliable network, including new substations and lines, modernized metering, and measures to bring down system loss. Meralco will be held to delivering these results,” he added.
Meralco, in a statement on Saturday, October 10, said it had yet to receive the full decision and would need to review it before determining its implications for the company and customers.
“We believe that this will allow Meralco to move forward with greater clarity as we pursue investments and initiatives to modernize our distribution network and enhance service delivery,” Jose Ronald Valles, Meralco’s head of regulatory management, said in a statement, pointing to investments in advanced metering infrastructure, cybersecurity, and other network modernization projects.
The increase comes as inflation soared to 7.2% in September, with faster price increases in food, transportation, electricity, and other household expenses.
Record profits even before latest hike
The higher distribution rate also comes as Meralco continues to earn record profits.
The company reported a record P50.6 billion in core profit in 2025. In the first half of 2026, its consolidated core net income reached P26.5 billion, up 3.8% from a year earlier.
The rate approval also comes just days after Manuel Pangilinan-led Metro Pacific Investments Corporation

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.
There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.
Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

items.title: #CourageON: A river in Cebu remembers
items.summary: The river has wisdom. If you walk slow enough to listen, then you learn that water always finds a way.
items.body_text:
AT A GLANCE
- Chris L. Villarino, an environmental advocate, shares his experience of a river walk in Cebu organized by the Cebu Citizens Initiative, highlighting the importance of respecting nature.
- During the walk, a team leader suffered an injury, which shifted the group's focus from leisure to the reality of nature's challenges, emphasizing the need for humility and community support.
- The experience reinforced the idea that environmental advocacy is not just theoretical but requires real engagement with nature, as they prepare for the upcoming #MoveCebu event aimed at promoting civic action and environmental resilience.
Hello, I am Chris L. Villarino. I am a tree hugger, having survived Super Typhoon Yolanda by hugging a tree in Tacloban. Since then, I have dedicated my life around advocacy for the environment by engaging individuals, organizations and communities through forest and watershed walk, wellness and regenerative activities in Cebu. 
We followed the water upstream; narrow, overgrown, stones covered in moss, plastic in some corners. But the river is still alive, still flowing. At some point, the water was knee deep.
They say that Cebu used to have a river like this. But now, the rivers are buried in culverts and flood control projects. Easily, we forgot the rivers. But as they say, the river never forgot us.
The river has wisdom. If you walk slow enough to listen, then you learn that water always finds a way. Even when choked with trash, blocked by concrete, the water still finds its way down to the sea. Just like life.
But during this walk, the river taught us its hardest lesson.
On a slippery stretch, our dear team leader had a bad fall; hard, face-first onto stones and sand. In a second, the laughter turned to blood, shock, and silence. He was hurt badly — needed stitches and emergency care.
We cared for him. Good thing we had an emergency kit (thanks Agence France!). We could not call for help. We were deep in the river ravine having walked more than an hour. At that moment, the leisurely walk became real.
And I realized: this is exactly what we did to our rivers.
We walked fast, distracted, taking a lot of pictures, looking at our phones, at the view. We forgot the river is not a backdrop. It is alive. It has sharp stones. It demands respect, presence, and slowness.
We also learned what community means. No one was left behind. Hands reached out. Someone held his head. Someone cleaned the blood. Someone prayed. Someone acted as buddy and walked the way back with him (thank you to our friend Karsten!).
The forest that felt so quiet suddenly felt like family.
He is okay now — stitched, resting, healing (driving around the city doing his work). We are grateful it wasn’t worse but the whole experience gave me an important life lesson.
He fell for all of us, in a way. A reminder that rewilding and re-rivering — whether through watershed walks, building urban pocket forests inspired by Laudate Deum, or carrying out the Handuraw Panaw project — is not just a nice workshop concept. It’s real terrain. It will wound you if you don’t walk with humility, much like surviving nature’s wildest forces as a tree hugger clinging to hope and life during Super Typhoon Yolanda.
Going for a river walk is not just going to a waterfall for Instagram or Facebook. It’s not for the faint of heart. It’s going back to our source.
Thank you Rappler, Jene Pangue, and John Sitchon for walking with us, for being brave, for teaching us courage and walking the talk. Thank you everyone for not leaving when it got hard.
I look forward to carrying this spirit forward into our upcoming partnership with Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH for #MoveCebu: Sugbo alang sa mga Sugboanon event this October 14–16, where fellow advocates, community leaders, and storytellers will gather to move together towards environmental resilience and civic action.
The river remembers. – Rappler.com

items.title: Gatchalian: No 'standard practice' of leaving Senate rooms bare
items.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman inspected the Senate office that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada stripped bare before handing it over to Sen. Tito Sotto, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian confirmed Saturday, October 10.
items.body_text:
Gatchalian: No 'standard practice' of leaving Senate rooms bare
MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman inspected the Senate office that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada stripped bare before handing it over to Sen. Tito Sotto, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian confirmed Saturday, October 10.
Gatchalian said the anti-graft office wrote him asking permission to inspect the room, after which a representative of the Ombudsman went to the Senate to check the facilities on Thursday, October 8.
"Wala naman silang sinabi kung ano 'yung pakay, but obviously naman 'yun, Ombudsman eh," Gatchalian said in an interview with DZMM. (They did not say what they were after, but that's obvious. It's the Ombudsman.)
Videos that spread online on Monday, October 5, the turnover deadline, showed the sixth-floor room stripped of most of its floor tiles and wall panels.
The room is reserved for the Senate president pro tempore, a post Estrada held from May 2024 to September 2025 under then-Senate President Chiz Escudero. Lacson and Sen. Loren Legarda, who later held the post, did not move in, and Estrada kept the room until he vacated it this month.
Images and clips also showed wires hanging from the walls and ceiling and electrical sockets pulled out, and what appears to be the removal of the toilet bowl, shower and pantry sink.
Gatchalian said he ordered the Senate secretary to cooperate with the Ombudsman, as the chamber does the same with the Philippine National Police and the National Bureau of Investigation.
The Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms assisted the Ombudsman's representative, who looked over the facility and the office.
Gatchalian said the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS), which owns the office as it is their building where the Senate is housed, also inspected the room a few days earlier after seeing photos of it.
The GSIS had been "concerned with the structural integrity" of the facility, Gatchalian said.
'Walang standard practice na ganoon'
Gatchalian rejected the claim of Estrada's camp that leaving a vacated office bare is standard practice in the Senate.
"Wala namang standard practice na ganoon. Ang standard practice ay pagbibigay-respeto sa isa't isa," he said. (There is no such standard practice. The standard practice is respect for one another.)
When Gatchalian moved offices in 2016, he said, then-Sen. Koko Pimentel asked whether he wanted the room as it was.
Sotto also asked whether he wanted the furniture when he vacated the Senate president's office on Friday, Gatchalian said.
Sotto ended up leaving the office as it was, down to his own chair and desk, which Gatchalian had expected him to take.
Gatchalian, whose term ends in 2028, said he would change only the work area for his staff to accommodate their larger number.
Asked if he was disappointed by Estrada's actions, Gatchalian said he was. "Nakita n'yo naman 'yung picture, bare na bare," he said. (You saw the picture. It was completely bare.)
He said Sotto would need considerable time to renovate the office and that the Senate would help in doing so.
"Sana nagkaroon ng magandang pag-uusap, sana nagkaroon ng magandang coordination para hindi made-delay 'yung paglipat ni Senator Sotto at hindi nagagastos ang gobyerno," Gatchalian said. (There should have been proper talks and coordination so Senator Sotto's move would not be delayed and the government would not have to spend money for this.)
In a statement Tuesday, Estrada's office said most of the removed items, including floor tiles, glass panels, lighting fixtures and cabinets, were bought with his personal funds because the Senate's budget for the office fell short.
It said "not a single centavo" of public funds was wasted and that the resident Commission on Audit auditor had been informed.
The statement said Estrada's chief of staff, lawyer Racquel Mejia, told Sotto's camp before the deadline that the fixtures and furnishings would be moved to Estrada's new office. It also claimed the room was already b

items.title: CALABARZON minimum wage earners get up to P45 daily raise
items.summary: Minimum wage earners in CALABARZON will get up to P45 more a day starting October 26, the region’s wage board announced Saturday, October 10.
items.body_text:
CALABARZON minimum wage earners get up to P45 daily raise
MANILA, Philippines — Minimum wage earners in CALABARZON will get up to P45 more a day starting October 26, the region’s wage board announced Saturday, October 10.
The raise, worth as much as P1,170 a month, will cover more than 1.56 million minimum wage earners across the region, according to the National Wages and Productivity Commission.
Not every worker will get the full P45 as the increase depends on the worker’s industry and on how the city or town where they work is classified, based on Wage Order No. IVA-23.
The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board 4A did not include that breakdown in its announcement. It said the rates per sector and area are listed in the official copy of the order.
The regional board and the NWPC, both made up of labor, employer and government representatives, approved the rates after reviewing the region’s economic and social conditions, as required by Republic Act 6727 or the Wage Rationalization Act.
Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino, who chairs the commission, led the meeting that set the new rates.
Tolentino said the Department of Labor and Employment’s CALABARZON office will closely monitor establishments to make sure they comply.
The new order follows Wage Order No. IVA-22, which raised daily pay in the region by P25 to P100 in two tranches, on Oct. 5, 2025 and April 1 this year.
Daily minimum wages in CALABARZON currently range from P508 to P600, depending on the sector and the municipality’s classification.
Prices at three-year high
The raise comes as inflation rose to 7.2% in September from 6.1% in August, matching April’s rate and the fastest since March 2023, the Philippine Statistics Authority reported.
Rice inflation climbed to a high 20.3%, and inflation among the poorest 30% of households reached 9%.

items.title: ICC allows seven more drug war incidents in Duterte case
items.summary: The International Criminal Court has allowed prosecutors to add seven killings to the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, but struck out an eighth because it fell outside the time period of the charge it was filed under.
items.body_text:
ICC allows seven more drug war incidents in Duterte case
MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court has allowed prosecutors to add seven more incidents to the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, but struck out an eighth because it fell outside the time period of the charge it was filed under.
In the same October 9 decision, the ICC Trial Chamber III also rejected a defense request to order the prosecutors to rewrite the charges against Duterte as a closed list of killings. Duterte’s lawyers had argued that because the prosecutors treat the listed incidents as examples, he cannot know which specific incidents he will have to answer for at his trial, which opens November 30.
The ruling brings the Duterte case's incident count to 56. The 49 incidents confirmed by the Pre-Trial Chamber in April charge Duterte with 76 murders and two attempted murders. The public version of this latest decision does not say how many murders or attempted murders are in the seven new incidents.
Police reported at least 6,252 deaths in anti-drug operations during Duterte's presidency, but rights groups estimate the true number is up to 30,000, including vigilante-style killings.
The charges
Duterte faces three counts, or separate charges, of murder as a crime against humanity.
Prosecutors must prove each count on its own and the judges are expected to rule on each separately, so Duterte could be convicted on one and acquitted on another. The counts are divided by time period and by type of killing.
- Count 1 covers killings in Davao City from 2013 to around June 2016, while Duterte was mayor. Prosecutors attribute these killings to the Davao Death Squad, which it accuses Duterte of having ultimate command over. This count lists 19 people killed in Incidents 1 to 9.
- Count 2 covers killings of "high-value targets," or alleged major drug figures, from July 2016 to July 2017, Duterte's first year as president. The count lists 14 people killed in Incidents 10 to 14.
- Count 3 covers killings of low-level suspects in police raids to clear barangays of drugs as part of "Oplan Tokhang," from July 2016 to September 2018. It lists 43 people killed and two who survived in Incidents 15 to 49, and is the only count that also charges attempted murder.
The eight new incidents
Prosecutors gave notice of Incidents 50 to 57 on August 31, the deadline the chamber set in May, and detailed them in their trial brief filed September 4.
On September 11, the defense asked the ICC judges to strike them or make prosecutors seek the Pre-Trial Chamber's approval, arguing that all eight involved new locations, victims, perpetrators and dates.
The chamber admitted Incidents 50 to 55 under Count 3 and Incident 56 under Count 2. It found that each falls within its count's time period and within the charges' scope of "locations across the Philippines."
However, the judges decided to reject Incident 57, filed under Count 2, because it falls outside the July 2016 to July 2017 period that Count 2 covers.
Witnesses for the new incidents are not expected to testify in the first months of the trial, and the chamber told both sides to ensure none is called before the defense has had reasonable time to prepare.
Request to refile charges rejected
Lead defense counsel Peter Haynes argued in an August 31 motion that charges built on "illustrative" and "non-exhaustive" incidents violate Duterte's right under the Rome Statute to be told in detail what he is charged with. He called the charges a "moving target" and asked the chamber to order prosecutors to refile them before the Pre-Trial Chamber with a complete list of acts.
However, in its decision, the chamber's judges said they have no power to do that as only the prosecutor can seek to change confirmed charges, and only with the Pre-Trial Chamber's permission.

items.title: HCMC teen with IELTS 9.0 and top English awards for gifted students chooses teaching career
items.summary: Winning first and second prizes in Vietnam's national English competition for gifted students, along with achieving a perfect IELTS score of 9.0, has earned a 12th grader direct admission to Ho Chi Minh City University of Education.
items.body_text:
Nguyen Tuan Phong is a former English major at Tran Dai Nghia High School for the Gifted in Ho Chi Minh City.
He is currently enrolled in the university's English language teacher education program.
He said he began considering a career in teaching early in 10th grade, after being selected for the national English competition team and winning second prize.
The achievement motivated him but also brought considerable pressure. Phong repeatedly questioned whether he could continue improving and maintain his performance.
Encouraged and inspired by the teachers who coached the competition team, he gradually regained his confidence and went on to win first prize in the competition for two consecutive years.
"I also want to become a friendly teacher with strong professional knowledge who inspires students, just like the teachers I have learned from," Phong said.
Phong took the IELTS test in 11th grade to strengthen his university application.
Because the test came immediately after the national English competition, he did not have much time to prepare and aimed for a score of 8.0.
He was therefore surprised to receive a perfect score.
"I couldn't believe my eyes. I thought the sheet showing a score of 9.0 was just a sample result. Only after reading it carefully did I confirm that it was actually mine," he said.
Phong said he had been exposed to English since the age of four and continued taking classes at language centers until the end of middle school.
Initially, he was eager to learn English so he could watch foreign reality shows, movies, and cartoons.
Over time, he shifted toward scientific content and materials related to his school curriculum.
English, to him, became a "gateway" that opened up a more diverse and expansive world.
Phong believes that practical application is essential to mastering a language. He regularly practices speaking English with classmates and native speakers whenever he has the opportunity.
In his view, learning a foreign language requires perseverance, and every small improvement deserves recognition.
"Don't put too much pressure on yourself or set too many goals. Haste makes waste, and the more stressed you are, the harder it becomes to absorb new knowledge," Phong said.
Tran Kim Duyen, head of the foreign languages department at Tran Dai Nghia High School for the Gifted, coached Phong for several years.
She described him as a well-rounded student who demonstrated creative thinking, independent learning skills, and a willingness to learn from teachers and peers without becoming arrogant.
"Phong is confident, independent and always willing to support those around him. He also helps teachers organize extracurricular activities," she said.
Building on his high school experience, Phong hopes to take part in a wide range of activities during his four years at university while striving for strong academic results.
He aims to become an English teacher at the high school level.
Vietnamese students currently take the same national high school graduation exams, but universities maintain their own admission standards.
Institutions are allowed to award additional points, or grant direct admission, to applicants for academic awards, language certificates such as IELTS or SAT, or extracurricular achievements.
However, the Ministry of Education and Training recently proposed eliminating university admission bonus points for IELTS certificates and excellent student awards starting next year.

items.summary: A 54-year-old renovation contractor from Malaysia's Sarawak state has won RM10.17 million (US$2.49 million) in a lottery jackpot on two numbers he said were inspired by a dream.
items.body_text:
He hit the Toto 4D Jackpot 1 in the Sept. 26 draw with the numbers 8622 and 5765, Malaysian daily The Sun reported.
"It was just the second time I bet on these numbers. I never expected the numbers to bring me such a huge win. It is something that I am still taking in," he said in a statement issued on Oct. 7 by STM Lottery, which runs the Sports Toto games.
The winner, a father of two who was not named, has been a Sports Toto customer for more than 30 years and spends about RM50 ($12) a week on the Toto 4D Jackpot, according to The Borneo Post.
Ticket bought over lunch
He was having lunch near one of his renovation sites when he noticed a Sports Toto outlet beside the restaurant, Free Malaysia Today reported.
"Something made me decide to buy the same numbers again. I did not think much of it at the time," he said.
He checked the results on the Sports Toto website that night and appeared calm and relaxed when he claimed the prize at STM Lottery's head office in Kuala Lumpur.
The payout was RM10,169,557.55, plus a System Play bonus of RM672, according to The Star.
"I intend to keep the money prudently and set aside a portion for the future well-being of my children. I believe it is important to plan carefully before making any major decisions," he said when asked about his plans for the winnings, The Sun reported.
STM Lottery, formerly Sports Toto Malaysia, is a subsidiary of Sports Toto Berhad and offers eight games drawn three days a week, according to the group's corporate profile.

items.title: Suspects flee country after B37m robbery of Turk in Pattaya
items.summary: Police are seeking help from Chinese authorities and Interpol to arrest five suspects who fled Thailand within hours after robbing a Turkish businessman of cryptocurrency, cash and valuables worth 37 million baht at his luxury home in Pattaya.
items.body_text:
Police are seeking help from Chinese authorities and Interpol to arrest five suspects who fled Thailand within hours after robbing a Turkish businessman of cryptocurrency, cash and valuables worth 37 million baht at his luxury home in Pattaya.
The robbery took place at about 3.30am on Oct 6, when three men dressed in black and wearing face coverings, armed with guns and knives, broke into a luxury residence at a housing estate in tambon Nong Prue of Bang Lamung district in Chon Buri.
The armed men reportedly threatened and assaulted Turkish businessman Kutay Aslan, 34, and a Myanmar cleaner before restraining them with handcuffs.
The gang forced the businessman to give them $824,000 in Tether cryptocurrency (USDT), 210,000 baht in cash, five Rolex watches and four mobile phones, with a combined worth of more than 37 million baht, before fleeing the scene.
Following the incident, investigators reviewed CCTV footage along the escape route and identified a Toyota Fortuner believed to be linked to the crime. The vehicle was subsequently found abandoned on Jomtien Soi 9 in Pattaya.
The officers examined the vehicle and collected 14 pieces of evidence, including balaclavas, gloves, clothing, footwear and an aluminium ladder, for forensic analysis. (Story continues below)
Images compiled from CCTV by police show the house of the robbery victim (1), the abandoned getaway car (2) and various other views of the suspects.
The investigators also pursued leads from witness statements, vehicle GPS data, car and accommodation rental records, hotel check-in information and suspects’ immigration records. They compared clothing details with the recovered evidence before identifying five suspects allegedly linked to the robbery.
The suspects were identified as Dong Ping, 38, who reportedly arranged car and accommodation rentals; Lixinle, 31; Wang Hongbo, 32; Mu Hongda, 33; and Zhiyu Wang, 31.
On Friday, investigators submitted evidence to the Pattaya Provincial Court, which approved arrest warrants for all five suspects.
The charges include armed robbery at night, property damage, using a vehicle in the commission of a crime, and causing physical or psychological harm to others.
The suspects also faced charges of detaining or confining others and depriving them of their liberty, and firearms-related offences.
However, subsequent checks of travel records showed that all five suspects had left Thailand within about six hours of the robbery.
Police are coordinating with the Chinese embassy and following procedures to seek Interpol Red Notices to locate the suspects and bring them to justice.
Police display evidence, including balaclavas, gloves, clothing, footwear and other items used by five suspects involved in the robbery of a Turkish businessman in Pattaya, in front of the Nong Prue police station on Saturday. (Photo: Provincial Police Region 2)

items.title: 11 foreign suspects arrested in nominee crackdown
items.summary: Authorities on Saturday launched the eighth phase of a crackdown on illegal foreign property ownership, raiding 17 locations at four luxury housing estates in Bangkok and arresting 11 suspects, including Chinese nationals, with assets worth more than 6 billion baht seized.
items.body_text:
Authorities on Saturday launched the eighth phase of a crackdown on illegal foreign property ownership, raiding 17 locations at four luxury housing estates in Bangkok and arresting 11 suspects, including Chinese nationals, with assets worth more than 6 billion baht seized.
National police chief Samran Nuanma led officers from the Immigration Bureau and Metropolitan Police Bureau in the operation, targeting foreigners who allegedly used Thai nominees to own houses and land.
The operation covered areas including Bang Na, Suan Luang, Rama IX, Srinakarin and Krungthep Kreetha.
Authorities had 86 arrest warrants for foreign suspects and arrested 11 people — 10 Chinese nationals and one American, Pol Gen Samran said at a media briefing.
The investigation was based on information shared by the Chinese embassy in Thailand concerning three suspects wanted by Chinese authorities.
The first suspect, identified only as Chao, held Chinese and Cambodian passports. He was wanted in connection with a murder case involving three deaths on Jan 30, 2018 in China.
Pol Gen Samran said investigators found that he was a business partner in a company holding houses and land in a luxury housing estate in the Rama IX-Srinakarin area, where properties were priced at 50 million to 69 million baht. He was also found to be linked to scam operations, said Pol Gen Samran.
The second suspect, Gui, held Chinese, Turkish and Cambodian passports. He was wanted in China for fraud and inducing people to cross borders illegally in April 2024, in Jinyun in southern Zhejiang province.
The third, Jian, held Chinese and Saint Kitts and Nevis passports and was wanted in connection with online fraud allegedly committed in December 2024 in Henan province.
The second and third suspects were found to be business partners in companies holding houses and land in a luxury housing estate in the Krungthep Kreetha area, where properties are priced at 77 million to 98 million baht. (Story continues below)
National police chief Samran Nuanma (seated, centre) gives details of the crackdown operation on foreign nominees following raids on 17 locations in Bangkok on Saturday. (Photo: Provincial Police Region 2)
95 nominee companies
Pol Gen Samran said authorities had also worked with local administrations, the Department of Business Development, the Department of Lands and the Revenue Department to investigate suspected nominee companies.
The investigation identified 95 companies suspected of using Thai nationals as nominees to own 94 houses and plots of land. It also found that two company partners were subject to Interpol Red Notices, while another was wanted under a warrant issued by the Phra Khanong Criminal Court. The three suspects were:
Mr Lin, a Chinese national and business partner in a company holding property in the Rama IX-Srinakarin area. He was wanted on an Interpol Red Notice issued on March 3, 2024, by authorities in Bengbu, Anhui province, for alleged involvement in an organised criminal group engaged in online fraud.
Mr Bai, a Chinese national and business partner in a company holding property in the Krungthep Kreetha area, was subject to an Interpol Red Notice issued on Aug 19, 2022, by authorities in Taiyuan, Shanxi, for alleged involvement in an organised criminal group engaged in online fraud.
Mr Huang, a Chinese national and business partner in a company holding property in the Bang Na-Ring Road area, wanted under a Phra Khanong Criminal Court warrant issued on May 25, 2023. The charges include importing goods without customs clearance, concealing or receiving goods connected to customs offences, involvement in a secret criminal society, and unlawful land ownership by a foreign national.

items.title: Hostages freed, but Gaza ceasefire’s biggest promises remain unmet
items.summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 10 — One year after US President Donald Trump declared the war in Gaza to be over, few of the long-...
items.body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 10 — One year after US President Donald Trump declared the war in Gaza to be over, few of the long-term promises of the ceasefire have come to fruition.
Here is a list of some of the key points of the October 10, 2025 ceasefire and where things stand:
Hostages released, calm in Israel
Three days after the agreement was announced, Hamas freed the 20 remaining living hostages seized during the group’s October 7, 2023 attack, the deadliest day in Israel’s history.
The captives’ return was a key priority for Israel, whose public had agonised over their fate.
The ceasefire anniversary also marks one year of quiet for Israel from the Gaza front, with no rocket attacks by Hamas.
The group’s missile inventory was depleted by near-constant Israeli bombardment, which damaged or destroyed the vast majority of buildings in the Palestinian territory.
The US military set up a command post with foreign allies near the Gaza border to monitor the truce.
No Israeli withdrawal or let-up
Israel has reduced its level of attacks but has kept striking Gaza on a near-daily basis.
Israeli strikes have killed some 1,450 Palestinians since the ceasefire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are considered accurate by the United Nations.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is in a tight election race, has vowed to kill everyone involved in the October 7 attack.
Netanyahu said on the attack’s anniversary that 4,000 out of 6,000 “Hamas monsters” had been killed.
Israeli forces were allowed to stay in 53 per cent of Gaza under the terms of the ceasefire, but a year later they control about 70 per cent of it, according to official accounts.
Hamas remains, with weapons
The second phase of the agreement was supposed to include a political transition away from Hamas, and technocrat Ali Shaath was appointed head of a new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
Hamas announced in July that it was disbanding its governing body and handing over Gaza’s administration to the US-blessed NCAG.
But Hamas effectively remains in charge of security in Gaza, and Shaath has taken a low profile.
The Palestinian Islamist movement elected a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, in July. Shortly afterwards, the group announced it would give up its weapons, a step hailed by Trump as a breakthrough.
But Israel has been sceptical, with Netanyahu demanding verifiable decommissioning of all weapons down to individual guns.
Hamas has not gone ahead with disarmament, and Israel has refused to reciprocate by starting to withdraw forces.
Reconstruction just talk
Trump set up a new global body for the deal dubbed the “Board of Peace”, tapping as key figures former British prime minister Tony Blair and Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov, who serves as “Gaza high representative”.
Trump, a critic of foreign aid, in January promised US$10 billion (RM41 billion) in US funding to the board he controls, and Gulf allies have pledged more, but no money is known to have made its way to Gaza reconstruction.
In September, the board proposed a US$2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan at a meeting of its members and stakeholders, in an effort meant to span over six months. — AFP

items.title: A year after Gaza ceasefire, families still queue hours for one meal a day
items.summary: KHAN YUNIS, Oct 10 — Every day, Gazan mother Niyaha al-Masri spends six exhausting hours or more queueing at a com...
items.body_text:
KHAN YUNIS, Oct 10 — Every day, Gazan mother Niyaha al-Masri spends six exhausting hours or more queueing at a community kitchen in the hope of getting some food for her family.
It has been a year since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was supposed to allow food to flood into the ruined territory, yet widespread hunger persists there.
Masri has little choice. Without the kitchen run by humanitarian groups, she and her eight children would have “nothing at all”, the 35-year-old told AFP.
Each day she sets out early in the morning and returns in the afternoon, this time bringing four containers of rice, lentils and a little chicken, which the family throws itself at.
Among them is her husband, wounded in both legs by an airstrike, meaning he “cannot go and fight with the others” to get food.
This will be the only meal of the day for the family of 10, living in a tent in Khan Yunis. There was no breakfast and they will have no dinner.
What little flour they have, Masri explained, has to be rationed.
In August 2025, a United Nations-backed body, the IPC, declared a state of famine in Gaza, though Israel quickly denounced it as a lie.
By December, the UN had lifted that declaration, saying that the ceasefire had allowed in enough supplies over the course of two months to ease conditions.
COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry organisation responsible for civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, told AFP that the humanitarian situation in Gaza was stable.
But Shaun Hughes, of the UN’s World Food Programme, was less sanguine.
The food security situation, he said, “is still extremely serious”.
The most recent figures, from July, show that “1.4 million out of the population of about 2.1 million people are acutely food insecure”, he said, with 200,000 of them “just one step below famine”.
‘Shameful’
While some food is getting in, a lack of sufficient nutritional variety continues to pose a health threat.
“Dietary diversity is a major food security issue in Gaza,” said Hughes.
“You cannot survive on dry goods and wheat flour and bread alone. Particularly children, particularly pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, they need the micronutrients that come with high protein foods, fresh vegetables, fresh fruits,” he explained.
Masri said that her children, aged between three and 14, “dream of eating fruit” but the family doesn’t have the means to buy any.
She said one of her sons suffered from malnutrition during the 2025 famine, although “little by little, his condition is improving”.
Malnutrition isn’t only caused by a lack of food, but also essential nutrients. It weakens the immune system of children, making them vulnerable to illnesses and stunting their growth.
“Repeated bouts of acute malnutrition amongst children is something that human beings just don’t recover from,” said Hughes.
Cognitive and physical impairments “continue into later life”, he added.
At Khan Yunis’s Nasser hospital, the head of the malnutrition unit, Israa al-Najjar, told AFP she had “observed an increase in syndromes and conditions” linked to malnutrition that affect the immune system.
In a report published on Thursday, the day after the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attack that sparked the Gaza war, Medecins du Monde published a study that found 93 per cent of pregnant or breastfeeding women had symptoms of anaemia, which is closely linked to malnutrition.
Just 17 per cent had a sufficiently varied diet to meet their nutritional needs, the group found.
All the while, Masri has kept visiting the community kitchen, despite asthma leaving her exhausted.
Her children spend their days collecting “pieces of nylon, bits of cardboard and chunks of foam” to try and reinforce their tent, which is in a poor state.
She said it was “shameful” that her children had to do so.
“I swear to God, this isn’t normal.” — AFP

items.title: Kremlin says Putin relayed Iran’s position to Trump, but gives no details
items.summary: MOSCOW, Oct 10 — Russian President Vladimir Putin has told Donald Trump about Iran’s position on a possible...
items.body_text:
MOSCOW, Oct 10 — Russian President Vladimir Putin has told Donald Trump about Iran’s position on a possible Mideast peace deal, the Kremlin said today.
The Kremlin said Tehran’s stance was relayed in a phone call held between the two leaders yesterday. It did not say how Trump responded, nor elaborate on Iran’s position.
Diplomatic efforts to end the more-than-seven-month-long Iran conflict, which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have been at an impasse since the summer.
Putin met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan earlier this week, where the Russian leader expressed an interest in helping broker peace.
“In coordination with the Iranian president, Putin conveyed the Iranian side’s views on a possible resolution to the conflict to Trump,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said today, according to Russia’s state RIA news agency.
The United States and Iran agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for ending their conflict, but Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz prompted a resumption of US military operations.
Recent indirect talks between Washington and Tehran on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly failed to produce a breakthrough. — AFP

items.title: Palmer signs Chelsea contract until 2034
items.body_text:
Palmer signs Chelsea contract until 2034
Oct 10 : Chelsea attacking midfielder Cole Palmer has signed a contract extension to keep him at Stamford Bridge until 2034, the Premier League club said on Saturday.
The 24-year-old England international has become a key figure since joining Chelsea from Manchester City in 2023, scoring 91 goals in 138 appearances across all competitions.
He was part of the squad that won the Club World Cup and UEFA Conference League.
"Speaking to the owners, to the sporting directors and obviously the manager, they gave me a lot of confidence so it was only right to sign," Palmer said.
"Speaking to players as well, everyone has the same ambitions. I feel like we win major trophies here consistently."
Chelsea have agreed long-term contracts Chelsea with several first-team players and emerging talent.
Forward Joao Pedro recently signed a deal through 2034, and winger Pedro Neto agreed a six-year contract last month.
Chelsea, 10th in the Premier League table, host Bournemouth on Saturday.

items.title: Verstappen wins Singapore sprint after chaotic start in wet conditions
items.body_text:
Verstappen wins Singapore sprint after chaotic start in wet conditions
SINGAPORE: Red Bull's Max Verstappen tasted victory in Singapore for the first time as the polesitter won a chaotic sprint on Saturday (Oct 10) after the start was delayed by over 30 minutes due to heavy rain while nine cars retired, a record for sprint races.
The victory was the first of any kind for the Dutchman in Singapore as he took the chequered flag ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc.
"I want to win tomorrow. I don't see this as a win in terms of actually winning a Grand Prix," Verstappen said.
Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli was gifted fourth place after the two McLarens collided on the final lap while his teammate George Russell crashed out of the lead on lap one.
The race was the first Formula 1 sprint race to be held in Singapore.
Verstappen had kept his pole position after escaping a penalty for overtaking under a yellow flag on Friday but the Dutchman made a slow start as Russell stormed ahead and Hamilton swiftly moved up from sixth to third.
Russell's sprint ended on the last turn of lap one when his rear tyre went over the kerb and he spun into the wall to bring the safety car out.
"The start was horrendous again, so that's definitely something that we need to improve on because if you have something like that tomorrow, that's your race over if nothing crazy happens," Verstappen added.
"After that, you just want to keep it calm and under control because you know that you can't pass around here."
'SILLY MISTAKE' FOR RUSSELL
Russell said a miscalculation caused him to spin out at the last corner.
"I came through the corner, had more battery deployment than I thought. Pushed me a little bit wider than I hoped and then I just went on the white line," Russell said.
"Yeah, silly mistake. Big, big consequences."
The carnage continued when Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez retired after they collided and Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was asked to stop his car due to a technical issue.
The safety car remained on track after Franco Colapinto's Alpine also came to a standstill and they did not resume racing until lap seven.
Verstappen led from the Ferraris of Hamilton and Leclerc while the McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were in the top five ahead of Antonelli.
MCLARENS COLLIDE ON FINAL LAP
McLaren's hopes of a podium vanished, however, when reigning champion Norris nudged into Piastri and the two cars spun out, allowing Antonelli to move up to fourth place and stretch his championship lead over Russell to 89 points.
"I checked in my mirrors and I saw red lights of the back of the cars of the McLarens. So I knew that something happened," Leclerc said.
The qualifying session for Sunday's race was delayed due to the rain.

items.title: 'Beyond the uniform': Singapore, Brunei officers share stories of lasting friendships as defence ties turn 50
items.summary: "We encouraged each other, learned from one another and, most importantly, knew that we were not navigating those challenges alone," says a Royal Brunei Air Force officer.
items.body_text:
'Beyond the uniform': Singapore, Brunei officers share stories of lasting friendships as defence ties turn 50
"We encouraged each other, learned from one another and, most importantly, knew that we were not navigating those challenges alone," says a Royal Brunei Air Force officer.
SINGAPORE: Amid long nights of military planning and discussions, Lieutenant Colonel (LTC) Shahreel Adam from the Singapore Army and Major (MAJ) Mahmud Afifi Mohd Kifli from the Royal Brunei Land Forces found common ground over their love of food and banter about weekly football scores.
The two officers, both now 37, first met in 2023 as coursemates at the Singapore Armed Forces' (SAF) Goh Keng Swee Command and Staff College.
They attended the Command and Staff Course, which brings together regular SAF officers, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs officers, and invited international officers with the ranks of Major, Lieutenant Colonel, Military Expert 5, Military Expert 6, and their equivalents.
LTC Shahreel remembers his Bruneian counterpart as outgoing and warm, bringing positive energy to the course. As for MAJ Afifi, he found LTC Shahreel to be professional, friendly, and someone who made him feel welcome from day one.
They spent long hours together in the planning room, unwinding and connecting over meals afterwards.
"Within the first interactions already, we knew that we will hit off. And actually, over time, we've realised how much we have in common with each other," LTC Shahreel told CNA.
"I think we sort of skipped a step a little bit. We jumped from being coursemates to friends almost immediately," he said, adding that they later found out how they shared the same alma mater in the University of Western Australia.
What began as a friendship between coursemates soon grew into a bond that transcended borders, with the pair meeting almost every year since.
For MAJ Afifi, their enduring bond is "testament to a friendship that goes far beyond the uniform".
Their friendship is one of many forged between servicemen and women from Singapore and Brunei over decades of military cooperation. This year marks the 50th anniversary of defence ties between the two countries, with Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong visiting Brunei to commemorate the milestone.
Mr Wong, who is also finance minister, and Brunei's Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah attended a joint parade at Muara Naval Base on Saturday (Oct 10), featuring 256 personnel and operational assets from the land, naval and air forces of both armed forces.
The parade was a key milestone in a year-long series of activities commemorating the 50th anniversary, including bilateral exercises across all three services and new areas of cooperation, the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) said in a news release.
The Singapore-Brunei relations stretch back to the early years of both armed forces. The Royal Brunei Armed Forces was established in 1961, followed by the SAF in 1965, with formal defence relations established in 1976.
Singapore's first Chief of Defence Force, retired Lieutenant-General Winston Choo, had also trained alongside many leaders from Royal Brunei Armed Forces.
"These early professional and personal ties laid strong foundations for bilateral defence relations and have endured across generations," MINDEF said.
"A NATURAL EXTENSION"
Five decades on, that spirit of camaraderie continues through servicemen such as LTC Shahreel from Singapore and MAJ Afifi from Brunei.
