items.body_text:
Encontrá las guías de servicio con tips de los expertos sobre cómo actuar frente a problemas cotidianos: Adicciones, violencia, abuso, tecnología, depresión, suicidio, apuestas online, bullying, transtornos de la conducta alimentaria y más.
Este probiótico cuenta con múltiples beneficios para la salud
- 4 minutos de lectura'
En el mundo de la gastronomía, ciertos alimentos han logrado trascender su función básica para convertirse en auténticos tesoros culinarios. Uno de estos es el chucrut, un producto fermentado que ha ganado una merecida fama, al punto de ser denominado por algunos como “oro blanco”. Este peculiar sobrenombre no es casualidad; el chucrut, originario de la región central de Europa, ha sido elogiado durante años no solo por su sabor distintivo, sino también por los numerosos beneficios que aporta a la salud.
Su riqueza en probióticos naturales lo convierte en un aliado de la flora intestinal, mientras que su capacidad para fortalecer el sistema inmunológico y mejorar la digestión lo ubica en un lugar privilegiado dentro de los hábitos alimenticios. De este modo, el chucrut no solo preserva una herencia culinaria centenaria, sino que también se presenta como un ingrediente esencial para quienes buscan un equilibrio saludable en su alimentación diaria.
El Código Alimentario Argentino define el chucrut como el producto obtenido mediante la fermentación láctica natural de hojas finamente picadas de diversas variedades de repollo blanco y duro (Brassica oleracea). Este producto puede contener o no condimentos y debe presentarse en buen estado de conservación. Según las normas, debe tener un contenido de cloruro de sodio no menor de 2% ni mayor de 3,5%; con una acidez expresada en ácido láctico no inferior al 1%, y un pH no mayor a 4,1. Además, el color del chucrut debe ser blanco amarillento.
Beneficios del chucrut
“Es un alimento probiótico porque en el proceso de fermentación sucede la colonización, es decir, se desarrollan bacterias/microorganismos vivos que luego uno incorpora a su propia microbiota”, indica Yael Hasbani, asesora en Dietética y Nutrición Natural.

items.title: Tamara Misewicz-Healey, 38 años, sobre las midterm 2026: “Ya no creo en ninguno de los dos partidos porque nos abandonaron”
items.summary: Conoce por qué Tamara Misewicz-Healey dejó de confiar en demócratas y republicanos antes de las midterm 2026 y qué cuestiona del sistema político.
items.body_text:
Tamara Misewicz-Healey, 38 años, sobre las midterm 2026: “Ya no creo en ninguno de los dos partidos porque nos abandonaron”
Una votante de Pensilvania reflejó el malestar de ciudadanos que cuestionan a las dirigencias políticas por sus vínculos con grandes empresas, el costo de vida y las decisiones del gobierno
- 4 minutos de lectura'
A pocas semanas de las elecciones legislativas, una parte del electorado estadounidense mostró un alejamiento de las estructuras tradicionales de los partidos políticos. Un análisis describió un escenario en el que demócratas y republicanos enfrentan cuestionamientos de ciudadanos que consideran que sus representantes dejaron de responder a las necesidades de sus comunidades.
¿Demócratas o republicanos?: cómo ven los ciudadanos las elecciones de medio término
Según The New York Times, Tamara Misewicz-Healey, de 38 años y madre de tres hijos en Pensilvania, representa uno de los casos de descontento con los partidos políticos en EE.UU. Durante años votó por candidatos demócratas, aunque no tenía una participación política activa.
Su postura cambió a partir de la oposición a la construcción de un centro de datos en Archbald, localidad donde reside. Junto con su esposo, Justin Healey, comenzó a organizar a los vecinos mediante el grupo de Facebook Stop Archbald Data Centers, que llegó a reunir 14.000 integrantes.
La pareja también impulsó una página de recaudación destinada a contratar a un abogado y presentó pedidos de información pública. Misewicz-Healey incluso inició una campaña por voto escrito para competir contra su representante estatal demócrata; sin embargo, recientemente anunció su retiro de la contienda.
“Ya no soy demócrata. Ya no creo en ninguno de los dos partidos. Ambos nos abandonaron”, dijo en una entrevista con The New York Times.
Pensilvania: los centros de datos y el desencanto con demócratas y republicanos
La experiencia de Misewicz-Healey terminó por modificar su identificación partidaria. Según explicó, la respuesta de los dirigentes políticos ante el proyecto empresarial le hizo perder la confianza en las instituciones.
Su conclusión fue que las dirigencias habían priorizado los intereses de las compañías sobre las preocupaciones de los residentes. “Tengo muchas ideas y visiones para un futuro más brillante para el noreste de Pensilvania. Pero primero, debemos asegurarnos de que siga existiendo una región segura, saludable y equilibrada a la cual llamar hogar”, señaló en un video publicado en Facebook.
El fenómeno no se limita a los votantes demócratas. En el condado de Carbon, Pensilvania, cientos de personas utilizaron la opción de escribir el nombre de Christian Bartulovich en las primarias. El republicano registrado, de 37 años y gerente en la industria de dispositivos médicos, terminó por obtener la nominación demócrata para las elecciones del 3 de noviembre.
“Estoy recibiendo un montón de mensajes de texto que dicen: ‘Nunca he donado a un republicano en mi vida. Espero que ganes’”, dijo el Sr. Bartulovich, según lo retomado por The New York Times.
La economía y Trump generan dudas entre los republicanos
El descontento también alcanzó a sectores que anteriormente respaldaban a Donald Trump. El análisis de The New York Times señaló que parte de sus antiguos seguidores cuestionan los resultados económicos y algunas decisiones de política exterior.
Para estos votantes, existe una diferencia entre las promesas realizadas durante las campañas y la situación que perciben en su vida cotidiana. Ryan Wagner, un conservador de 41 años de Michigan que había apoyado con fuerza a Trump, comenzó a distanciarse del presidente por estos motivos.
“Nos dejamos engañar, y nos equivocamos”, dijo Ryan Wagner a The New York Times. “Ya ni siquiera puedo escucharlo hablar”, dijo en referencia a Trump.

items.title: Chinese whispers
items.summary: Sino-Argentine links slightly predate the Wuchang Uprising of 115 years ago – in 1909, the dying Manchu empire started to grope towards establishing formal relations with an almost centennial Argentina but ran out of time. Leer más
items.body_text:
Today is the 115th anniversary of the Wuchang Uprising, the start of the 1911 revolution ending four millennia of Chinese imperial dynasties four months later, so perhaps as good a time as any to talk about China – rarely at the top of the news here but always lurking somewhere.
While the first day of this month is celebrated in mainland China as the anniversary of the 1949 proclamation of the People’s Republic, “Double Ten,” as today is called in Taiwan, remains the national day across the straits on that island – Beijing’s Malvinas, something also making that part of the world topical today, given the centrality of that issue here in the past couple of months. With almost five percent of the mainland’s economic output produced on 0.4 percent of its area by 1.6 percent of the population (closer to being among the world’s top 20 economies than G20 member Argentina) and still recognised as China’s legitimate government by a dozen countries around the world (including our neighbour Paraguay), Taiwan deserves respect but today’s column will focus on the superpower.
So how did China evolve from the ramshackle empire starting to collapse 115 years ago today into sporadically being Argentina’s top trading partner. plus having our long-haired president by the short hairs via a currency swap on a par with Donald Trump’s midterm lifeline last year to beef up the always precarious Central Bank reserves? As it happens, Sino-Argentine links slightly predate Wuchang – in 1909, the dying Manchu empire started to grope towards establishing formal relations with an almost centennial Argentina but ran out of time. A long vacuum follows – the Middle Kingdom is introspective at the best of times and the next three decades were the worst under the thumb of the treaty ports and warlords (until 1928) with Communist subversion as from 1927 and escalating Japanese encroachments as from the invasion of Manchuria in 1931. In those years Argentina might just as well have been Timbuktu.
At the end of May, 1945, with the war in Europe already over, a hitherto Axis-leaning Argentina completed its switch to the winning side by formally recognising Kuomintang China, although the first embassy was in western Chungking (today Chongqing) with Japanese troops still occupying much of the country. This move was quickly wrongfooted by the Communist triumph in 1949. Nevertheless, Taiwan continued to run the Chinese Embassy here for over two decades, enjoying some enthusiastic support from anti-Communist military dictators (especially General Juan Carlos Onganía) but viewed as increasingly irrelevant by almost everybody else.
The world changed with United States President Richard Nixon’s historic visit to Beijing in 1971 as part of Henry Kissinger’s strategy of driving a wedge into the Sino-Soviet bloc, while the United Nations recognised the People’s Republic as the sole Chinese UN representative in the same year. Latin American governments, even the military dictatorships, had no choice but to follow suit and on February 19, 1972, diplomatic relations between Argentina and the People’s Republic were formally established in Romania with Nicolae Ceaușescu as middleman – Argentina has consistently maintained a “One China” policy ever since.
Although then Vice-President Isabel Perón visited China the following year, there was no immediate empathy between the new interlocutors – in the early years Chairman Mao’s biggest fans were not to be found in any Argentine government but in the Ejército Revolucionario del Pueblo (ERP) guerrillas (who never reached the intensity of Peru’s Sendero Luminoso, however). Nevertheless, junta President Jorge Videla, whose anti-Communist principles led him to delete thousands of fellow-Argentines, had no compunction about making an official visit to Beijing in 1980 at the same time he was defying Jimmy Carter’s grain embargo against the Soviet invaders of Afghanistan (although joining the boycott of the Moscow Olympics).

items.title: Argentina gets taste of global data-centre boom
items.summary: Argentina has 67 registered data centres, including 13 announced projects, with 52 operational; Government eyes billions in digital infrastructure investment but concerns mount over energy use, water consumption and job creation. Leer más
items.body_text:
Javier Milei is determined to turn Argentina into a technology hub and he travels the world to promote the country’s advantages: vast expanses of land, water, cheap energy and the promise of a legal framework tailored to the needs of major digital corporations as they develop data-storage infrastructure.
Data centres are the big talking point of the present, both in Argentina and abroad. The President presents them as a source of billions of dollars in investment and economic development.
The problem is that the term – data centres – covers everything from facilities that have been operating for years to projects that exist, for now, only in the form of an announcement.
Not for the first time, promises are some way ahead of reality.
A data centre is a physical facility designed to house technological infrastructure, including servers, storage systems and networking equipment, that allow large volumes of information to be processed, stored and distributed.
In truth, they are nothing new. Data centres have existed since businesses and governments first needed dedicated facilities to handle large quantities of data. But the digital explosion, and particularly the development of artificial intelligence (AI), has transformed their scale: they increasingly require greater processing and storage capacity and, above all, more energy.
Argentina has already seen two high-profile announcements. In October 2025, just before the midterm elections, OpenAI and Sur Energy signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) to develop a data centre in Patagonia, with a potential investment of up to US$25 billion. To date, no final investment decision has been confirmed, and the project's location has yet to be verified.
In July, Poland’s Green Capital announced plans for a data centre in Trelew, Chubut Province. According to the company, the first phase is intended to deliver 300 megawatts (MW) of power, with an eventual target of 3,000 MW dedicated to technological infrastructure. The company aims to conclude discussions with investors and potential clients by 2027, while construction is projected to begin in 2028.
Outside of these grand plans, it’s worth noting that data centres are already part of Argentina’s digital infrastructure and the sector is looking to expand. The proliferation of projects and announcements is also creating a need to organise the available information and establish what actually exists on the ground.
Pablo Serdán, a lawyer and lecturer at the University of Buenos Aires, developed the Tengo Data data-centre observatory. Its public register identifies 67 data centres in Argentina, of which 52 are operational, one is under construction, 13 have been announced and one has been cancelled.
The Cámara Argentina de Internet (CABASE) chamber group has also begun compiling its own register. The organisation, chaired by Ariel Graizer, has focused on data centres currently providing services to third parties. It has identified 14 facilities in this category with a capacity of more than 1 MW and a combined installed capacity of nearly 32 MW.
These mapping exercises help explain the sector and will identify its needs as it develops. Last month, the national Energy Secretariat established the Régimen de Demandas Extratendenciales (Extraordinary Demand Regime, XDEM) within the wholesale electricity market (MEM), which will require major projects to provide and pay for their own energy supply.
The aim is to prevent the overloading of existing infrastructure and safeguard uninterrupted electricity supplies for households, PyMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises, or SMEs) and businesses.
Where are Argentina’s data centres located?

items.title: Brazil’s second MAGA moment
items.summary: South America has truly turned to the right politically in a move that mirrors the “pink tide” of the early 2000s. Leer más
items.body_text:
While the decisive leg of the election is still to be run, the results of the presidential election in Brazil between Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro last weekend have created deep ripple effects that will have lasting impact. If Bolsonaro ultimately wins in the run-off scheduled for October 25, a true “blue wave” of right-wing presidents will have swept across Latin America; if he doesn’t, the make-up of the Brazilian Congress and the distribution of governors across the largest and most important country in the region will heavily favour the Partido Liberal (PL) leader and deliver momentum to its agenda, with the impeachment of Supreme Court Justice Alexandre De Moraes and an official pardon for his father, ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, at the top of that list. It will also mark the consolidation of a new hegemony, built in the image of US President Donald Trump and his MAGA movement. President Javier Milei is the most prominent expression of it in the Southern Hemisphere, yet Brazil is the ultimate prize.
The election was tight. Bolsonaro topped Lula by 1.87 percentage points, the slimmest margin in history. The final tally came in at 47.03 percent for Flávio (the firstborn of former president Jair who remains under house arrest after an attempted coup in 2023), compared to 45.16 percent for the sitting president, who is seeking his fourth term in office. Some 33 million Brazilians didn’t vote last Sunday, a 21.08 percent abstention rate. Right-wing parties secured 59 percent of the Chamber of Deputies and 43 of 81 Senators, giving it a strengthened position in Congress, and five governorships outright for Bolsonaro’s party. In São Paulo, Tarcisio de Freitas crushed Fernando Haddad of Lula’s PT, 62.65 percent to 36.42 percent, in favour of the incumbent right-wing governor.
Flavio has received the endorsement of several parties, including Ronaldo Caiado of the Partido Social Democrático (PSD), who took 2.18 percent of the vote in the first round. The third-place finisher, Augusto Curry (2.89 percent) has indicated he will not take sides, while Renan Santos (2.24 percent) appears to be politically on the right but has campaigned on disillusionment with the Bolsonaros clan. Lula will bank on trying to increase the turnout in order to overturn his loss of support compared to the 2022 election.
While in Argentina we generally analyse the rise and consolidation of the Milei phenomenon as a reaction to never-ending economic decrepitude, results in Brazil indicate that the electoral appeal of the “new-right” is not strictly ideological and economic, but more of an aesthetic. Founded by Trump in the United States, the anti-system, anti-woke crusader of the “culture wars” is an international phenomenon. Indeed, Jair Bolsonaro was probably the second chronologically and in importance, given the geopolitical significance of Brazil. He followed in Trump’s footsteps by refusing to accept an electoral defeat at the hands of the historic “lefties” (Lula), and then attempted to launch a coup d’état. Given that Jair is effectively barred from holding office, he’s managed to transpose his votes onto his less charismatic son and they may succeed in making it to the Planalto Presidential Palace in Brasília.
There is no doubt that Milei has perfected the MAGA art in his own way. He added elements including the chainsaw, the “caste,” the lion and the “heavenly forces,” extremely seductive branding from an electoral standpoint. Total submission to MAGA and alignment with the United States in terms of foreign policy have granted Milei a direct line to POTUS, who has had no qualms in intervening in other countries’ domestic politics and internal electoral processes. In Argentina, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered Milei a US$20-billion bailout at the toughest moment of the campaign last year and both he and Trump have made it clear that support is off the table if Milei is kicked out. Así pasaron la primera noche los habitantes de la zona cercana al epicentro del terremoto de magnitud 7,7 en Panamá: vigilancia y gente en las calles
Las diferentes circunstancias y el miedo de las personas llevaron a que se desarrollara un fin de día que no era habitual.
Los vecinos de la pequeña ciudad de Penonomé, una de las zonas más afectadas por el terremoto de magnitud 7,7 que sacudió este viernes 9 de octubre a Panamá, continúan al caer la noche con la adrenalina en el cuerpo mientras vigilan sus negocios derruidos.
Una de las infraestructuras afectadas fue un hotel de apenas cuatro niveles en el corazón de esa ciudad, ubicada a más de doscientos kilómetros al oeste de la capital panameña.
La fachada y los balcones del hotel están colapsados. Parte del edificio cayó sobre los automóviles estacionados en la base, lo que imposibilita su traslado, pese a no haberlos destruido.
EFE habló con dos trabajadores del hospedaje que estaban dentro cuando el terremoto de magnitud 7,7 -según el Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos (USGS, por sus siglas en inglés)- agitó al país centroamericano.
“Fue una gran adrenalina. Nadie está preparado para esto (…) estábamos sacando a la gente cuando escuchamos crujir la infraestructura”, dijo a EFE Eduardo González, trabajador del hotel, mientras hace “guardia” durante toda la noche sentado en una silla de playa frente al hotel.
González, como otros vecinos, está pendiente ante la posibilidad de robos a lo largo de la noche.
Pese a que el fuerte movimiento telúrico, de apenas diez kilómetros de profundidad, tuvo como epicentro las cercanías del pequeño pueblo costero de Tonosí, a casi cien kilómetros de Penonomé, esta pequeña ciudad fue una de las zonas más resentidas.
“Fue bastante fuerte (…) entré a mi carro (vehículo), pero cuando intentaba salir, detrás de mí había otros interceptándome y comenzó a caer el concreto”, comentó a EFE otro de los trabajadores hoteleros, que prefirió no dar su nombre.

Sistema de Falla Azuero-Soná: esto se sabe de la estructura geológica detrás del fuerte terremoto de magnitud 7,7 en Panamá y sus más de 100 réplicas
Néstor Luque, director del Instituto de Geociencias de Panamá, entregó algunos detalles.
El Instituto de Geociencias (IGC) de Panamá informó que más de cien réplicas han seguido al terremoto de magnitud entre 7,5 y 7,7 que sacudió este viernes 9 de octubre el sureste del país, mientras fuentes de protección civil dan cuenta de al menos dos heridos y una persona atrapada en los escombros de una iglesia.
Néstor Luque, director del IGC, dijo a la cadena de televisión TVN que todas las réplicas del evento principal suman hasta ahora unas 107 que se han sentido en todo el país, e incluso al momento de sus declaraciones se dieron un par de temblores secundarios más.
El terremoto inicialmente fue registrado por el IGC como de magnitud 7,2, pero entrada la noche lo actualizó a 7,5, según lo confirmó Luque a la televisión, mientras que el Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos (USGS, por sus siglas en inglés) lo reportó en un principio con una magnitud de 7,6, que luego fue actualizada a 7,7.
"Todas estas réplicas son aquí en esta área que es donde se encuentra el 'Sistema de Falla Azuero-Soná', lo cual corrobora efectivamente que el evento principal fue una liberación de energía súbita de una porción de la falla activa", indicó Luque.
Según el primer informe oficial del Gobierno panameño, el terremoto dañó casi todas las plantas potabilizadoras del país, iglesias, hoteles, comercios, edificios públicos y carreteras, pero no se reportaron hasta el momento víctimas mortales.
El movimiento telúrico, con profundidad de diez kilómetros, generó daños en varios edificios y carreteras cercanas a la localidad de Tonosí, epicentro del temblor, en Penonomé, capital de la provincia central de Coclé.
Arturo González, director del Sistema de Protección Civil (Sinaproc) en la provincia central de Veraguas, dijo por su parte a la televisión local que en esa región hubo dos heridos, y que además fue rescatada con vida una persona atrapada entre los escombros de una iglesia colapsada.

items.title: Is the Spanish Transition a Model for Venezuela?
items.summary: Spain's democratization yielded a stable party system and longstanding agreements, but didn’t address the past. Should we follow its steps?
items.body_text:
Is the Spanish Transition a Model for Venezuela?
Spain's democratization yielded a stable party system and longstanding agreements, but didn’t address the past. Should we follow its steps?
King Juan Carlos I summons party leaders after the failed 1981 coup. From left to right: Santiago Carrillo (Communist Party), Agustín Rodríguez Sahagún (Defence Minister), Adolfo Suárez (Prime Minister), Juan Carlos I, Felipe González (PSOE) and Manuel Fraga (People’s Alliance, later PP).
(“Gosh, no! Not another hyper-comparative article about two distant political conflicts…” Apologies. We’ll try to make it a fun read).
More often than not, our intellectual circles have felt tempted to look at alien historical episodes in a never-ending search for resolute answers that shed light on our present. In 2023, when Maduro flirted with attacking US-supported Guyana, some revisited the Falklands War as a sign that a serious military incursion would be a fatal mistake that would lead to the dictatorship’s downfall. Then came the road to the 2024 presidential election; many feared (rightfully, in the end) that the country would plunge into the “Nicaragua scenario” if the dictator refused to recognize his defeat. Others momentarily wondered if enough external pressure could give way to a Guatemala-style transfer of power and a weak transition government.
The days of terror seem to be behind us, yet there’s no progressive reformer like Raúl Alfonsín steering the wheel of justice. Instead, Donald Trump gave us the Pizza Hut scenario. Here, Delcy Rodríguez has become the poster girl of the MAGA international franchise. Here, too, US geopolitical ambitions and business interests at times seem to be competing with the need for free elections and a democratic regime.
Is Rodríguez our Mikhail Gorbachev, trying to open the economy and political system just enough while attempting to save the chavista State from outright collapse? What if chavismo is already dead and she’s the Yeltsin of the Caribbean, the feeble leader who will give away the country’s riches to oligarchs in an arbitrary fashion, laying the ground for a new form of autocracy?
Or might Delcy be the chavista version of Adolfo Suárez, the not-so-brilliant and obscure but highly charismatic Francoist insider? Suárez finished the job after a remarkable run, surviving a period of meagre political support, declining approval rates and a coup d’etat that could have killed him. The comparison now sounds like an insult to the Spaniard. Like Gorbachev in today’s Russia, Suárez has become a sort of mythical statesman abroad while Spanish right- and left-wing critics dispute his legacy.
There are genuine similarities between the process currently unfolding in Caracas and the outset of Spain’s democracy, as well as room for gross contrasts. While 2026 has been insane for Venezuelans, Spain exactly fifty years ago was astonishing due to the speed at which Suárez acted in unilaterally dismantling the regime from within the regime. The dictator was finally gone, and as soon as he had the chance, the new King ordered a politician without strong ideological convictions to establish a full parliamentary democracy.
Suárez took office in June 1976. The Law for Political Reform, meant to pave the way for a new democratic legislature (with the King acting as a key enforcer), was through six months later. Spain held general elections within a year. That was just the start. What followed was a sequence full of the raw materials that tend to feed these history-making episodes: secret meetings and grand bargains between rivals and strange bedfellows, journalists acting like hinges, political violence, and leaders who soon become overwhelmed by their own decisions and actions.
How the transition worked out

items.title: Diplomatic Defeat for Delcy: The UN Will Keep Probing Chavismo
items.summary: Distancing from old allies made the regime look lonelier than ever in the Human Rights Council
items.body_text:
Diplomatic Defeat for Delcy: The UN Will Keep Probing Chavismo
Distancing from old allies made the regime look lonelier than ever in the Human Rights Council
Police officers block a protest demanding decent wages as public workers, students and pensioners try to reach the presidential palace. Photo by Associated Press, April 2026.
On October 6, the UN Human Rights Council voted to renew the mandate of its Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Venezuela for two additional years. For victims, their families, and society at large, it means an independent investigation must continue as long as the machinery of repression remains operational, and through any transition that finally allows more of the truth to emerge.
The vote must be read alongside the negotiation that made it possible. A striking 25 of the Council’s 47 members voted in favour, 5 against and 17 abstained. The result sends a clear signal, but must be read carefully: governments can allow an investigation to continue while disagreeing over findings or the way forward because of considerations beyond the Council room.
The diplomacy behind
This renewal reflected some of those wider considerations. It also deserves recognition as the outcome of sustained diplomatic work by the Core Group: Argentina, Canada, Chile, Ecuador, Guatemala, Paraguay and Uruguay. As one diplomat told me, this included outreach to Washington DC through privileged diplomatic and regional channels to explain the stakes of the vote, and to build an understanding over the need for renewal. These delegations have been instrumental in scrutinizing the regime since the Mission’s establishment in September 2019. This time, they endorsed the Mission again and built the political space for continuation.
The 49 sponsors (including North Macedonia, which the Venezuelan regime accused of hacking the electoral system during the 2024 presidential election) chose a short, carefully balanced resolution. During negotiations, they emphasized that this would encourage more Council members to accept it. The text acknowledges initial prisoner releases and renewed cooperation with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), before supporting continuing the independent investigation and demanding accountability.
Negotiations also revealed strains in the traditional protections chavista governments had come to rely on at the UN over the past decade. Venezuela’s diplomatic allies, coordinated through the Group of Friends in Defence of the Charter of the UN, face an increasingly uncomfortable dilemma: how to reconcile opposition to US intervention with support for Venezuelan authorities now working closely with Washington. Their own relations with the US add to that difficulty.
In my view, the cohesion that once sustained their defence of the chavista regime is under tension and may give way to new problematic circumstances. The Caracas delegation did not articulate a strategy among the “Friends of the Charter.” A representative of a long-standing Venezuelan NGO who recently visited Geneva offered this explanation for the apathy: “The regime is walking on eggshells, and bullies have no experience on that.”
The Havana delegation was particularly cooperative during negotiations, a marked departure from its usual role in defending Venezuela.
Informal consultations had already suggested this change. Although most delegations maintained their statements of principle, chavismo’s traditional allies didn’t put up major obstacles and proposed few, if any, amendments.
A senior human rights defender who attended a meeting with some of these allies later told me: “Am I dreaming, or did they just turn a blind eye?”

items.title: Dear Mr. Rubio, Don’t Forget About the Non-Oil Economy
items.summary: Your weekly reminder that Venezuela remains a terrible place to do business. Please try fixing that too
items.body_text:
Dear Mr. Rubio, Don’t Forget About the Non-Oil Economy
Your weekly reminder that Venezuela remains a terrible place to do business. Please try fixing that too
The Venezuelan economic debate has been dominated by headlines over hydrocarbon deals and speculation around the future of the mining sector. The focus is understandable. It’s a petrostate with an abundance of natural resources, capable of propelling us out of the prolonged economic and humanitarian crisis that chavismo inflicted upon us. But as we must continue to discuss the future of the oil, gas and mining sectors, we must not forget the reforms required to allow the non-oil economy to flourish.
Although a large share of the state’s revenues and the country’s GDP is ultimately tied to hydrocarbons, the overwhelming majority of Venezuelans are not oil engineers, geologists or miners. Nor are most Venezuelan companies directly involved in extracting natural resources. The non-oil economy is there, operating under a highly restricted business environment of price controls, extortion, a minefield of a tax system and labour laws hostile to companies. All while facing a contraction in its market due to the migration crisis and severely restricted access to credit.
Venezuela is still among the hardest places to do business in the world. It is time to discuss how to give the sector, which includes formal and informal businesses of all sizes, the breathing space it needs to grow.
Let’s first put the power grid and infrastructure issues aside. The reforms required span virtually every aspect of the business environment, from the institutions that oversee the economy at the macro level, to the banking system and the nitty-gritty of tax and labour law. At the most basic level, the private sector needs confidence that contracts will be respected, property will be protected, and disputes can be resolved through institutions that are predictable and independent. Without these basic reassurances, investing in Venezuela remains a gamble that many businesses and outside investors will simply not be willing to take.
Dollarization without the institutional and financial framework to back it will fail in its mission to stabilize the economy.
As previously explained regarding the macro level, the Venezuelan Central Bank (BCV) needs to regain its independence and establish a credible monetary policy based on transparency and clear rules, supported by a board and president who are not subordinate to Miraflores. Burning through the petro-dollar cash pile to curb the Bolivar devaluation won’t cut it. The central bank is estimated to have used 65% of the oil sale proceeds to shore up the Bolivar. This has proven to be futile without a proper macro framework to support such interventions. It is the BCV’s credibility that is fundamental to correcting the distortions in the FX market and preserving confidence in the Bolivar, in order to lower the still extraordinary inflation rate hovering around 500%.
A credible BCV will also be fundamental to back whichever currency policy the State decides to embrace. Debates over dollarization have spread. However, the measure is not a magic wand, and going for it without the institutional and financial framework to back it will fail in its mission to stabilize the economy. Monetary stability with a functioning BCV will not suffice, but it’s a necessary foundation to correct the distortions that pervade the Venezuelan economy.
Surviving without credit
Reforms aimed at stimulating the non-oil private sector must not stop there.
Venezuela needs its banks to be banks again. The country has by far the region’s lowest credit portfolio relative to GDP thanks to draconian restrictions from regulators, which limit the capacity of banks to function as credit facilitators, and reduce them to mere transactional businesses. A functioning banking system is fundamental for the private sector’s recovery. Venezuelan businesses need the capital, as much as consumers need the

items.title: EXPLAINER: What to know about the refugee ruling that sparked riots in Durban and Soweto
items.summary: Violent protests erupted in Durban and Johannesburg this week following widespread misinformation about a Home Affairs directive on how asylum seekers should be processed. Here’s what you need to know.
items.body_text:
A total of 24 cars were torched during protests in Durban and Soweto on Thursday, 8 October 2026. To understand the violence, we have to go back to a court ruling on asylum seekers and the anti-foreigner movement that has been building throughout the year.
In July, the Constitutional Court declared certain provisions of the Refugees Act unconstitutional and invalid. The ruling said specific procedural barriers to lodging an asylum claim must be removed.
In late September, Home Affairs issued a directive to implement that ruling. That led to the violence in Durban and Soweto, which was amplified by online misinformation.
On Friday, the director-general of the Department of Home Affairs withdrew the directive. The department says it will start from scratch to draft a sustainable plan that meets the requirements set by the Constitutional Court.
Hereâs what you need to know.
So, what happened in Durban and Joburg?
On Tuesday, 6 October, members of March and March disrupted asylum applications at the Durban Refugee Reception Office on Che Guevara Road, where hundreds of people had queued to apply for asylum.
Anti-foreigner protests in Durban have continued throughout the week, with violence escalating. People have been injured and multiple vehicles have been torched while foreign-owned shops have been looted.
In Soweto on Thursday, anti-foreigner demonstrators clashed with foreign shop owners amid reports of gunshots and property destruction. Vehicles were also set alight.
Protesters gathered outside the Constitutional Court in Braamfontein on Friday, 9 October. The riot, which drew more than 300 anti-foreigner demonstrators, escalated and became violent. A vehicle was torched and police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds.
Whatâs the Constitutional Court ruling about?
The Refugees Act required asylum seekers to enter South Africa through a designated port of entry to receive an asylum transit visa, which is valid for five days. Within that period, they were required to present themselves at one of the five refugee reception offices and to lodge an application for asylum.
If they were unable to do so, asylum seekers had to provide immigration officers with âcompelling reasonsâ or show âgood causeâ for not following the prescribed process.
If unsatisfied with an explanation, officers could prevent an individual from lodging an application or reject them on the spot.
The court found that these procedural barriers could prevent genuine asylum seekers from accessing a merits-based assessment of their claim, particularly given the constitutional right to dignity and the principle of non-refoulement, which prevents states from returning people to countries where they face persecution or other serious harm.
What did Home Affairs do?
On 28 September, Home Affairs issued a directive instructing refugee reception offices to receive people who report in person and indicate that they intend to apply for asylum, and to help them lodge their applications.
It applied to people who had entered the country unlawfully, had entered somewhere other than a designated port of entry, did not have a visa, or had failed to report to one of the countryâs five offices within five days.
Why the uproar?
The uproar over the asylum ruling and directive comes amid a growing wave of anti-foreigner mobilisation in South Africa.
Groups such as March and March have been at the forefront of demonstrations throughout the year, culminating in a 30 June âdeadlineâ for foreign nationals to leave the country.
Demonstrations became more frequent as the deadline approached, while vigilantes targeted people they believed to be foreign nationals. Some were intimidated and assaulted, others were forcibly removed from their homes, and foreign-owned businesses were shut down.
The unrest has, at times, turned violent, resulting in the destruction of homes and businesses, the displacement of communities, and people fleeing the country. The violence has also claimed lives.

items.title: GROUNDUP: Anti-immigrant mob threatens to burn women and children in Pretoria
items.summary: Home Affairs has backtracked on reopening the asylum system after violent clashes in various cities. In Pretoria, anti-foreigner groups made violent threats before they were dispersed.
items.body_text:
âYour time is up! We will lock you in your shops and set them on fire,â anti-immigrant protesters, armed with sticks and sjamboks, told immigrant shopkeepers, mainly women and their children, in Pretoria on Friday, 9 October.
Anti-immigrant groups, including March and March, Operation Dudula and the United Progressive Peopleâs Alliance Party, gathered outside the Refugee Reception Office in Marabastad.
âWe are staying here until the Home Affairs staff leave and make sure no immigrant accesses the services. We will be back on Monday and every day after that until they change this policy,â said Operation Dudulaâs Tsaka Tsepedi.
Immigrants were chased, water bottles were thrown at them, and they were spat at. The police stood by and did not intervene.
âSome of the police support our cause as they are part of our community,â claimed one of the protesters.
Later on, the crowd moved to Luttig Street, where many shops are run by immigrants. About 20 people, some carrying sticks and sjamboks, went around forcing the owners to close the stores. Some residents, including South Africans, tried to defend the immigrant shop owners.
The situation became more volatile, with threats of physical harm and death hurled at the immigrants and their children if they âdid not leave the countryâ. During this altercation, GroundUp reporter Seth Thorneâs phone was taken out of his hand. He was slapped on the face several times. He was told he should not take photographs of the protesters.
The crowd dispersed when four police officers arrived to separate the protesters and shop owners.
Police officers told GroundUp that there had been several demonstrations at the Refugee Reception Office over the past few days, but this was the first time shops had been forced to close.
There were long lines outside Refugee Reception Offices across the country this week after Home Affairs announced its offices would start accepting new asylum applications again in line with a Constitutional Court ruling in July.
Online misinformation, including that the court ruling guaranteed all applicants asylum and those granted asylum would be able to vote in the upcoming election, contributed to these groups harassing asylum seekers at the offices.
On Friday, protesters also gathered at the Constitutional Court in Johannesburg and set a car alight. They reportedly tried to enter the court building.
The oversubscription of refugee offices this week, and the anti-immigrant violence seen at many offices, forced Home Affairs to close its offices.
âThe 28 September directive has led to unintended consequences, noting national interest, security considerations and its impracticality in terms of operationalisation by Refugee Reception Offices,â an internal Home Affairs memorandum stated.
Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber was reportedly unaware of the directive to reopen asylum offices.
Aftermath of Durban violence
Fourteen cars were set alight in Durban on Thursday as hundreds of people, including March and March members and affiliated groups, targetd people they suspected of being immigrants. The group vandalised and looted stores as they marched.
On Friday morning, many shops remained closed. Some had been burned or looted. Abed Khan, who owns a business in the Durban CBD, said March and March needed to be dismantled because âitâs going to bring nothing but hunger in this countryâ. He added that businesses owned by immigrants employ many people.
âOnly the government can put an end to the March and March madness,â said Khan.
Samuel Michael, who owns several businesses around Durban, had two of his shops on Gillespie Street vandalised. The group smashed his doors and windows while trying to gain entry, he said. âIâve been here for 24 years. My wife and son are both South African,â said Michael, who originally comes from Nigeria.
A liquor store near the beachfront, owned by Vinay Maharaj, was also vandalised. He told GroundUp that the shop has been in there for 20 years.

items.title: STRANGE TIMING: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after South African judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
items.summary: Hours after South Africa’s Navi Pillay, a former judge of the International Criminal Court, was named as this year’s recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, the US slapped sanctions on the court.
items.body_text:
US President Donald Trumpâs administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, 9 October, hours after one of âits former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, South Africaâs Navi Pillay, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The ICCâs deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal's work.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court, which was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Fridayâs move would go far further, âby potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
âPresident Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,â Secretary of State Marco Rubio âsaid in a statement, first published by Reuters.

items.title: Global reaction to US sanctions on International Criminal Court
items.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with the ICC, what he called a "rogue court".
items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
The United States announcement of new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to one of its former judges Navi Pillay, has provoked widespread international criticism.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court".
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," he added.
European nations and the United Nations have led the opposition, while Israel has welcomed Washington's decision.
Here are key reactions:
'Serious blow': UN
UN chief Antonio Guterres condemned the US decision, saying he was "deeply alarmed by the expected impact" of the measures, a spokesman said.
"Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar," spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
"The secretary-general reiterates his unwavering support for the independence of the court and its officials."
UN human rights chief Volker Turk said the sanctions, "the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel... are unacceptable".
Netanyahu support
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised the US sanctions, a rare show of support for Washington's action.
"The ICC is not a court," Netanyahu's office posted on X.
"It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty."
Stay informed. Subscribe to our newsletter
Dutch call for dialogue
The ICC is based in The Hague and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten described the sanctions as "deeply regrettable".
"At the same time," he added, "these sanctions will not take effect immediately, Jetten told reporters.
"And this is crucial because it provides us vital space for dialogue in the upcoming months."
EU vows to help court
The European Union also described the US sanctions "deeply regrettable".
"The EU will work closely with the ICC to ensure it continues to operate effectively," the European Commission added.
It, too, called for dialogue in the six months before the sanctions start.
Key ICC members back court
Britain, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands, also backed the court.
"As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," said a joint statement from the countries' foreign ministers.
Amnesty says resist
Rights group Amnesty International called on countries to "resist".
President Donald Trump's "sanctions are designed to isolate and ultimately destroy the International Criminal Court", Amnesty's Erika Guevara Rosas said in a statement. "This existential attack must fail. States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures."

items.title: US imposes sanctions on the International Criminal Court
items.summary: US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court, cites threats to its citizens; calls for diplomatic and legal solutions within 180 days.
items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
The United States on Friday announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court, vowing to cripple the tribunal's operations just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to a former ICC judge who warned of mounting political attacks on the court.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court," escalating a long-running campaign by President Donald Trump's administration against the Hague-based tribunal.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said in a statement.
But the immediate impact of the sanctions was softened by a series of exemptions that offer a de facto six-month grace period.
The State Department said that was meant to give the court's member states time to show "meaningful progress" toward addressing US concerns.
The grace period could be adjusted depending on the "success or failure" of those efforts, the department added.
The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that "history will judge this moment."
Countries including Canada, France, Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom said in a joint statement that they "strongly disagree" with the announcement.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar."
The European Union called the sanctions "deeply regrettable" and said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work."
The European Commission, the EU's executive arm, said it hoped the six-month delay meant "there is room for dialogue."
Rights group Amnesty International urged countries to "resist" the move, saying the sanctions were "designed to isolate and ultimately destroy" the court.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces an ICC arrest warrant over alleged crimes in Gaza, praised the US action.
"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," his office posted on X.
Never allow
Stay informed. Subscribe to our newsletter
The move came on the same day the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the peace prize to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old jurist who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal, served on the ICC and later led a UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.
Rubio's statement did not mention Pillay or the Nobel award.
He said the sanctions were needed to protect security personnel and elected officials from prosecution by a court the United States has never joined.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said, adding that the measures would cut off the court's resources and cripple "its ability to operate."
The top US diplomat said Washington had for more than a year spelled out "basic gestures of good faith" it expected from the court, and had held off on the designation in hopes that the ICC or its member states would change course.
He said no "meaningful steps" had been taken to address US concerns.
Rubio also called on US allies that belong to the court and "rely on American service members for their defense" to rein it in, warning that otherwise Washington would keep working to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick."
The Trump administration had already sanctioned 17 people linked to the court, including its prosecutor and several judges, over the ICC's investigations involving the United States and Israel, which is also not a member.
Trump last month called on all ICC member states to quit the body, denouncing it as "out of control" and a "rogue institution."

items.title: Mozambique's Graca Machel among 21st-Century's 'Top of The Top-10 Merit Sovereigns'
items.summary: 21st-Century's Top of the Top-10 Merit Sovereigns Hierarchy Crowns Graca Machel alongside Stephen Soldz, King Charles III, Francesca Albanese, Polymath Aurangzeb Hafi and Greta Thunberg among others.
items.body_text:
Audio By Vocalize
Graca Machel of Mozambique has emerged as one of the era-defining standout names in a sweeping new global merit ranking, cited twice over for her decades of work on behalf of children caught in armed conflict, as Impact Hallmarks (IH©) unveiled its list of the ‘Sovereign Merit Icons of the 21st Century’.
The Britain-based cross-disciplinary indexing system names 38 individuals across humanitarian work, science, athletics, monarchy and youth activism, scored against a 1,000-point framework that its authors say was designed to reward documented achievement over public visibility.
Machel, credited as architect of a landmark United Nations report assessing the impact of armed conflict on children over a 25-year span, scored more than 940 points to place second in the Humanitarianism and Social Justice category, a distinction she shares with Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, recognised for her 2024 report ‘Anatomy of Genocide’ and for facing sanctions over her work.
She appears a second time in the Icons of Dignified Asceticism category, alongside former Finnish president Tarja Halonen and former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, each scoring above 910 points, and is named a third time among the Quarticentennial Merit Vanguards, a tier recognising researchers who provided evidentiary baselines for major UN constitutive documentation.
Topping the Humanitarianism and Social Justice category outright is Stephen Soldz of the United States, who scored 967 points for what assessors called his monumental documentation of psychologically coercive interrogation tactics used against war prisoners — work IH© described as the first academic condemnation of using sacred religious texts as instruments of torture, and which the assessors named the ‘Magna Carta’ of ethics and human inviolability.
Also recognised is Greta Thunberg of Sweden, indexed in two separate categories: third place in Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity with 933 points, for an arc running from her solitary school-strike movement to leading high-risk flotilla missions carrying aid toward Gaza, including the Freedom Flotilla in June 2025 and the 44-nation Global Sumud Flotilla in September 2025, whose interception led to the detention of 450 activists and sparked protests across three continents, and again in the Young Trailblazing Icons category with 920 points.
In the Scientific Endeavours category, physicist Dr Fritjof Capra of the United States shares first place with Arch-Polymath Sir Aurangzeb of Pakistan with 950+ points for both.
Dr Capra is credited for his systems theory of life and for framing a composite worldview against the Newtonian-Cartesian mechanistic paradigm.
Prof Aurangzeb Hafi is recognised for integrating the ‘scientific pentarchy’, for identifying the mega-toxification of underground water reserves, which is linked to prevailing sewage-drainage practices in developing countries, for presenting the first ‘Deca-Archic Phygital Literacy Model’, and for the discovery of Magneto-Hydro-Tropism (MHT).
Prof Hafi is named in three separate categories overall, also placing in Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons with 910 points and second in Multiple Iconicities with 957 points, cited for research spanning 93 subject fields.
King Charles III of the United Kingdom is named in the Paradigm-Trailblazing Icons category with 930 points, cited as a decades-long advocate for world peace, interfaith harmony and global ecology, now serving as head of state of multiple nations.
Pope Francis leads the Resilience, Endurance and Nature-Centricity category with 940 points, and James Harrison of Australia, the ‘’Man with the Golden Arm’, tops the Multiple Iconicities category for blood-plasma donations credited with saving roughly 2.4 million lives.
Both figures were living iconicity-participants during the retrospective evaluation timeline (2000–2025), but are deceased at the time of the gazette's o

items.title: Nigeria: American Lobbying Firms Disagree Over $57m U.S. Lawsuit Against Tinubu
items.summary: [Premium Times] DCI Group has rejected allegations in a $57 million US lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu and others, while Femi Fani-Kayode's office says he has not been formally served.
items.body_text:
DCI Group has rejected allegations in a $57 million US lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu and others, while Femi Fani-Kayode's office says he has not been formally served.
American lobbying firm DCI Group has rejected allegations made by Washington-based lobbyist Karl Von Batten in a $57 million lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, former aviation minister Femi Fani-Kayode and the firm.
DCI has been hired by the Nigerian government for lobbying activities in the United States, while Mr Von Batten is doing the same work for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.
Mr Fani-Kayode's office also told PREMIUM TIMES that he had not been formally served with the court papers and maintained his earlier denial of the allegations.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
The case, filed at the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on 28 September, concerns allegations of defamation and a conspiracy to kidnap and physically harm Mr Von Batten. The claims are disputed and have not been established by a court.
DCI, Fani-Kayode respond
In an email to PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday, Craig Stevens of DCI Group dismissed the allegations.
"Mr. Von Batten's allegations are so far past unfounded that they reach the point of the absurd," Mr Stevens said.
He said DCI's work for the Nigerian government focused on strengthening relations between Nigeria and US policymakers and referred the newspaper to the firm's disclosures under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
Mr Stevens did not address the specific allegations individually.
Mr Fani-Kayode's office, responding separately, answered "No" when asked whether the former minister had been formally served. It also confirmed that he stood by his earlier denial of the allegations.
Mr Fani-Kayode had previously indicated that he would pursue a $100 million counterclaim against Mr Von Batten.
Asked whether the counterclaim had been filed or lawyers instructed to commence proceedings, his office replied: "All in good time."
The response did not confirm any filing.
What the lawsuit alleges
The US federal court docket identifies the case as Von Batten v. Tinubu et al., No. 1:26-cv-03374, before Judge Randolph D. Moss.
The defendants include President Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, Mr Fani-Kayode, DCI Group AZ, LLC, and 10 unidentified persons.
In a public announcement, Von Batten-Montague-York said it was seeking $36 million jointly from President Tinubu and the Nigerian government, $3 million from Mr Fani-Kayode and $18 million from DCI.
The firm alleged that the defendants were involved in efforts to defame, kidnap or physically harm Mr Von Batten over his advocacy concerning US government records relating to President Tinubu.
The publicly accessible docket records the filing and issuance of summonses, although this does not establish that the defendants have been formally served.
PREMIUM TIMES has requested the complete file-stamped complaint and exhibits to examine the allegations and the damages sought.
Presidency, others yet to respond
PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Presidency through Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to President Tinubu on Information and Strategy, seeking its response to the allegations, confirmation of any formal service and its position on the court's jurisdiction.
The enquiries were sent by email and WhatsApp, followed by telephone contact and reminders.
The newspaper also contacted Mr Atiku's ADC campaign to establish whether the former vice president or his representatives knew about the lawsuit before it was filed and whether they endorsed its allegations.
The campaign was further asked about the status of Mr Atiku's $1.2 million lobbying agreement with Mr Von Batten's firm, payments made and their source.
Mr Von Batten was separately contacted for the full complaint, supporting documents and his response to the denials by DCI and Mr Fani-Kayode. PREMIUM TIMES also sought clarification on the alleged th

items.title: Kenya: U.S. Report Flags Kenya's Failure to Act On Officials Linked to Human Trafficking
items.summary: [Capital FM] Nairobi -- Kenya has failed to report meaningful enforcement action against public officials and recruitment agencies allegedly linked to human trafficking, with a new United States report warning that official complicity continues to undermine the country's efforts to prosecute the crime.
items.body_text:
Nairobi — Kenya has failed to report meaningful enforcement action against public officials and recruitment agencies allegedly linked to human trafficking, with a new United States report warning that official complicity continues to undermine the country's efforts to prosecute the crime.
The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report said Kenyan authorities investigated three Ministry of Labour officials suspected of accepting bribes to facilitate potential trafficking involving migrant workers travelling to the Middle East, but highlighted broader concerns over alleged collusion between public officials and recruitment networks.
The report also found that the government had not reported action against recruitment agencies allegedly owned by government employees and suspected of facilitating trafficking, with authorities frequently pursuing lesser offences such as failure to register recruitment companies.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
"Corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes remained significant concerns, inhibiting law enforcement action during the year," the report stated.
The findings raise questions about accountability within institutions responsible for regulating overseas recruitment and protecting Kenyans seeking employment abroad.
Media reports cited in the assessment indicated that more than 10 per cent of Kenyan government officials held ownership interests in private employment agencies, including firms recruiting migrant workers for jobs overseas, creating potential conflicts of interest.
Observers also alleged that criminal syndicates colluded with law enforcement and immigration departments at border checkpoints and airports to transport trafficking victims into and within Kenya.
The report further cited allegations that some Kenyan embassy officials in Saudi Arabia demanded sex or cash payments from women seeking government assistance to escape abusive employers and return home.
The allegations come against the backdrop of declining anti-trafficking prosecutions and convictions.
Kenya convicted six traffickers in 2025, down from 21 in 2024, while prosecutions fell from 44 cases to 14.
The government investigated 43 trafficking cases during the year, compared with 42 in 2024.
The report also detailed allegations involving the fraudulent recruitment of more than 1,000 Kenyan men to fight for the Russian military in the war against Ukraine, with officials reporting that Kenyan and Russian officials had colluded with illicit recruiters to facilitate the recruitment.
Despite the concerns, Kenya remained on Tier 2 in the US assessment, which recognises significant efforts to combat trafficking while finding that the government has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating the crime.
The report credited Kenya with identifying more victims, repatriating citizens exploited in overseas online scam operations, and securing its first civil judgment against a fraudulent recruiter.
However, it said persistent concerns over official complicity continued to hamper law enforcement and victim identification, while protection services for adult survivors remained limited.

items.title: South Africa: Navi Pillay's Nobel Win Draws Attention To Her Work Defending Media Freedom And Beyond
items.summary: [Bird Story Agency] Recognised by the Norwegian Nobel Committee for her efforts to promote peace and international law, Navi Pillay is being celebrated by African media, legal and civil society voices for a career advancing justice, accountability and human rights -- including the right to report freely and safely.
items.body_text:
Recognised by the Norwegian Nobel Committee for her efforts to promote peace and international law, Navi Pillay is being celebrated by African media, legal and civil society voices for a career advancing justice, accountability and human rights — including the right to report freely and safely.
Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize, announced on Friday, 9 October, is drawing attention to her support for media freedom and a career spanning some of the most consequential developments in international human rights law.
The South African jurist has backed initiatives to strengthen legal protections for free expression and promote a free and pluralistic information space.
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
Pillay is the fifth South African to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, following Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk.
Announcing the Nobel, Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes linked Pillay’s early legal work under apartheid to her later role in international justice, from defending Nelson Mandela and others who opposed apartheid to serving as a judge in major international cases.
The committee said she had helped strengthen the international legal order and institutions responsible for holding perpetrators of serious crimes accountable. It also highlighted the uneven application of international law and the ability of powerful states and leaders to evade responsibility.
“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence," the committee said.
Pillay’s win is particularly being celebrated by the media fraternity in Africa, most of whom are citing her efforts in defending media freedom.
Reacting to the announcement, Moky Makura, executive director of Africa No Filter said Pillay “embodies African agency”.
“For decades, she has worked tirelessly to create the change she wants to see in the world. This Nobel Prize shines a well-deserved spotlight on her extraordinary contribution. It is a reminder that African progress is not always about what is happening, but also about what the world is failing to see,” Makura said.
Churchill Otieno, president of The African Editors Forum (TAEF), also said Pillay’s record held particular significance for journalists because of its emphasis on accountability and the right to report freely.
“From her struggle against apartheid to her work in international human rights and law, she has shown that peace cannot endure without accountability,” Otieno said.
“For us journalists and media workers, her record also speaks directly to the right to report freely and safely. As UN High Commissioner, she called for journalists to be protected from political interference and physical threats. Her recognition affirms that defending human dignity, press freedom and the rule of law takes courage, especially when powerful interests resist scrutiny.”
In February 2025, Pillay delivered the keynote address at the launch of South Africa’s Free Expression Legal Network in Johannesburg. Developed by the South African National Editors’ Forum (SANEF), the Press Council, the Campaign for Free Expression and other organisations and legal experts, the network connects journalists and others facing legal threats over their expression with support, including legal representation.
Information and digital rights activist Izak Minnaar notes that Pillay had actively supported the network and advanced media freedom initiatives internationally.
“As the only South African on the global Information and Democracy Commission, she has been spearheading initiatives to support media freedom in South Africa and beyond,” Minnaar explained.
Anton Harber, director of the Henry Nxumalo Foundation, said Pillay had been particularly consistent in defending independent journalism.

items.title: Fitch revises Nigeria’s outlook to positive on monetary, exchange rate reforms
items.summary: “The outlook revision reflects ongoing reform of the policy framework and Fitch's increased confidence that momentum will not be disrupted by upcoming elections,” Fitch said. The post Fitch revises Nigeria’s outlook to positive on monetary, exchange rate reforms appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
Fitch Ratings, a leading provider of credit ratings, commentary and research for global capital markets, has revised the outlook on Nigeria’s long-term Issuer Default Ratings (IDR) to positive from stable, citing economic reforms that are yielding positive outcomes.
The rating agency, in its rating action report issued on Friday and seen by PREMIUM TIMES, also affirmed the IDRs at ‘B’.
An IDR is a forward-looking view by Fitch Ratings on an entity’s relative vulnerability to default on its financial obligations.
‘B’ ratings imply that a material default risk exists, while the capacity for continued payment is prone to deterioration in the business and economic environment, even though there is a limited margin of safety.
“The outlook revision reflects ongoing reform of the policy framework and Fitch’s increased confidence that momentum will not be disrupted by upcoming elections,” Fitch said, alluding to the potential economic impact of Nigeria’s general elections coming up early next year.
“Monetary and exchange rate reforms have supported greater naira flexibility, disinflation and faster-than-expected FX reserve accumulation, while improved reserve quality enhances resilience to shocks,” it went further to say.
The rating agency’s outlook on Nigeria derived support from improvement in Nigeria’s external position, which saw gross FX reserves jump to $54.9 billion on 9 September 2026 from $32 billion in mid-April 2024, supported by higher formalisation of FX deals, robust portfolio inflows and increased export receipts and remittances.
Stay Ahead with Premium Times

Add as a preferred source on Google
Fitch anticipates that reserve coverage will reach 6.3 months of current external payments by the end of this year and stay above peers in 2027-2028. Nevertheless, it noted that big net errors and omissions remain a source of uncertainty.
The rating agency also expects the naira to trade broadly around the current level through the end of this year, in spite of the likelihood of weaker oil prices in 2027-2028.
It believes sustained reform implementation is bolstering policy transmission and should aid further disinflation, much as inflation is expected to remain well above peers.
According to Fitch, Nigeria’s ratings are indicative of its big economy, comparatively developed and liquid local debt market, substantial oil & gas reserves and a stronger macroeconomic policy framework.
However, weak governance indicators, high hydrocarbon reliance, sticky inflation, security challenges and structurally low government revenue compared to peers are among major constraints.

Fitch envisages broad economic policy continuity, including in relation to reforms that have contributed to higher policy credibility, increased external liquidity and improved resilience to external shocks, adding that the incumbents are on track to win the 2027 elections on account of the ruling party’s control of most of the states in the country.
It highlighted a restrictive monetary policy position, moderating inflation and higher oil production and refining output among key rating drivers.

items.title: AI boom lifts trade but raises financial risks – UNCTAD
items.summary: UNCTAD warned that a slowdown in demand for AI hardware could remove a major source of momentum from global merchandise trade. The post AI boom lifts trade but raises financial risks – UNCTAD appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has become a major driver of global merchandise trade, but its growing concentration in technology-related goods and investment exposes the global economy to financial risks if demand slows.
The new insights are contained in the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) latest Trade and Development Report 2026.
UNCTAD said global trade in goods and services grew by 4.4 per cent in real terms in 2025 and was projected to expand by about four per cent in 2026.
However, the report said the growth rested on a narrow base, with AI-related goods, including chips and servers used in data centres.
The growth accounts for about one-sixth of global goods trade by value in 2025 and contributing 42 per cent of its growth.
UNCTAD warned that a slowdown in demand for AI hardware could remove a major source of momentum from global merchandise trade.
The organisation added that higher prices have also driven much of the recorded growth in trade values since March 2026.

“The AI boom shows signs of earlier financial bubbles. A fall in share prices could trigger selling and squeeze credit well beyond the technology sector,” the trade body said.
AI concentration
The report also highlighted the concentration of AI investment, which is dominated by spending on advanced chips and model development in 2026.
While such spending generates relatively little employment, UNCTAD said data centres were helping to stimulate economic activity.
According to UNCTAD, investment remains concentrated in China and the United States, with Europe benefiting to a lesser extent.
Also, Brazil, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand are also benefiting to varying degrees.
It said investment in US data centres would reach $400 billion in 2026 and approximately $600 billion in 2027.
This represents projected growth of about 300 per cent in 2026 and 50 per cent in 2027, compared with a projected seven per cent increase in fixed investment across all sectors of the US economy in 2026.
“Without data centres, the investment picture would look profoundly different,” the report said.
Investment flows
UNCTAD said the concentration of economic activity was also evident in international investment, with global foreign direct investment (FDI) rebounding to $1.6 trillion in 2025, a six per cent increase that ended two consecutive years of decline.
However, the recovery was uneven, as FDI inflows to developed economies rose by 11 per cent, compared with a two per cent increase in developing economies, according to the UNCTAD’s 2026 data.

The report attributed the changing pattern of investment to geoeconomic fragmentation, industrial policies and technological competition, which increasingly influence where capital flows.
It said investors were directing funds towards capital- and technology-intensive projects in strategic sectors, including AI computing infrastructure, data centres and critical minerals, rather than focusing primarily on short-term profitability or the cost of capital.

items.title: Access Holdings executive director retires
items.summary: The company said the retirement would ensure compliance with the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) Corporate Governance Guidelines for Financial Holding Companies in Nigeria. The post Access Holdings executive director retires appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
items.body_text:
Access Holdings Plc has announced the retirement of Olanrewaju Bamisebi as Executive Director, Information Technology and Digitalisation, following the expiration of his term contract.
The retirement took effect on 30 September, according to a regulatory filing by the financial holding company, signed by Sunday Ekwochi, the group company secretary on Friday.
The company said the retirement would ensure compliance with the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) Corporate Governance Guidelines for Financial Holding Companies in Nigeria.
Under the guidelines, a financial holding company is permitted to have a maximum of two executive directors: the managing director/chief executive officer and one other executive director, who must be the chief financial officer, subject to the CBN’s approval.
Access Holdings said its board appreciated Mr Bamisebi’s contributions to the digital transformation and growth of the Access Group during his tenure.
“The Board expresses its sincere appreciation to Mr. Bamisebi for his dedicated service and contributions to the digital transformation and growth of the Access Group during his tenure and wishes him every success in his future endeavours,” the notice stated.
With over 20 years in IT and digitalization, Mr Bamisebi oversaw the group’s digital strategy across 19 countries and serving over 68 milLion customers.
