items.title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
items.summary: Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill.
items.body_text:
Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-UÃ©lÃ©, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border
items.normalised_title: questions remain over ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected

items.title: Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr on making history at her NFL half-time show
items.summary: The Nigerian star will become the first African artist to headline the show at an international NFL game.
items.body_text:
Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr on making history at her NFL half-time show
- Published
Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr has already broken numerous records, and her NFL half-time performance this weekend is set to level up her list again.
The Nigerian star will become the first African artist to headline one of the American football league's international games when the Philadelphia Eagles take on the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on Sunday.
Ahead of the performance at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Starr told BBC Newsbeat her history-making performance "itself is a message".
Earlier this year, Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny used his Super Bowl half-time show to celebrate Latin American culture.
The 32-year-old also made history by becoming the first musician to perform entirely in Spanish at the sporting event, normally the most-watched each year on US TV.
Starr said it's "very important" for singers to seize opportunities like this.
"At the end of the day, as artists, we speak for the culture and we speak for the people that listen to us," she added.
"And we have to represent any way that seems fit, that they need."
She didn't want to give away too much about her performance, but confirmed it would feature tracks from her new studio album, Starrgirl, which was released in August.
"Sunday is gonna be amazing," she said.
"I'm still in rehearsals. It's a lot of work we're putting in so I'm really excited."
The 24-year-old has been making waves in recent years, becoming the first African woman to win best international act at the Mobo Awards and the first Nigerian woman to surpass one billion video views on YouTube.
But before she became a superstar, the singer studied for a degree in political sciences and international relations - and said this has influenced her work.
"When it comes to matters of women and equality and the girl child and even just children - I'm very outspoken on any platform that sees fit.
"Even with my music, my music is very much like 'I will do what I want' and freedom."
The Afrobeats genre, which originates from West Africa, has massively grown in recent years - dominating playlists and seeing artists, including Starr, featuring at major festivals such as Glastonbury.
She said the rest of the world is just "catching up" to a style that's been "popping in Africa for the longest time".
The singer added that becoming one of the dominant faces of the music she grew up listening to, alongside artists such as Wizkid and Burna Boy, is "crazy".
Starr acknowledged it's a male-dominated field and would like female artists to have more "space in the genre" and be "allowed the same privileges".
But she also feels this is just the beginning.
"Afrobeats just keeps evolving, it keeps growing and it just keeps getting better... I want it to be one of the top genres in the world."

items.summary: Pillay is recognised for her "efforts to promote peace and international law", the Norwegian Nobel Committee says.
items.body_text:
Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
- Published
Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.
Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee JÃ¸rgen Watne Frydnes.
"Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said.
"At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity."
Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'".
Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃa Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom".
Pillay dedicated her award to "all the survivors of international crimes" and the practitioners of international justice "whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign".
Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban.
She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court.
Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president. She was elected to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2003.
From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law.
The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements.
The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies".
The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes.
Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice".
It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."

items.summary: How did the world reach a tipping point, and who holds the leverage?

The Global Diesel Crisis, Explained
How did the world reach a tipping point, and who holds the leverage?
The price of diesel fuel—which moves tractors, trains, and ships around the world—has recently surged, almost doubling in the last two years. The causes of that increase are wide-ranging, from the wars in Iran and Ukraine to policy decisions in Europe and Asia. The resulting crisis is already hitting anyone who uses a diesel-powered vehicle and could soon affect consumers everywhere.
What exactly is diesel? How did Europe become so dependent on it? And who has leverage in the current crisis?
The price of diesel fuel—which moves tractors, trains, and ships around the world—has recently surged, almost doubling in the last two years. The causes of that increase are wide-ranging, from the wars in Iran and Ukraine to policy decisions in Europe and Asia. The resulting crisis is already hitting anyone who uses a diesel-powered vehicle and could soon affect consumers everywhere.
What exactly is diesel? How did Europe become so dependent on it? And who has leverage in the current crisis?
Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.
Cameron Abadi: What is diesel exactly, and what makes it distinct as a fuel?
Adam Tooze: In the process of refining oil, which we’re all getting familiar with as a result of this crisis—it does feel like [U.S. President] Donald Trump’s foreign policy is God’s way of teaching us all chemical engineering—you basically cook the heavy oil, and as you warm it up, different fractions of the oil come off in the refining in these tall towers they have, right? There are very light gases that come off first, because they evaporate off the heavy oil first, and then you get regular benzene and petrol.
Then, lower down, you get heavier products—bigger molecules, basically. At the very bottom, you get something that’s basically tar and is used in road surfacing. But in the middle tier, you get heavy molecules with lots of carbon atoms that are still in various ways easily combustible—not quite as prone to combusting under ignition as petrol, but nevertheless combustible. Diesel is a cocktail of these ingredients in the middle range of the refining stack.
When you encounter diesel, it’s much more oily than regular fuel. Regular fuel is kind of terrifyingly … it feels light if it splashes on your skin, right? Diesel is oily. The thing with diesel is that you want it to spontaneously ignite in hot air, which has to do with the design of the diesel engine. Whereas the classic internal combustion engine injects an emulsion—a cloud of air mixed with petrol and then igniting it with a spark plug—the diesel engine instead compresses air, generating enormous heat in the air.
You don’t really need a spark plug if you have a fuel type like diesel, which when it’s injected into the hot air will spontaneously combust. The result is it produces a much more uniform flame. The problem with a standard internal combustion engine is you basically got a cloud of petrol in air and then you ignite it, so you get an uneven spread of the flame. There’s an awful lot of fancy engineering I used to be totally into as a kid about how you design that combustion chamber and where the air-fuel combination comes in and how you maximize it.
All of that disappears with diesel because you’re just going to compress the air and then inject the fuel into the right place. The beauty of that is several different things, but one crucial one is that you can make the engines really, really big because you can control the way in which the combustion takes place, because it’s going to be uniform across the chamber. Arnold Toynbee’s Chinese Century
A forgotten historian enjoys a strange afterlife in Beijing.
“China has a more promising chance of shepherding mankind into political unity than any other country,” wrote Britain’s most famous historian in 1974. Arnold Toynbee, historian and prognosticator, was once famous enough to appear on the cover of Time magazine in 1947, but he is almost unheard of in the West today. Yet his legacy lives on in Asia, where Zhang Guangzhi of Fudan University’s history department can recall Toynbee rising from obscurity to acclaim as the greatest modern historian. Today, Zhang is one of dozens of scholars working to translate the entirety of Toynbee’s 3-million-word magnum opus, A Study of History, into Chinese.
Toynbee, born in 1889, came of age as World War I transformed the philosophy of history. Pessimism came to dominate a field once marked by attempts, like those of Hegel and Marx, to track mankind’s ascent from barbarism towards liberation. The German polymath Oswald Spengler offered the first volley with his two-volume Decline of the West, first published in 1918. For Spengler, civilizations resemble organisms; they are born, they live, they die.

Before Spengler’s work was translated into English, it was reviewed for the Times of London by Toynbee, fluent in German. A classicist by training, Toynbee grew to question Western historical narratives during his time as a delegate to the Paris Peace Conference and a correspondent covering the Greco-Turkish War. In both cases, he felt the British public misunderstood the legitimate grievances of the colonized. By age 33, Toynbee was director of studies at Chatham House, Britain’s premier international relations institute, where he stayed for three decades.
Years later, Toynbee remembered that he “wondered at first whether my whole enquiry had been disposed of by Spengler.” Spengler’s account of cycles of advanced cultures categorically rejected any notion of Eurocentrism. He elevated civilizations from Mesoamerica to China, ridiculed by 19th century imperialist historiography, to the same level as anything Europe had produced. But Toynbee soon realized that his project was distinct. Spengler’s differentiation of civilizations was so radical that he jousted at windmills to separate every fragment from culture to culture, even arguing that mathematics was a relative construct.
Toynbee’s alternative came with his A Study of History, published in 12 hefty volumes between 1934 and 1961. The 7,000-page work made Toynbee a household name, particularly after an abridgement sold at least 300,000 copies. While the idea of transnational civilizations remained at its core, it featured more sociology than Spengler’s quasi-mysticism. In place of iron laws of historical decline, Toynbee attempted to find trends between 21 civilizations across millennia.

items.title: Trump Is Gutting America’s Core Geopolitical Advantage
items.summary: Robert Zoellick, an expert on the global economy who served as U.S. trade representative and World Bank president, makes the authoritative case that President Donald Trump’s antagonism toward Canada and Mexico is destroying an economic and security partnership that that enables the United States to project power globally.
items.body_text:
The Trump administration’s attack on Canada and Mexico is cracking the foundation of the United States’ global power. Friendly relations with neighbors enhance security, promote mutual economic gain, and make it easier to handle transnational challenges. Weak neighbors export trouble. Today, Canadians perceive U.S. President Donald Trump’s high tariffs and belittling of their country as the “51st state” as assaults on Canada’s economy and independence. In Mexico, Trump’s economic coercion and threats of military intervention have revived deep historical anxieties about gringo hegemony.
The North American partnership took generations to forge. During the nineteenth century, the United States’ foreign policy concentrated on its home continent, where it competed with France, Mexico, Russia, Spain, the United Kingdom, and indigenous peoples for dominance. As the United States became a global power in the twentieth century, U.S. strategists took North American relations for granted. Washington turned its attention to Europe, the Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East. Since the closing years of the Cold War, however, U.S. presidents have recognized the need to invest in North America. Ronald Reagan laid out the strategic rationale clearly when he launched his presidential campaign in 1979: “The key to our own future security may lie in both Canada and Mexico becoming much stronger than they are today,” he explained. “It is time we stopped treating our nearest neighbors as foreigners.”
Geopolitics begin with geography, and the United States’ geography gives it an enormous advantage over the world’s other major powers. China and Russia each have to manage relationships with 14 neighbors, many of which are unfriendly or carry resentments from histories of conflict. India must deal with six, including a nuclear-armed rival. All three powers’ access to the world’s seas depends on passage through maritime chokepoints. In contrast, the United States borders two benign neighbors and enjoys open sailing on two vast oceans. Close cooperation with Canada and Mexico enhances homeland security, attracts investment, promotes innovation, creates a huge market rich in resources and talent, and helps all three countries deal with criminal networks, illegal immigration, and threats to clean air, water, and wildlife.
A safe, resilient, and adaptive North America is the starting point of U.S. global strategy. Washington is best positioned to navigate an uncertain world when the United States, Canada, and Mexico present a common front. Yet Trump’s bullying is driving the United States’ natural partners away. The president is destroying a precious geopolitical asset: a strong continental base from which Washington projects power.
CONTINENTAL VISION
William Seward, who served as U.S. secretary of state from 1861 to 1869, first appreciated that good relations with the United States’ neighbors would boost the country’s global influence. He asserted that to have “control of this continent is to be . . . the controlling interest in the world.” When he was negotiating the U.S. purchase of Alaska in 1867, Seward observed that Alaska and the Aleutian Islands “extend[ed] a friendly hand to Asia.” He also tried to buy Greenland, Iceland, the Hawaiian Islands, and islands in the Caribbean, hoping that the purchases would help secure the United States’ oceanic approaches.
Seward recognized, however, that the United States could also boost its power by strengthening economic links, not just by adding territory. He abhorred European imperial conquests of foreign lands. He had also opposed the 1846–48 U.S. war with Mexico. At the end of the U.S. Civil War in 1865, Seward prevented Generals Ulysses S. Grant and Philip Sheridan from invading Mexico to depose the Habsburg archduke whom the French had installed as emperor. He reasoned that an invasion would arouse Mexican hostility and that the Mexicans could depose the interloper themselves—which they did, in 1867.

items.title: Iran’s Theory of Victory
items.summary: Tehran’s fight for great-power status in the post-American Middle East.
items.body_text:
When it comes to Iran, the Trump administration has a decidedly dismal record. It failed to wear down the Islamic Republic with months of intense bombings. It could not bend Iran’s will at the negotiating table. Yet despite seven months of setbacks, U.S. officials believe that they have turned the page. They have implemented fresh sanctions while maintaining the existing American blockade of the country’s southern coast, throttling its access to outside commerce. As a result, they have concluded that the Islamic Republic will soon either concede or be downed. “We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared on September 1.
There is no doubt that Washington has dealt significant damage to Iran. But the Islamic Republic does not believe it is unraveling. In fact, Tehran thinks that it will defeat the United States—and it isn’t hard to see why. The Iranian government did not merely survive the U.S.-Israeli bombardment. It retaliated ferociously, damaging American military bases and obstructing the Strait of Hormuz. Its people are paying a hefty economic price thanks to damage caused by the war and Washington’s cutoffs, but much of the population has rallied around the flag and seems to accept that hardship is necessary if Iran is to defend itself. As a result, Tehran has been emboldened. Its officials may not see eye to eye on each tactic. But they share the same ambitions: evicting U.S. forces from the Persian Gulf, forcing Washington to remove all its sanctions, and getting the United States to accept that Iran is a great power.
This agenda might sound overly audacious, given that Iran has been materially weakened. But the Islamic Republic thinks its aims are within reach. It believes its military can drive U.S. troops from the Persian Gulf by continuing to strike American bases directly and by getting Arab countries to push the United States to leave. It thinks that by wreaking havoc on energy markets, it can force Washington to lift economic restrictions, as well. Tehran’s theory of victory, in other words, is that it can hold out and inflict enough pain that the United States will end its containment of Iran.
CLOSING RANKS
No one doubts that Iran has been battered by war. Months of American and Israeli bombs have damaged the country’s industries and infrastructure, spiking unemployment and pushing more Iranians into poverty. Washington’s sanctions and naval blockade have caused rampant inflation. And the American and Israeli militaries can count many tactical successes, including the assassination of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
But strategically, the conflict has been disastrous. U.S. officials believed that punishing aerial bombardments and sweeping efforts to degrade the Iranian economy would bring the Islamic Republic to its knees. They didn’t. Washington hoped that assassinating Khamenei would prompt a mass antigovernment uprising. That scheme also failed. Instead, Khamenei’s death brought out the Islamic Republic’s ardent supporters. They marched every night in the country’s main cities and were eventually joined by Iranians of other political hues, who rallied in support of their homeland. When the war started, Turkey planned to accommodate 70,000 Iranian refugees. But few people fled. In fact, as the war progressed, many Iranians living abroad returned home, including long-exiled cultural figures, journalists, and politicians, such as the singers Mohsen Namjoo and Bijan Mortazavi.
This surge in nationalism is not an endorsement of the Islamic Republic. Many Iranians remain deeply unhappy with the country’s leadership. But the anger at their government has been subsumed by their anger at Washington. items.title: The Case for Economic Espionage
items.summary: America should spy on foreign companies to help its own.
items.body_text:
For decades, both adversaries and allies of Washington have spied on American companies to gain insights into innovation in the United States. During the Cold War, KGB spies routinely sought to steal trade secrets from U.S. industries. In the 1980s, French intelligence stalked American technology firms. In recent years, China has been especially aggressive on this front. The Center for Strategic and International Studies recorded 224 incidents of Chinese-sponsored espionage against the United States that occurred between 2000 and 2023, of which more than half targeted commercial technologies. Invariably, the goal of this kind of espionage is to help key sectors in the spying country rapidly replicate or surpass American advances. As the former National Security Agency director Keith Alexander memorably put it, cybertheft of U.S. technologies amounts to “the greatest transfer of wealth in history.”
Yet amid this brazen robbery, the U.S. intelligence community has long maintained a policy against spying on foreign companies to provide a commercial advantage to U.S. businesses. That self-imposed ban on economic espionage was reaffirmed repeatedly throughout the Cold War and in the decades since, including by President Barack Obama, who codified it in 2014 and tried to get China and other countries to follow suit. At the time, this made sense. U.S. economic policy had long forsworn government intervention in the private market, and providing select firms with secret intelligence would unavoidably distort the economy. In any case, through much of the Cold War and early post–Cold War era, most technological innovation important to national security emerged under government auspices rather than in the commercial market. Moreover, its lead in many technologies meant that the United States had much more to lose than to gain by legitimizing commercial spying.
Today, these rationales no longer hold. To an ever-growing extent, U.S. national security now depends on private-sector innovations. In such disparate areas as artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum science, bioengineering, next-generation energy, and space, breakthroughs that are crucial to the country’s power and influence are emanating from private companies. At the same time, even as technological supremacy has become increasingly central to national security, the U.S. lead in many crucial advanced technologies is being contested or even erased by China. By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.
To right the balance, the United States should allow U.S. intelligence agencies not only to collect commercial secrets from foreign companies but also to deliver that intelligence where it could have the greatest impact: to the firms producing the frontier technologies that will be vital to U.S. national security in the years to come. In September, the Trump administration appeared to take a step in this direction when it disclosed that the CIA and other intelligence agencies had begun to broaden their long-standing espionage efforts against China, including Chinese industry.
But a comprehensive strategy requires the United States to formally lift its existing prohibition on economic spying. The government must also establish robust rules and oversight to ensure that commercially valuable intelligence shared with the private sector serves the national interest, preserves competition, and, critically, is not used to advance partisan, political, or personal ambitions. Although economic espionage is not without risk, unilaterally renouncing the practice in the current global environment is far more dangerous.

items.title: What’s Driving the French Student Protests
items.summary: A movement born in the Paris banlieues has mobilized young people against diminished school conditions and accumulating problems at home and beyond.
items.body_text:
Among the hundreds of thousands of people who took to the streets in France on Tuesday were Paolina and Violette, eighteen and seventeen years old, arguing politely with a white-haired man sucking apple juice from a juice box. The two young women carried signs: “EVEN PEDOPHILES don’t FUCK US as much as THE EDUCATION DEPARTMENT” declared one, handwritten in ink a few shades darker than Paolina’s blueberry-colored manicure. “FOUR RIOT POLICE FOR ONE STUDENT / ONE PROFESSOR FOR THIRTY-FIVE.” Paolina is studying fine arts at the Sorbonne Nouvelle; Violette is a communications major at the Institut Universitaire de Technologie. They had come out to the Place de la République, in Paris, to protest the conditions at French schools. The familiar scent of grilling merguez wafted through the air as Violette began to enumerate the system’s failures. “This year, the government eliminated four thousand teaching positions,” she said. (Her stats were dead-on.) The man, who declined to give his name, thought that the problems facing French schools could be resolved quite easily: all the authorities had to do was “put more A.I.” into the curriculum.
“That’s not something that interests me, in an intellectual sense or in a moral sense,” Paolina shot back. “Prompting ChatGPT? I think I know how to do it better already than professors who are forty-five years old and hardly know how to use the technology.”
The man accepted defeat and slunk off, slurping, toward the Boulevard du Temple.
The protests began on September 17th, at a single high school, Lycée Saint-Exupéry, in the Parisian suburb of Créteil. Students and teachers had grown tired of not having a nurse or a deputy head teacher, dealing with leaks and clogged toilets, and trying to concentrate in un-air-conditioned classrooms, where the temperature could soar to more than a hundred degrees in summer. They decided to do something about it, erecting a blocus, or “blockade,” at the entrance to the school, mostly with trash cans. A few days later, some students launched explosive devices into the school lounge, injuring two people.
Nobody at “Saint-Ex” expected that the blocus would spread across the country, but social media did its work, awakening in French students a determination to make themselves heard after years of diminished means and accumulating problems—and providing, for their detractors, a pretext for blaming the country’s ills on febrile, feckless adolescents. Two weeks in, students at some six hundred and forty lycées and thirty universities across forty cities have joined the movement, drawing in adults as well, including many of their parents and teachers; elected officials, mostly from the left and the far-left; and trade unions like the powerful C.G.T.
The demonstrations have been met with aggressive and often outrageous policing. Around seven thousand protesters, most of them minors, have been arrested. During Tuesday’s march alone, officers arrested around two hundred more people than they did on the day the gilets jaunes sacked the Arc de Triomphe, in 2018. Protesters have sometimes resorted to violence, too, and they have set fire to or otherwise damaged at least twenty-four schools. But the majority of students have been peaceful, and many come off in interviews as almost freakishly mature. “What we have is a classic lycéen movement, using routine blockade methods, that speak of the conditions they’re facing,” the sociologist Sebastian Roché observed, on Radio France. “They constitute a threat to the government, because it’s weak, but not to the Republic.” In northern France, a police officer threw a tear-gas grenade directly into a fourteen-year-old’s face and shattered his jaw. Another child picked up a stun grenade that the police had launched and lost a hand.

items.title: A Woman with a Past
items.summary: My cousin Laura had a diva’s charisma and a siren’s voice. She also had a mysterious past. When she died, she left me to tell the story of her defiant reinvention.
items.body_text:
When my cousin Danny introduced me to his new wife, almost forty years ago, Laura was in her early thirties, a radiant beauty of Taíno heritage with a lithe figure and a model’s cheekbones. She wore her hair in a thick plait that swayed when she moved, and she emanated a sensuality that stirred anyone with a pulse. Without meaning to, she seduced my son’s puppy on the day we brought it home from the shelter, and whenever she came to visit, it went mad with joy. But Laura’s most striking feature was her voice, a smoky contralto, rich in irony, with an unplaceable accent, the product of self-invention.
Danny and Laura made an odd couple. His appearance was unprepossessing—frizzy red hair, a fleshy nose, a Teddy bear’s physique—and he effaced himself in her company, as if to deflect notice. (Divas often have such a husband, a recessive figure who pays the bills and basks in their charisma.) But then I hadn’t paid him much notice when we were growing up together in Queens, in garden apartments that bordered a cemetery. We were both members of the Meisner clan, a family of Hungarian Jewish immigrants, but Danny was six years my junior, and we weren’t close. When his parents moved away, our worlds diverged.
Over the years, I’d heard that Danny had studied acting and joined a theatre group. He might have succeeded on television, playing cops or hit men in procedurals, but he lacked the aura of menace those parts require. His looks destined him for comic roles, and the ones he landed couldn’t pay the rent, so he trained as a computer tech.
Laura entered my life at a fraught moment. My parents had just died, six months apart. My son, Will, was a baby with a distant father, and my maiden aunt Arkie was helping me raise him. I was living in a former pushcart stable in Yorkville, hidden behind a storefront and surrounded by an overgrown garden. Its bohemian décor struck Laura as romantic, and so did my life as a single mother who lived by her pen. “Not needing a man,” she sighed theatrically. “What a luxury.”
Later, Laura would visit me when Danny was at work. I’d set a pretty table for her, and she’d dress for the occasion. Along with a fondness for thrift-shop china, one of our bonds was a sense of imposture; we were both guarded women who seemed outgoing. I had just started work on a biography of Colette, whose title would be “Secrets of the Flesh,” and even before I knew Laura’s history she struck me as a character Colette might have imagined. An uncle of mine made the connection. He was an old rake who avoided family gatherings, though not after he met Laura. He flirted shamelessly with her, then told us approvingly, “There’s a woman with a past.”
The better I knew Laura, the more I puzzled at her pure-heartedness. Life had wounded yet somehow not embittered her. She believed in love, and her capacity for loving was like a boxer’s heavy bag, sturdy and inured to blows. You could confide your chagrins to her knowing she wouldn’t try to assuage them with pat reassurances. items.title: Year of the Horse
items.summary: After a young tourist was killed in a Central Park carriage accident this summer, the City Council is considering whether to ban horse-drawn carriages forever.
items.body_text:
Romanch Mahajan, an eighteen-year-old from Pathankot, India, visited New York City with his family in June to celebrate his high-school graduation. A tall, ambitious kid who loved cars, playing guitar, and collecting Jordans, Romanch dreamed of expanding his father’s travel business. On the third day of their trip, the Mahajans went to Central Park and took a ride in a horse-drawn carriage.
The carriage—white, with tufted seats—was pulled by a seven-year-old horse named Samson, who had been working in the Park for just six weeks. The carriage paused at Cherry Hill, a plaza with a cast-iron fountain (originally a drinking spot for horses). The driver, Ertan Gokdepe, stepped out to take a photo of the family in their seats. Suddenly, Samson bolted. The Mahajans screamed for help, and as they rounded a corner Romanch’s mother was thrown to the ground. Shouting, “Mom!,” he lunged to save her and fell out. He landed on his head.
The horse ran south toward Tavern on the Green, where the carriage collided with another and toppled over, smashing to pieces. Hours later, Romanch was pronounced dead, from blunt-force trauma. Samson was retired, and Gokdepe was put on indefinite suspension. “We lost a gem,” Romanch’s shell-shocked father, Deepak, told me. “We were four, and we came back as three.”
The tragedy couldn’t have come at a worse time for the Park’s carriage industry, which has weathered a series of fiascoes. One hot day in August, 2022, a carriage horse named Ryder collapsed in Hell’s Kitchen, en route to his stable. As cops sprayed him with water, onlookers took videos, aghast at his emaciated ribs. Ryder was sent to a farm upstate, where, after a seizure, he was euthanized; a necropsy revealed that he’d had leukemia. His driver, Ian McKeever, was tried and acquitted for animal cruelty. At the time, a bill to ban carriage horses was before the City Council. After the incident, it was renamed Ryder’s Law.
The industry tightened its equine-first-aid protocol, but the disasters kept coming. In May, 2025, a runaway horse crashed into a fleet of parked pedicabs. That August, a mare named Lady died of an aortic rupture at an Eleventh Avenue intersection. Days later, the Central Park Conservancy, which had remained neutral on the issue of carriage horses, formally endorsed the ban, citing hazards to public safety, damage to the roadways from horseshoes, and sanitation problems (manure). Nevertheless, Ryder’s Law died in committee.
This past January, an elderly horse named Destiny, apparently spooked by an e-bike with a cargo trailer, darted into Sixth Avenue traffic. In May, a startled horse reared and knocked over a carriage. On June 9th, a horse named Deniz nibbled from a Japanese-yew bush, which is highly toxic to horses, and dramatically expired. But it was Romanch’s death, a week later—the only human fatality from a New York carriage accident in modern memory—that juiced the political momentum. The revived ban, now called Romanch’s Law, is headed for a vote this month and would phase out the carriages by June, 2028. It has twenty-nine co-sponsors and the support of the Council’s speaker, Julie Menin; Mayor Zohran Mamdani is likely to sign it. The Mahajans are suing the city for a hundred and five million dollars. (Their lawyer, Sagar Chadha, is a co-founder of Hindus for Zohran.) In July, a crowd gathered at Cherry Hill for a memorial. Deepak, calling from India, told the mourners that his son, a vegetarian, had “sacrificed his life for the animals.”
Carriage horses share Central Park with owls, blue jays, red-tailed hawks, mallards, red-eared sliders, chipmunks, Virginia opossums, raccoons (who make cameos at Shakespeare in the Park), a small and elusive community of coyotes, and more than two thousand Eastern gray squirrels. items.title: Nobel laureate Karl Deisseroth on how light is changing what we know about the brain
items.summary: From algae to a Nobel prize: listen to The Conversation Weekly podcast to hear Karl Deisseroth explain his brain science breakthrough.
items.body_text:
When Karl Deisseroth was studying to be a doctor in the 1990s, he took a rotation working with psychiatric patients. It would start him down a path of discovery about how the brain works that would eventually lead him to become a Nobel laureate.
The brain is billions of fragile, extremely vulnerable, transparent, very fast-acting cells. It’s a very challenging system to study, and of course, buried within the skull and doing very complex things … I was very much impressed with the magnitude of the challenge.
Deisseroth, today a professor in the schools of medicine and engineering at Stanford University in the US, spoke to The Conversation Weekly podcast about his research, and the experience of being jointly awarded the 2026 Nobel prize for physiology or medicine with two German scientists, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
Deisseroth’s contribution was for pioneering the field of optogenetics, the ability to control nerve cells with light to investigate how their activity shapes our feelings and behaviour. To do this, he used a gene from a single-celled pond algae, discovered by Hegemann and Nagel.
We were able to find cells that were involved in hunger and thirst, basic survival drives. We were able to identify cells and pathways controlling aggression and defensiveness and parenting, nurturing of the young … all the different parts of anxiety … memory, motivation. The general applicability became clear over the subsequent years.
Listen to Deisseroth talk about his research journey, and his hopes for the future of optogenetic research, on The Conversation Weekly podcast.
Disclosure statement
Karl Deisseroth has received funding from the NIH and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. He was the founder of MapLight Therapeutics, a biopharmaceutical company.

items.title: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature – how she discovered new possibilities within language
items.summary: At a time when scholarship and creative writing are often treated as separate pursuits, Carson has shown how deeply they belong together.
items.body_text:
For over four decades, Anne Carson has been quietly redrawing the map of contemporary literature. Poet, translator, classicist, essayist, performer and visual artist, she has produced a body of work that refuses easy categorisation.
Yet what is most striking about Carson, the 2026 Nobel prize winner in literature, is not her formal originality, extraordinary though that is. It is her ability to make thinking itself like a literary event.
At a time when scholarship and creative writing are often treated as separate pursuits, Carson has shown how deeply they belong together. Her work is a reminder that thought and imagination don’t compete with one another, but continually enrich each other. The result is a body of writing that is at once intellectually demanding and creatively daring.
Carson moves effortlessly between ancient and modern worlds, not by collapsing historical difference but by inhabiting it. In her hands, antiquity is never a repository of cultural authority or a storehouse of exemplary texts. It is a living, unsettled terrain of voices, fragments, silences and absences.
This is perhaps most evident in her treatment of ancient Greek literature. Carson’s Sappho, Simonides, Sophocles and Euripides, do not emerge as objects of scholarly reconstruction. They are interlocutors. Their words cross centuries in order to illuminate experiences that continue to elude us: desire, grief, longing, estrangement, mortality. Carson’s dialogue with antiquity reveals that the ancient world survives not because it is preserved, but because it continues to generate new meanings.
Again and again, her composition returns to questions of distance. Between lovers. Between languages. Between the living and the dead. Between what can be known and what must remain elusive. Desire in Carson is rarely a movement towards possession; it is an encounter with absence. Her writing dwells in the gaps and intervals that structure human experience, finding there both pain and possibility. Few contemporary authors have written so perceptively about longing and the many forms it takes.
This concern with distance is inseparable from her radical experimentation with form. Fragmentation, quotation, interruption and collage become ways of thinking through memory, desire and loss. Publications such as Eros the Bittersweet (1986), Autobiography of Red (1998), The Beauty of the Husband (2001), Nox (2010) and Float (2016) continually challenge readers’ expectations of what poem, an essay, a translation, or a book might be. Yet Carson’s formal innovations never feel merely innovative. They arise from the demands of the subjects she explores. Form is never decoration; it is inquiry.
Carson’s influence
What distinguishes Anne Carson from many of her contemporaries is the combination of intellectual audacity and emotional restraint. She approaches language, literature and human experience with uncommon boldness – yet her work remains marked by a profound attentiveness to absence, uncertainty and what cannot fully be said. Witty, sometimes devastating and almost always unpredictable, her writing asks a great deal of its readers, but rewards that attention with rare intensity. Readers have the sense, reading Carson, of an author who discovers new possibilities within language while remaining acutely aware of its limits.
The influence of Carson’s output is already evident in a younger generation of writers and scholars who move freely between criticism, translation, poetry and creative prose. Many, including myself, have learned from her example that these activities need not be separated from one another. What Carson has bequeathed is not a method to imitate but a sense of intellectual freedom: a willingness to experiment, to embrace uncertainty and to trust that rigorous thinking can itself become an act of literary creation.

items.title: French student protests: comparisons with 1968 will only serve the political extremes
items.summary: Both far left and far right will try to make political capital out of the unrest.
items.body_text:
The student demonstrations that have spread across France in recent weeks are not unprecedented. Indeed, commentators have been quick to point to comparisons with the events of May and June 1968, where, at their peak, more than 10 million students and workers took to the streets.
In 1968, as now, there were legitimate reasons for protest. The unrest began at the Nanterre campus of the University of Paris, which was miles from the city centre and poorly equipped for the changing social norms of the 1960s. In particular, the ban on women and men being able to enter each other’s accommodation was the catalyst for initial demonstrations that then spread into central Paris and beyond.
Today’s parallels with the past are unmistakable. What began in September as a demonstration at the poor quality of high school (lycée) buildings in the Parisian suburbs (this time Saint-Denis) has escalated into wider protests about the conditions facing young people in France today.
In addition to the disproportionate number of missed days of teaching in underprivileged areas, students have been complaining about the appalling insulation of school buildings and the complexity of the post-school training and education application platform.
In 1968, the regime of General Charles de Gaulle came under severe pressure. De Gaulle was so convinced that he would lose control of the situation that he travelled to Germany to meet representatives of the French Army, who would be prepared to “invade” France to protect the general if required.
Despite the best efforts of de Gaulle’s prime minister, Georges Pompidou, police actions against the students, and later the millions of striking workers, were brutal. Now – as then – the police across France have also been accused of heavy-handedness, including firing tear gas directly at protesters. The use of stun grenades has been banned, after a 15-year-old reportedly lost a hand after picking one up at a protest.
Sébastian Lecornu, France’s beleaguered prime minister, has stated that he believes the students and young people have genuine concerns, while also defending the police response.
Revolt and rebellion are nothing new in France. There is a strong history of taking to the streets to protest, dating back to the revolution of 1789 via various revolutions and rebellions – in 1830, 1848, 1871 and 1944, along with many others.
No president of the current Fifth Republic has avoided some form of protest during their time in office. But what makes this wave of demonstrations so interesting is the way that political actors have sought to capitalise on events.
In May and June 1968, the Parti Communiste Français (the French Communist Party, once the biggest political party under the Fourth Republic) condemned the students as bourgeois and were slow to realise the potential of the demonstrations.
Far-left gets the 1968 spirit
By contrast, Jean-Luc Mélenchon of La France Insoumise (LFI), also on the far-left, has been quick to respond. Elected LFI representatives have joined the protests in the street and have in some cases put themselves between police and students. A savvy media operator, who in the past has used holograms to appear in multiple locations at the same time, Mélenchon has made much use of social media to garner support among the youth.
Many of the images developed by LFI and indeed by the protesters themselves have evoked the spirit of May and June 1968. One student was caught on camera with a placard proclaiming that the “6-7” Generation, after the popular meme, was “redoing” May 68.
This nostalgia for protests of the past is serving the far left rather than the political centre. Indeed, Emmanuel Macron, already the least popular president of the current Fifth Republic, is hamstrung by the political stalemate in the National Assembly caused by his own disastrous decision to call elections in June and July 2024.

items.title: Former DR Congo president says the country is 'in peril'
items.summary: Joseph Kabilla said the situation in the country has ‘steadily worsened’ and criticised the government's failure to engage in initiatives to restore peace.
items.body_text:
Rwanda
Speaking to the Congolese people on Friday via his Reconstruct the DRC YouTube channel, former president Joseph Kabilla said the situation in the country has ‘steadily worsened’.
Without naming President Félix Tshisekedi, he denounced personal power guided by the “sole will of the head of state” who “considers the Congo as private property”.
“This has resulted in a system of governance more concerned with maintaining the status quo than with the welfare of the people,” he said.
According to him, the DRC “is no longer a Republic, much less a democratic one," denouncing a governance marked by " the institutionalization of tribalism and nepotism”.
Kabila described what he sees as the discrimination against minorities, the exploitation of state power for political ends, and the mismanagement of state asset and public property.
He also criticised the government’s handling of the conflict in the eastern DRC, saying that continuing the war there would not solve the country’s political and security problems.
Kabila accused Tshisekedi of refusing to engage in initiatives aimed at finding a political solution to the crisis.
“Dialogue is not an option" but rather a necessary path to restoring peace and strengthening national cohesion, he said.
He notably mentioned steps taken by regional organisations in east, southern, and central Africa, as well as by the African Union and certain partner countries.
Kabila reiterated his call for an inclusive national dialogue, an approach he claims is necessary to reconcile the Congolese people, restore national cohesion, and re-establish democracy and the rule of law.
In May last year, he presented a 12-point plan that included ending the war, restoring state authority and the rule of law, reconciling communities, neutralising armed groups, and withdrawing foreign troops.
His statement on Friday comes after Tshisekedi officially launched a “National Dialogue for Peace, Cohesion, and the Refounding of the State” in August.
Scheduled to last a maximum of three months, this process is intended to start at the grassroots level before moving up to national institutions, according to the presidency.
However, its format is seen as divisive. Kabila's political allies contest its modalities and are demanding guarantees of its inclusiveness.
Meanwhile fighting continues on the ground between the Congolese army and the AFC/M23 rebels, supported by Rwanda, while mediation efforts by Washington and Doha are struggling to reach a conclusion.

items.title: Mauritanian PM reappointed hours after resignation over power outages
items.summary: President Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani has tasked Mohamed Ould Cheikh with forming a new government.
items.body_text:
Mauritania
Mauritania's prime minister was reappointed on Friday, just hours after he had resigned over a scathing report into fires at two main electricity substations in the capital Nouakchott.
President Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani met with Mohamed Ould Cheikh and tasked him with forming a new government.
The fires broke out less than 24 hours apart on 21 and 22 August, striking transformer substations belonging to the Mauritanian Electricity Company (Somelec) in Nouakchott and its suburbs.
Subsequent power outages affected large areas of the capital, as well as the towns of Ouad Naga, Idini and Aouleigat, and lasted three to five days.
The report by an independent commission outlined "serious shortcomings regarding prevention, electrical protection, work supervision, and emergency management".
It said the fires were caused by electrical connectors that did not meet required technical standards and had been imported by a private company.
It linked the issues to three newly installed electrical power lines, identifying overheating as the most likely scenario leading to the fires rather than sabotage or operational error.
But it held the company and officials at the Energy Ministry responsible for the incidents.

items.title: Panic in Panama as 7.7 quake hits, cathedral collapses and tsunami warnings spread
items.summary: Panama was hit by a powerful 7.7 earthquake, a 6.6 aftershock and many tremors, damaging buildings and prompting evacuations but no deaths reported.
items.body_text:
Panic in Panama as 7.7 quake hits, cathedral collapses and tsunami warnings spread
A series of strong earthquakes hit Panama on Friday, 9 October, causing damage to buildings and triggering evacuations. Residents rushed into the streets of Panama City, while tremors were also reported in Colombia. In Penonomé, part of a cathedral collapsed, including one of its spires, while footage showed extensive damage to a nearby hotel. Residents in Herrera province also reported cracks and damage to their homes. Tocumen International Airport briefly suspended operations before reopening, while the Panama Canal continued operating normally. According to the US Geological Survey, the first earthquake struck at a depth of 10 kilometres, around 10 kilometres southwest of Pitaloza Arriba in Herrera province. Tsunami warnings were issued for Panama and several neighbouring countries. Panama's president said no deaths had been reported in the immediate aftermath, as emergency teams continued assessing the damage. The country lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a vast zone of seismic and volcanic activity where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

Enemies of Convenience: Ethiopia’s New Opposition Alignment and the Question of What Comes Next
On September 20, 2026, seven Ethiopian armed and political movements announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival, declaring that they sought to remove the Prosperity Party-led government and establish an inclusive transitional government. The announcement was followed by a major TPLF offensive on September 23 across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Federal and allied forces have since regained ground, including Mekelle’s airport, which government-aligned forces said they had retaken on October 3. The fighting is the most serious escalation since the 2020–2022 war.
The coalition’s announced membership included the Amhara Fano National Movement, Oromo Liberation Army, Tigray People’s Liberation Front, Ogaden National Liberation Front, an Afar armed group, Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement. But within days, GPDM and ONLF publicly denied joining. That matters: even the coalition’s composition is contested.
Former Adversaries, Conflicting Objectives
The three most consequential armed actors are the TPLF, Fano and OLA. Their histories and political objectives are sharply different. Shared opposition to Addis Ababa does not erase those differences.
Ethiopian politics has repeatedly produced alliances of convenience. TPLF and OLF were once partners in the 1991 transition, but the TPLF pushed the OLF out in 1993. The OLF was later outlawed, while thousands of suspectedsupporters were detained or killed during successive security campaigns. When the OLF returned from exile after Abiy came to power, it entered politics as a legal party, but armed factions continued fighting as the OLA.
The contradiction with Fano is even deeper. Fano presents the post-1991 political order and ethnic federalism as a source of Ethiopia’s fragmentation and as an arrangement hostile to Amhara interests. The OLA, by contrast, continues to pursue an Oromo nationalist project, with prominent OLA figures publicly describing independence as an objective. Fano and Oromo armed movements have also accused each other of atrocities and territorial aggression. These are not minor disagreements that can simply be postponed until after victory.
From Wartime Enemies to Unlikely Allies
The most striking feature of the new alignment is the relationship between the TPLF, Fano and Eritrea. During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean forces and Fano fought alongside the federal government against the TPLF. The Pretoria Peace Agreement ended that war in November 2022, but Eritrea and Fano were not parties to the agreement. Though some analysts have argued that their exclusion left important grievances unresolved, the deeper source of their discontent was their belief that they were in a position not only to defeat the TPLF but potentially to eliminate it as a military and political force, and that the federal government had effectively rescued the TPLF by agreeing to the peace deal.
The agreement also created a new dispute between the TPLF and Addis Ababa over disarmament, territory and the administration of Tigray. The TPLF’s subsequent struggle with the federal government in violation of the Pretoria peace agreement contributed to a deeper political and military split inside Tigray. Tigrayan fighters dissatisfied with the TPLF’s course broke away in 2025 and formed the Tigray Peace Force, which has received apparent support from federal authorities. The TPF has since fought alongside federal forces against TPLF forces.
This history makes the current alignment remarkable. Former battlefield enemies are now cooperating against the government they once fought alongside or, in the TPLF’s case, fought against.

items.body_text:
Ethiopia’s volatile politics: the June 2026 parliamentary elections, the National Dialogue, and violent conflict
In a surprise to absolutely no one, Ethiopia’s ruling Prosperity Party (PP) led by PM Abiy Ahmed won the 1 June 2026 parliamentary elections in a landslide. The outcome has evoked few commentaries in the global media or even in Ethiopia itself. There was a c. 90% win of parliamentary seats for the PP. This is, like in previous elections (2021, or 2015), a kind of Communist country result. It indeed was a well-organised operation, a classic case of what in Ethiopia since the Derg-regime (1974-1991) is called an “organisational operation” (Amharic: dirigitawi sera). That may be regretted or lauded but reflects political reality. Ethiopia still has no deep-rooted democratic political culture, certainly not on the national level: there was always violent competition for power and lack of freedoms, and people mostly went to the polls because of a mixture of duty, pride, and fear.
At around the same time, in August, some results of the ‘National Dialogue’ process were announced – a nation-wide ambitious consultation initiated in 2022 and closed off after a conference (15 July-22 August), and they may prove to be more important than the elections as such. The yet unpublished full recommendations of this unique although not perfect Dialogue were offered to the federal government on 3 October and will have to be addressed by the newly elected parliament. Interesting in the discussions and the recommendations was a growing ambivalence about ‘ethnic politics’.
First about the June elections. What did they show? Technically efficient, they were a repeat of the process of elite consolidation: the incumbent can continue as usual. The security situation also prevented voting in at least 143 polling stations in 46 constituencies. Since early September we also saw an escalation of violent strife, especially in Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia Regions, and the national political arena seems to further fragment: clearly, the elections did not have a stabilising effect.
What few people talk about is the electoral system that facilitates the return of the incumbent party, time and again. Ethiopia does not have proportional representation but a district system, with a ‘first past the post’ mechanism (created by the previous, EPRDF regime). It means that the more parties participate (there were 48 registered parties..), the more the chances are that the most powerful and influential party – of course the one in power, i.e., the PP – will reach the threshold first, even if it has, say, only 15% of the votes in the voting district. In addition, there is a, to many analysts, unhealthy preponderance of ethnic-based parties: a divisive element in any election system, leading to uncritical, loyalty block-voting rather than a focus on issue politics and coalitions or on evaluating the concrete results and human impact of policies. My argument is that this ‘district system’ and the ethno-federal formula mean that the incumbent cannot lose. This hinders effective democratic representation. In an alternative system, however, ‘ethnic’ parties should be discouraged, because that would, under current conditions of elite politics’, de facto continue the ethnic block voting. Realistically, however, this will not happen soon, and thus, political quagmire and conflicts will continue.
With PP hegemony in parliament confirmed and only a marginal role for opposition parties or civil-society forces, the question is if pressing national concerns will be tackled in a new way. These include the (effects of) ongoing armed conflicts, the large number of IDPs, regionally unbalanced developmental policies, the weak justice system, and the perpetual economic problems. This is not to deny the achievements: the completion of the Blue Nile dam for hydro-electric power generation, the new initiatives in infrastructure expansion, digitalisation of the economy and services, agra

items.body_text:
How Zambia Defeated an Election Petition Without Ever Arguing the Case
Zambia’s 13 August general election was already fraught before anyone tried to challenge its result, according to an account human rights lawyer Linda Kasonde has since published on her Substack. The army had been deployed to polling stations, she writes, a role outside its constitutional mandate. The Electoral Commission suspended vote tallying for six hours over reports of attacks on polling agents, during which only police and soldiers had access to the ballots. Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile’s home was raided and eleven of his associates were abducted. Former Cabinet Minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot in the same raid. Authorities denied the killing for five days, until a habeas corpus application forced them to confirm it. Hakainde Hichilema was declared the winner on 18 August with around 61 percent against Mundubile’s 38 percent, though the Christian Churches Monitoring Group’s own assessment of its parallel vote tabulation had projected a closer 56 percent.
It is against that backdrop that Linda Kasonde decided to petition the result. Kasonde is a human rights lawyer and former president of the Law Association of Zambia. She petitioned under Article 103(1)(b) of the Constitution, which allows any citizen to challenge an election on the ground that it was not free and fair. She had seven days from the declaration to file, under Article 101(4). She did not get seven days. On 24 August, a day before her deadline, the government shut down the courts. The closures covered the Constitutional Court, the Supreme Court, the High Court in Lusaka, and premises in Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone. The stated reason was unspecified security concerns. Police later described the closuresas nationwide security risk assessments at government premises, without saying what threat had prompted them. The closure lasted until 27 August. In an essay she has since published on her Substack, Kasonde describes what she did next.
In her account, she writes that she had tried to file electronically before, under new e-filing rules introduced in May 2026, and had been told the rules were not yet operational. With the courthouses sealed, she tried again anyway, emailing her petition to the Chief Registrar’s official address. The judiciary’s website, she says she was told, had been disabled. So she sent the documents to Chief Justice Mumba Malila’s personal email instead, explaining that the shutdown had left her no other option. A day later, Kasonde recounts, the judiciary’s public relations office confirmed receipt, and the Chief Justice himself said that while the method was “highly irregular,” he would forward the documents to the Constitutional Court. Kasonde describes the relief as short-lived. A separate statement soon followed from the Chief Administrator, asserting that no petition had been received by the deadline. The Secretary to the Cabinet then announced that Hichilema’s inauguration would proceed on 1 September, citing that same claim.
This is worth pausing on, because it is not the same story as an election being rigged. The government never had to win an argument about the vote count. It only had to keep the question of whether a petition existed unresolved for as long as the Constitution’s window allowed. It then declared that no petition existed, even though its own Chief Justice had said otherwise days earlier. Human Rights Watch called the closures a direct denial of access to justice. Zambia’s Chapter One Foundation has since petitioned the Constitutional Court to declare the shutdown itself unlawful, a case the judiciary has yet to determine.
That distinction matters more than it might look. An election stolen at the ballot box is a familiar kind of theft, and African courts, however imperfectly, have a template for adjudicating it. items.title: Tigray insurgency withers as federal forces enter Shire and resume flights to Mekelle
items.summary: Defections and retreating rebels leave a power vacuum in northern Ethiopia, raising the stakes in an escalating diplomatic standoff over sea access.
items.body_text:
Ethiopia and Eritrea each accused the other of starting a war on Friday as an internal Ethiopian conflict threatened to escalate into a regional war.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and they fought a brutal border war from 1998 to 2000.
Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of backing rebels in its northern Tigray state, who launched attacks against federal forces last month.
The two countries severed diplomatic relations last week, and since then, Eritrean forces have invaded Ethiopian territory, with a foreign security source estimating it has 5,000 to 8,000 troops in Tigray.
Eritrea’s conduct is “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos wrote in a letter to diplomats.
Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, responded on X that it was facing “an unprovoked war of aggression” from Ethiopia.
Over the past week, the Ethiopian army has pushed back the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and seized their capital, Mekelle.
It has also launched drone strikes against the Eritrean troops in the region, forcing them into an apparent retreat, though a lack of access for media makes verification difficult.
Rebels lose cities
Witnesses told AFP on Friday that the rebels had lost two other cities in Tigray: Shire and Adigrat.
A Shire resident said pro-government forces had entered the city on Friday afternoon.
“People are coming out to watch the armed fighters arriving. Shops are closed. To prevent looting, residents have organised themselves in their respective neighbourhoods and are guarding their areas,” the resident said.
An aid worker in Shire said rebel fighters and the local administration abandoned the city on Wednesday, and that four people had been killed in exchanges of fire related to the looting.
Eritrean forces were seen in Adigrat in recent days before being targeted by Ethiopian drone strikes, according to a conflict monitor and witnesses.
The rebels were retreating to Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, according to a Tigrayan official from a TPLF dissident faction.
In a sign of renewed government confidence, Ethiopian Airlines said flights to the Tigrayan capital would resume from Sunday.
Kjetil Tronvoll, regional specialist at Oslo New University College, told AFP the government would likely appoint a new interim administration for the region.
He said the TPLF was “withering”, with low morale and frustration with their leaders.
“Many are defecting and going back to their villages,” he said.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed could press his advantage and push into Eritrea, Tronvoll warned.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly insisted that it has a right to direct sea access, which Eritrea interprets as a threat to invade and seize its port at Assab.
“The hysterical infatuation with the Red Sea must also be seen with previous intentions to wage a war of invasion against Eritrea,” the Eritrean information minister said.
Authorities in both countries have not responded to AFP requests for comment.
Relations initially improved when Abiy came to power in Ethiopia in 2018, and Eritrea even fought alongside Ethiopia during the latter’s 2020-2022 civil war against the TPLF.
But relations deteriorated after the war, with Eritrea angry over the way it was concluded, and fearing an Ethiopian invasion.

items.title: US vows to ‘cripple ICC’ as former judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
items.summary: ‘Unapologetic pursuit of national power’ butts heads with ‘unaccountable global arbiter’, as America sanctions the International Criminal Court.
items.body_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay of South Africa won the Nobel Peace Prize.
“President [Donald] Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said in a video statement. “That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told Reuters the sanctions “must be condemned” and vowed that the court would fight on. “The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing,” Khan said.
The new sanctions mark a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s fight to undermine a global body that has infuriated the US by issuing arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant and investigating alleged war crimes by US service members in Afghanistan. Pillay chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
Neither the US nor Israel are a party to the Rome Statute that established the ICC.
International campaign to dismantle ICC
The second Trump administration first announced visa restrictions and financial penalties for people who help the ICC investigate US citizens and US allies in February 2025. Since then, the US has sanctioned more than a dozen judges and other court officials.
In July, Rubio launched an international campaign to dismantle the court, calling it a threat to US sovereignty. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defence, to rein in the court,” Rubio said. “If they do not, the US will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.”
The pressure campaign has had some effect. The authoritarian states of Chad and Venezuela withdrew in late July, with Chadian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul citing US pressure.
The putschist-run Sahel countries of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso announced their withdrawal last year, calling the court an “instrument of neocolonial repression in the hands of imperialism.” All three are allies of Russia, whose President Vladimir Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant over his invasion of Ukraine.
Opposing visions
The timing of the sanctions pits the US squarely against a global activist community that applauds Pillay’s recognition as a victory for human rights around the world.
At a press conference this afternoon in the historic Nuremberg courtroom where Nazi dignitaries were tried in 1945-1946, Pillay dedicated the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes”.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, who clashed with Trump over false accusations of “white genocide” in his crime-ridden country, celebrated “the progressive contributions [Pillay] has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally”.
“She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can, and should be, a better place,” Ramaphosa said.
Using altogether different rhetoric, Rubio heralded the Trump administration’s “unapologetic pursuit of national power” while embracing a united West “at the head of the world” at a speech at the Acropolis in Greece earlier this week that fuelled speculation of his 2028 presidential ambitions.
Sour grapes
Trump has made it abundantly clear that he believes he should win the prize, falsely claiming that he has ended eight wars – even as he started one with Iran – while undeservedly accepting the Nobel offered up by 2025 winner of Venezuelan opposition activist Mar
