items.title: Why Afghanistan’s Neighbors Have Not Backed Pakistan’s Strikes on the Taliban
items.summary: China, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan are less exposed to the impact of cross-border terrorism – and less willing to risk smooth relations with Kabul over the issue.
items.body_text:
On October 5, Moscow hosted the eighth meeting of the special representatives and senior officials from regional countries for the Moscow Format to discuss political and economic relations with Afghanistan and counterterrorism and counter-narcotics cooperation. The Moscow Format includes Afghanistan, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan.
But the meeting failed to adopt a joint statement because the Pakistani and Afghan delegates disagreed over the language on terrorism. The Taliban objected to the frequent mention of terrorism in reference to Afghanistan.
Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, said the Afghan delegates accepted similar language last year. He believed that the changed relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan might have caused Kabul’s objection this time.
The meeting was held only a week after the most recent confrontation between Islamabad and Kabul. On September 18 and 26, Pakistan suffered deadly terrorist attacks in its northwestern province, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, that together killed about 44 people and injured about 138. Pakistan responded with airstrikes on different targets in Afghanistan that it believes were the training camps and hideouts of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its associated factions responsible for the cross-border attacks.
At the Moscow summit, Pakistan’s delegation said the Taliban were complicit in those attacks in Pakistan because the terrorist groups were operating on Afghan soil with impunity. The Taliban said Pakistan was using military aggression in violation of international law for an issue that could be resolved through political negotiations.
The Moscow Format meeting failed to bridge these differences enough to allow for a joint communique. What’s noteworthy is that other countries that share borders with Afghanistan – such as China, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – did not use their diplomatic capital to reach an understanding on language that included everyone’s concerns.
Afghanistan’s neighbors have different levels of concern about militancy there. Their strategies, especially on counterterrorism, are a function of the nature of their border with Afghanistan, the extent of the threat from militant groups on Afghan soil, and the Taliban’s scale of cooperation regarding those groups. From their perspective, military force is not the most effective solution to address the issue.
China shares a border of only about 92 kilometers with Afghanistan, high in the Wakhan Corridor, marked by rough terrain and the nearly 5,000-meter high Wakhjir Pass. In terms of a terrorist presence in Afghanistan, Beijing considers the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) its main concern and has pressed the Taliban to act against the group. The Taliban have reportedly relocated ETIM fighters away from the border, and they now have a dispersed presence. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat to China is smaller, and any movement across the pass is easy to detect.
Uzbekistan similarly shares a short border of 144 kilometers with Afghanistan, almost entirely along the Amu Darya. Regular cross-border movement is concentrated at the closely guarded Termez-Hairatan road and rail crossing. But the militant groups in Afghanistan that concern Tashkent have shown only a limited capacity for cross-border attacks. There was one incident in 2022 of rockets being fired toward Termez, which didn’t cause any casualties. Therefore, the immediate cross-border threat is relatively small and easier to contain.
Tajikistan’s case is closer to Pakistan’s in terms of the long border and threat. Dushanbe shares about 1,374 kilometers of border with Afghanistan, much of which runs along the Panj River and passes through remote and mountainous territory and is difficult to monitor consistently. items.title: The US and China Cannot Slow the AI Race, But They Can Make It Safer
items.summary: The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in AI safety cooperation.
items.body_text:
The most important shift in artificial intelligence (AI) is not that models are becoming more intelligent, but that they are becoming more capable of acting.
Much of the first wave of AI safety governance focused on misinformation, bias, deepfakes, privacy violations and harmful content. Those risks remain. But increasingly capable AI agents can plan, write and execute code, use tools, obtain credentials, and interact with external systems. Recent incidents in which OpenAI’s autonomous systems slipped past their constraints show that as agents gain tools and autonomy, the boundary between a model and the outside world becomes harder to enforce.
That makes AI safety a collective-action problem. The AI superpowers face a prisoner’s dilemma. If one laboratory slows while competitors continue, it may lose its edge. Disclosure creates a similar tension: reporting failures can make the wider ecosystem safer, but the discloser bears the costs and may expose vulnerabilities to attackers. Governments face the same strategic impasse as the firms. Washington fears that slowing its AI development will allow China to catch up; Beijing fears that doing so will leave it further behind.
Yet cooperation can be narrow on AI safety. The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in such cooperation. It has an interest in ensuring that AI-enabled cyber incidents are contained before they cascade through third countries, shared software infrastructure and global supply chains. China has the same systemic interest.
This collective action has significant implications for middle-power countries. Helping others repair a vulnerability can be a form of systemic containment and a public good.
The Accelerating AI Race
The AI arms race is intensifying.
U.S. President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow U.S. AI development, framing continued technological leadership as essential to winning the AI race. On September 29, he convened major technology companies at the White House, where six firms – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia – signed a voluntary accord built around four layers of oversight: internal capability assessments, internal audit teams, independent external auditors, and board-level review. His administration ordered federal agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence,” presenting the technology as a source of economic and strategic leadership.
Taken together, these moves point to a U.S. approach combining continued AI power with developer responsibility, voluntary industry controls, external scrutiny, and ex-post legal accountability.
China approaches the problem through a more centrally coordinated system. In May 2026, guidelines on AI agents, issued jointly by the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, made “safety and controllability” a baseline requirement for agent development and deployment. Governance is tiered, with tighter filing, testing and recall requirements for agents used in sensitive sectors.
On September 14, China’s AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 reiterated “safety and controllability” while updating its classification of AI risks and associated technical and governance measures.
Despite their institutional differences, the two approaches converge on one point: neither country wants safety policy to halt AI development, and both increasingly recognize that greater autonomy creates new problems of control.
Common Ground and Shared Risks
AI systems rest on overlapping technological foundations. Chinese AI development has relied heavily on U.S. chips and, in some cases, U.S. cloud infrastructure. Export controls may weaken those hardware links, but the stronger case for joint risk management lies in the software and services AI systems share.

items.title: Myanmar’s Leaders Tried to Erase My Rohingya Identity 11 Years Ago
items.summary: The repression of Rohingya identity is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order. It's time for ASEAN to realize that.
items.body_text:
In July 2015, I was invited to the residence of U Aung Thaung, a senior and influential leader of Myanmar’s Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP), in Naypyidaw. We discussed the approaching general elections and parliamentary nominations for the constituencies in northern Rakhine state.
What happened during that meeting has remained outside the public record for more than 11 years. I want to disclose it now because the political question at its center – the recognition of Rohingya identity and rights – remains unresolved. It is also relevant to how ASEAN engages with Myanmar’s military leadership today.
I was elected to Myanmar’s house of parliament, the Pyithu Hluttaw, from Buthitaung township of Rakhine state in November 2010 as a USDP candidate. In the summer of 2015 I was preparing to secure my office for another term. But, during our private conversation, U Aung Thaung proposed a condition that went far beyond ordinary electoral politics.
As I recall it, he told me that he, the USDP leadership, President U Thein Sein, and then Commander-in-Chief Min Aung Hlaing did not accept “Rohingya” as an ethnic identity. He urged me to stop advocating for that identity and to persuade my constituents to identify themselves as “Bengali” instead. He presented this change as a pathway toward obtaining citizenship documentation and restoring political participation. He also advised me to give a media interview stating that “there is no Rohingya but Bengali,” without mentioning our private meeting and his name.
My parliamentary nomination, he indicated, depended on my willingness to support that position.
I refused.
I could not ask my constituents to surrender their identity in exchange for the possibility of receiving documents, voting rights, or another parliamentary term. Political representation should protect the rights of a community, not become an instrument for bargaining those rights away.
U Aung Thaung encouraged me to consult my constituents and reconsider. I subsequently informed community leaders and constituents about the conversation. They supported my position and we were all on the same page. I did not disclose the meeting to the media at that time because of the political consequences of making such an account public while living in Myanmar.
During my visit, I saw large portraits of President Thein Sein, Min Aung Hlaing, and nationalist Buddhist monk U Wirathu in an office at the residence. An assistant told me that the office also served U Wirathu whenever he comes to Naypyidaw. These are my recollections of what I saw and I was told 11 years ago.
The statements about Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing were made to me by U Aung Thaung. I cannot claim that I heard either man personally authorize the proposal. But U Aung Thaung confirmed the proposal with Union Immigration Minister U Khin Yi, today’s USDP chairman and speaker of Pyithu Hluttaw, over the phone in front of me.
The central proposition was unmistakable: I was being asked to abandon public advocacy for the identity of the people I represented as a condition of continuing my political career.
On August 4, 2015, I resigned from the USDP. Two days later, I applied to contest the upcoming Pyithu Hluttaw election as an independent candidate for Buthitaung.
On August 22, the Maungdaw District Election Subcommission rejected my candidacy. Its decision concluded that my parents had not been Myanmar citizens at the time of my birth in 1965. I appealed, together with concrete documents, to the Rakhine State Election Subcommission, which upheld the rejection on September 1, 2015. The Union Election Commission subsequently affirmed the decision, communicating its ruling in a letter dated September 6, 2015.
This outcome presented a profound contradiction in my political life.

items.title: Samsung dangles $560,000 bonuses to keep engineers from China
items.summary: A Samsung memory chip worker earning about $60,000 a year could receive roughly $560,000 in bonuses before tax, according to the company’s largest union. Its estimate includes both Samsung’s existing profit-sharing bonus and a new special payment. Samsung hasn’t confirmed the amount. On October 7, the company outlined how that special bonus would work: 10.5% […] The post Samsung dangles $560,000 bonuses to keep engineers from China appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
A Samsung memory chip worker earning about $60,000 a year could receive roughly $560,000 in bonuses before tax, according to the company’s largest union. Its estimate includes both Samsung’s existing profit-sharing bonus and a new special payment. Samsung hasn’t confirmed the amount.
On October 7, the company outlined how that special bonus would work: 10.5% of its chip division’s 2026 operating profit would go into an uncapped pool. Samsung plans to pay it in shares, subject to shareholder approval.
The next morning, Samsung estimated third-quarter operating profit at 107.4 trillion won, roughly $80 billion, almost nine times the year-earlier figure.
Those profits explain how Samsung can afford the payout. Findings released for a parliamentary audit the same week show the competition for the engineers it wants to keep.
What did the audit find?
The office of Choi Soo-jin, a People Power Party lawmaker on the National Assembly’s science and ICT committee, reviewed LinkedIn and other public career records. It traced at least 27 senior engineers from Samsung and SK Hynix who went on to work at ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China’s biggest DRAM maker.
Together they had spent 415.9 years at the two Korean companies, an average of 15.4 years each. Six were principal or executive-level staff with more than 20 years in mass production.
Eight worked in circuit design and seven in process integration. Others came from equipment, yield analysis, and advanced packaging, a mix that Dong-A Ilbo said was enough to run a whole chip factory.
Messages from Chinese headhunters obtained by Choi’s office offered pay increases of 60% to 100%, three to five years of guaranteed employment, rental housing, and help with children’s school costs.
Fifteen of the 27 didn’t go straight to CXMT. They first took jobs at equipment or materials suppliers, foreign companies, or universities. Choi’s office said that may have been a way around non-compete agreements, which usually last one to two years.
Why does it matter that they left CXMT?
The engineers stayed at CXMT for 2.9 years on average. According to their public profiles, 26 of the 27 have since left, and seven moved on to other Chinese chip companies, including Huawei’s Hong Kong research center and HiSilicon.
Public career records don’t establish why they left or whether any technology was transferred. But CXMT grew quickly over the same years. Its research and development staff rose from 2,606 at the end of 2022 to 7,491 in June 2026, and in September it said its fifth-generation DRAM was in mass production.
Choi’s office suggested CXMT had drawn on the engineers’ experience to build its factories and stabilize production. That illustrates the retention problem: experienced engineers can help a competitor build capabilities that remain after they leave.
Why bonuses rather than bans?
Seoul’s legal tools are limited. “There is no legal basis to crack down on or restrict lawful overseas hiring,” Korea’s industry ministry said, according to Dong-A Ilbo. Non-compete clauses expire, and the detours through suppliers and universities suggest they can be waited out.
Interest in working abroad extends beyond the chip industry. In a Bank of Korea survey of 2,694 researchers with master’s or doctoral degrees, 42.9% of those working in Korea said they were thinking about moving abroad within three years.
So the companies are competing on pay. SK Hynix moved first. Its profit-sharing system sets aside 10% of operating profit for employees, and a labor deal in late 2025 removed the old cap of 1,000% of base salary for the next 10 years.
The first payout under the new terms came to 2,964% of base salary, with a fifth of each payout deferred over two years, KED Global reported. A company official told the outlet the system was expected to curb talent losses to domestic and overseas rivals.
Samsung’s new plan follows the same logic. The special bonus arrives as shares, and most of them can’t be sold right away

items.title: Anduril’s plan to save US sub edge from China’s undersea surge
items.summary: A multibillion-dollar private initiative to overhaul US submarine manufacturing marks an urgent push to revitalize naval industrial capacity at a pivotal moment in the Indo-Pacific balance of power. This month, multiple media outlets reported that defense technology firm Anduril Industries will invest US$3.7 billion of its own capital to build a 2-million-square-foot “software-defined shipyard” at […] The post Anduril’s plan to save US sub edge from China’s undersea surge appeared first on Asia
items.body_text:
A multibillion-dollar private initiative to overhaul US submarine manufacturing marks an urgent push to revitalize naval industrial capacity at a pivotal moment in the Indo-Pacific balance of power.
This month, multiple media outlets reported that defense technology firm Anduril Industries will invest US$3.7 billion of its own capital to build a 2-million-square-foot “software-defined shipyard” at Sparrows Point in Baltimore County, Maryland, to expand US Navy submarine production capacity, according to company and defense officials.
Under a complementary US Navy contract worth up to $2.9 billion, with disbursements tied strictly to demonstrated production outcomes, the total $6.6 billion public-private venture aims to relieve severe bottlenecks in the Virginia-class nuclear attack submarine (SSN) program.
Dubbed “Arsenal-2,” the coastal facility will feature a 1,200-foot graving dock, direct rail access, and digitized workflow tracking, creating 3,100 direct manufacturing jobs and adding roughly nine million annual labor hours — a vital 15% capacity boost to the nation’s strained nuclear shipbuilding industrial base.
The intervention comes as legacy shipbuilders General Dynamics Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Newport News Shipbuilding continue to struggle to meet the US Navy’s minimum goal of two hulls annually.
To bridge near-term operational needs, Anduril will begin delivering critical gating components, such as torpedo tubes, from a certified Costa Mesa site by 2028, before Maryland operations begin around 2030, with long-term plans to supply full hull modules and help meet domestic fleet goals alongside AUKUS defense pact delivery commitments to Australia.
This private-sector expansion raises the question of whether the US can overcome domestic shipbuilding bottlenecks to maintain its undersea warfighting edge as China rapidly expands and modernizes its submarine fleet. The facility could boost US submarine production at a time when conventional shipyards repeatedly miss scheduled delivery milestones.
The scale of that industrial deficit is severe. A January 2026 US Congressional Research Service (CRS) report notes that while the US Navy aims to achieve a fleet goal of 66 SSNs, actual construction has never reached that threshold and has averaged just 1.1 to 1.2 boats per year since 2022 because of persistent workforce shortages, supplier bottlenecks, and component delays.
The CRS report notes that the US Navy is now pushing to raise production to 2.0 boats annually and eventually 2.33 per year to reduce backlogs, sustain domestic fleet requirements, and build replacements for three to five Virginia-class SSNs slated for sale to Australia under the AUKUS security pact.
These ongoing industrial delays affect Western Pacific operations, where attack submarines are vital to the US in a possible conflict with China over Taiwan, and forward deployments reaffirm their strategic importance.
Demonstrating that operational footprint, a June 2026 report by the South China Sea Probing Initiative (SCSPI), a Chinese think tank, found that in 2025 the US operated at least 11 nuclear-powered submarines in three Western Pacific operational corridors—the South China Sea, East China Sea, and Java Sea—to demonstrate forward presence and signal a clear undersea deterrence posture against China.
In a high-intensity Taiwan conflict, that forward undersea posture forms the tip of the US spear. In a May 2026 article for the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Seth Jones says US SSNs provide an asymmetric operational advantage over China by exploiting the latter’s persistent anti-submarine warfare (ASW) deficiencies.
Jones notes that in simulated Taiwan Strait conflict scenarios, SSNs play a critical warfighting role by inflicting heavy attrition on Chinese invasion forces and hunting high-value amphibious vessels, surface escorts, and logistics ships.

items.title: Moving B-1 bombers from UK to US is no drone warfare solution
items.summary: On October 4, the US pulled its 12 B-1 strategic bombers out of Fairford, UK and returned them to the United States. Reports say the planes returned to Ellsworth Air Force Base in Rapid City, South Dakota. The bombers were pulled out when intelligence reported that an attack by armed drones against Fairford was imminent. […] The post Moving B-1 bombers from UK to US is no drone warfare solution appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
On October 4, the US pulled its 12 B-1 strategic bombers out of Fairford, UK and returned them to the United States. Reports say the planes returned to Ellsworth Air Force Base in Rapid City, South Dakota. The bombers were pulled out when intelligence reported that an attack by armed drones against Fairford was imminent.
While the US may have prevented an unnamed enemy, generally believed to be Iran, from executing a strike on the bombers and support infrastructure at Fairford, bringing the bombers back to the United States does not mean they are out of danger.
There were over 350 unauthorized drone incursions detected across roughly 100 domestic US military installations, alongside widespread civilian mass sightings in late 2024, particularly across the Northeast and in New Jersey.
In 2025, the high volume continued across both domestic military sites and borders, including tracking tens of thousands of drone movements along the southern border, and prompting congressional investigations and enhanced counter-UAS authorities. In 2026 (so far) the frequency remains high.
In the UK a series of unauthorized drone incursions affected four primary Royal Air Force bases utilized by the US Air Force in England including RAF Lakenheath, RAF Mildenhall. RAF Feltwell and RAF Fairford. In addition at RAF Akrotiri, the British Royal Air Force base in Cyprus, was struck by an Iranian-manufactured Shahed-type loitering munition on March 1, 2026.
The US uses Akrotiri for regional reconnaissance, intelligence operations, and force deployments. This includes hosting US Air Force units—such as Detachment 1 of the 9th Reconnaissance Wing supporting reconnaissance aircraft like the U-2—as well as shared intelligence and security detachments.
At Fairford intelligence suggested that the possible attack would be launched from trucks carrying drones, similar to the way Ukraine attacked Russia in Operation Spiderweb in June 2025.
In that operation, Ukrainian operatives smuggled large quantities of first-person-view (FPV) attack drones deep inside Russian territory, concealed inside wooden cabins mounted on the back of commercial trucks.
The drones were then launched from close proximity to the targeted airfields. The drones hit multiple deep-interior Russian air bases spanning multiple time zones, including Olenya, Ivanovo Severny, Dyagilevo, Belaya (Siberia), and Ukrainka.
The operation targeted Russia’s long-range strategic bomber fleet (such as Tu-95MS and Tu-22M3 aircraft used to launch cruise missiles against Ukraine), destroying or damaging multiple high-value aircraft.
The severity of the drone threat to US airbases and other sensitive sites (including dams, nuclear power plants, communications and energy infrastructure) is unclear. US and UK authorities do not typically release information on drone incursions unless they have to do so from public pressure.
Ellsworth is not necessarily safe. Local law enforcement and base officials previously reported multiple unauthorized drone sightings and incursions in restricted airspace near the base.
For instance, the Meade County Sheriff’s Office issued warnings regarding multiple waves of unauthorized drones spotted north of the base, prompting local authorities and base defense to remind the public that the installation is a strict “no-drone zone.”
It would be highly unusual for a single drone operator to run multiple waves of drones, suggesting that Ellsworth, like Barksdale and other sensitive sites, have been extensively reconnoitered by an adversary or adversaries.
A few drones recovered around US bases do not tell us a great deal. All of them are commercial drones (primarily of Chinese origin), just as the drones flying across the US southern border are commercial drones from China, sometimes modified to carry explosives or transit drugs such as fentanyl.

items.title: Africans disproportionately targeted by ICC – investigative journalist
items.summary: David Hundeyin has accused the ICC of disproportionately targeting Africans and failing to prosecute war crimes elsewhere Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Africans disproportionately targeted by ICC – investigative journalist
The International Criminal Court (ICC) disproportionately targets Africans while failing to hold perpetrators of war crimes elsewhere accountable, Nigerian investigative journalist David Hundeyin has told RT.
Hundeyin questioned the court’s record, claiming that Africans account for more than 90% of those prosecuted under the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. “It’s either crimes against humanity only happen in Africa, or Africans are disproportionately targeted by the ICC,” he said. The journalist disputed the ICC’s impartiality, asking whether it has become an instrument of selective justice.
Hundeyin said the ICC could be considered “useless or toothless” at best, or, at worst, a tool used specifically to target Africans.
Geopolitical analyst and author Kim Heller has also questioned the ICC’s credibility, accusing it of pursuing decades-old cases involving African figures while failing to address ongoing atrocities elsewhere. Speaking to RT following the sentencing of two former militia leaders from the Central African Republic last July, she described the court as embodying a “hierarchy of justice” in which Western political and military leaders escape accountability.
Established in 2002, the court is tasked with prosecuting genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression, and relies heavily on the cooperation of its 125 members. However, some of the world’s most powerful states, including the US, China, India and Russia, reject its authority.
The court has long faced accusations of selective justice and political bias. Chad recently notified the UN of its decision to withdraw from the ICC, accusing the tribunal of disproportionately targeting countries in Africa. The Chadian Foreign Ministry claimed that nine of the 13 investigations it counted concerned African states, describing the court’s effectiveness as “limited and uneven.”
Chad’s decision followed similar moves by Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, which previously denounced the ICC as an “instrument of neocolonial repression.” The ICC has warned that such withdrawals risk weakening international efforts to end impunity.

Another Sudanese rebel commander defects to army – media
Another senior commander of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has defected to the Sudanese army, bringing around 300 fighters and 30 military vehicles with him, The Sudan Times reported on Thursday.
Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq al-Fanjari, who identified himself as commander of the RSF’s Special Tasks Group, announced his departure in a video circulated on Thursday. He described the conflict as a “futile war.”
“I, Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq al-Fanjari ... announce my resignation and withdrawal from all military duties and responsibilities within the ranks of the Rapid Support Forces,” he said. Fanjari apologized to Sudanese families who had lost relatives, been displaced or suffered during the fighting.
The local news agency said the number of personnel accompanying Fanjari could not be independently verified, while the RSF has not publicly confirmed the scale of the reported defection.
The move comes as Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has ruled out negotiations with the RSF, pledging to continue military operations until the paramilitary group is defeated. “We say it again: We have no negotiations with anyone, we are not speaking with anyone, and we have nothing to do with anyone,” Burhan said on Tuesday during a visit to Northern State.
Sudan’s conflict erupted in April 2023 following months of tensions between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
Several senior RSF commanders have switched sides since 2024. Abuagla Keikal, commander of the Sudan Shield Forces, defected in October that year, followed by Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, known as Al-Nour al-Qubba, in April 2026 and Ali Rizqallah, also known as Al-Savana, in May 2026.

items.title: Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of ‘all-out invasion’
items.summary: Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an “all-out invasion” and appealed for international support, citing its right to self-defense Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of ‘all-out invasion’
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of sending troops deep into its territory and warned that it must defend itself against an “all-out invasion,” escalating a confrontation between the former allies.
Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos alleged that Eritrean forces, including mechanized units, had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray. His October 8 letter was addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and circulated to other UN Security Council members, Reuters reported Friday. The letter described the incursion as a “blatant act of aggression” and sought international support for Ethiopia’s right to self-defense.
Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Gedion briefed UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed on what it called Eritrea’s “continued aggression,” demanded the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean forces and urged a “clear and principled UN response.”
In separate talks with senior UN officials, Ethiopian State Minister Berhanu Tsegaye alleged direct Eritrean military involvement “across different fronts along the border” and called for the UN to unequivocally condemn the “flagrant violations of sovereignty.”
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected Ethiopia’s accusations on Friday, calling them “audacity and duplicity in their most extreme forms.” He accused Addis Ababa of pursuing a war of aggression for more than three years, citing statements by Ethiopian leaders about acquiring sovereign access to the Red Sea and taking control of the port of Assab.
There are fears that renewed clashes between federal forces and Tigrayan fighters could plunge northern Ethiopia back into war. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which formed an alliance with six other armed groups seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, declared a “defensive war” last month. Its forces seized airports in Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, and the cities of Axum and Shire, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the region.
On Sunday, the government-allied Tigray Peace Force announced it had retaken Mekelle following the TPLF’s withdrawal. The TPLF said it had decided to “temporarily leave” and operate from another location while continuing military operations.
Conflict monitor ACLED reported suspected Ethiopian drone strikes against Eritrean forces near the border town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday. A resident told Reuters that explosions continued overnight into Friday.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Egypt, and Sudan of supporting the rebel alliance. The three countries have rejected the allegations. Last week, Addis Ababa expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara, prompting Eritrea to sever diplomatic ties. Eritrean troops previously backed Ethiopia’s federal army during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, which ended with the Pretoria peace agreement.
Relations with Eritrea have deteriorated over Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Asmara views Addis Ababa’s ambitions as a threat to its sovereignty.
The African Union has urged restraint, while UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for dialogue to resolve the disputes between the Horn of Africa states and prevent further escalation.

items.summary: On the fourth day of the Amoris laetitia meeting in the Vatican, Cardinal José Cobo Cano calls for ongoing pastoral accompaniment, while theologian María Marcela Mazzini emphasizes that the Sacrament of Marriage must be lived as well as celebrated. Read all
items.body_text:
Amoris laetitia: Marriage is a shared commitment to nurture each day
By Francesco Ricupero
âThe Churchâs pastoral conversion therefore calls us to listen closely to the experience of young married couples: to how they speak about what they are learning together, or about what prevents them from learning and growing; the resources they discover in the sacrament of marriage; what they expect from Christian communities; and how they understand their own missionary responsibility.â
Cardinal Kevin Farrell, Prefect of the Dicastery for the Laity, Family, and Life, offered this reflection on Saturday morning, October 10, as he introduced the fourth day of the meeting, âTen Years after Amoris laetitia: Proclaiming the Gospel with Families Today,â in the Paul VI Hall.
The gathering, which runs through October 14, brings together Pope Leo XIV, the heads of the Eastern Churches, presidents of Bishopsâ Conferences, married couples, and experts.
A decisive time
Introducing the dayâs theme, âMarried life. The first years of marriage: a decisive time,â Cardinal Farrell highlighted the considerable pastoral efforts made since the Second Vatican Council to enrich marriage preparation.
These efforts, he said, have drawn on the experience of married couples and offered engaged couples the opportunity to experience fellowship and prayer within the Christian community.
âYet we see that this is not always enough to help newly married couples understand and deepen the conjugal love that is taking shape within them during the first years of marriage, or to face the difficulties that may arise with the birth of children or as they come to know one another more deeply.â
The need for ongoing accompaniment
Cardinal José Cobo Cano, Metropolitan Archbishop of Madrid, reflected on how to listen to and accompany couples at the beginning of married life.
He emphasized that Amoris laetitia has âhelped us to view the reality of marriage in a different light and has opened up new pastoral horizons. However, the first challenge is not to design new programmes. The question comes before and is more decisive: do we truly understand, right from the start, the reality of the couples we wish to accompany?â
According to the Cardinal, the post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation invites the Church to rediscover marriage as both a sacrament to celebrate and a vocation to live and nurture throughout life.
Getting married means choosing to give oneself to another, building a shared future, and learning to love amid the joys and difficulties of everyday life. Marriage ministry therefore needs to make a fundamental shift: from preparation focused primarily on the wedding to accompaniment that supports couples before, during, and after their wedding.
Dialogue, patience, and forgiveness
âAmoris laetitia highlighted two focus points from the moment a couple approaches the Church: accompaniment and discernment,â Cardinal Cobo Cano said.
âThe question: âWhat do they need to know in order to get married?â is different from the deeper question: âWhat do they need to discover in order to know whether they are called to commit themselves definitively to one another?ââ
Providing engaged couples with the knowledge needed to celebrate the sacrament is not enough. They also need help understanding the choice they are making, discerning their vocation, and getting to know one another.
Marriage is a journey that continually develops. The early years, the birth of children, work responsibilities, financial difficulties, illness, and personal changes all call for dialogue, patience, forgiveness, and a renewed commitment to remain united.
The âengaged couplesâ clockâ
âAs in many dioceses, here in Madrid we are trialing, alongside pre-marriage courses, initiatives such as El reloj de los novios (The engaged couplesâ clock),â Cardinal Cobo Cano explained.
These are âbased on a simple insight: a couple needs to set aside quality time for each other to talk, reflect on their story, recognize their stre

items.summary: Pope Leo XIV reaffirms the Catholic Church’s rejection of the death penalty, recalling that the common good can be “safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment.” Read all
items.body_text:
Pope Leo XIV rejects death penalty as attack on dignity of human person
Vatican News
Pope Leo XIV has posted on his official X account that the Catholic Church holds the death penalty to be âinadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person.â
In a post published on Saturday, on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, the Pope noted that justice can be upheld and the common good of humanity can be safeguarded without relying on capital punishment.
He said criminals can be effectively detained in order to protect citizens, while still allowing those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.
âThe death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption. #NoDeathPenalty,â wrote Pope Leo.
The Popeâs post came a day after Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin and the President of the US Bishopsâ Conference made statements against the planned public execution of Nidal Hassan.
Mr. Hassan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others at Fort Hood in November 2009. A military court sentenced him to death in 2013.
On Thursday, the Pentagon announced his execution by firing squad scheduled for December 3, 2026, although further legal proceedings could delay it.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Cardinal Parolin said plans for a livestreamed execution were unacceptable.
âIt is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this method in this day and age,â he said. âI do not know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle. However guilty the person may be, there are other ways.â
He reiterated that the death penalty âis incompatible with human dignity and does not serve as a deterrent.â
Earlier on Friday, Archbishop Paul Coakley, President of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, expressed âshock and great sorrowâ and urged reconsideration.
âIn no way can Hassanâs actions be condoned, but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,â he told Vatican News.
He warned that a public execution would undermine the nationâs moral fabric and prayed that Americans would always choose life.

items.title: Pope appoints Archbishop Viola as Archpriest of St. Peter’s Basilica
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV appoints Archbishop Vittorio Francesco Viola as Archpriest of St. Peter’s Basilica and Bishop Aurelio García Macías as Secretary of the Dicastery for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope appoints Archbishop Viola as Archpriest of St. Peterâs Basilica
Vatican News
Pope Leo XIV has appointed Archbishop Vittorio Francesco Viola, O.F.M., as Archpriest of the Papal Basilica of St. Peter in the Vatican, Vicar General of His Holiness for Vatican City, and President of the Fabric of St. Peter.
The Holy See announced the appointment in a press release on Saturday.
Archbishop Viola previously served as Secretary of the Dicastery for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments.
Born in Biella, Italy, on October 4, 1965, he made his solemn profession in the Order of Friars Minor in 1991 and was ordained a priest in 1993.
He holds a doctorate in sacred liturgy from Romeâs Pontifical Liturgical Institute of SantâAnselmo and was appointed Bishop of Tortona in 2014, before becoming Secretary of the Dicastery in 2021.
New Secretary for Divine Worship
Pope Leo also appointed Bishop Aurelio García Macías as Secretary of the Dicastery for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments.
He has served as the Dicasteryâs Undersecretary since May 27, 2021, when Pope Francis also named him a bishop.
Born in Pollos, Spain, on March 28, 1965, Bishop García Macías was ordained a priest for the Archdiocese of Valladolid in 1992 and holds a doctorate in liturgy from the Pontifical Athenaeum of Saint Anselm.
A former rector of Valladolidâs diocesan seminary, Bishop García Macías began working at the Dicastery in 2015.
